extraction.body: Only tech companies are seeing growth from the AI boom, Apollo Global Management says. Apollo says that though some big companies are spending big on AI, they may soon pull back. Corporate America is starting to see AI spending not as a source of growth, but as a cost center. One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie . In an economic analysis published on Saturday, Apollo Global Management said that while the Magnificent Seven — a group of established tech companies that includes Nvidia and Meta — are seeing revenue growth during the AI boom, this growth isn't being shared by other industries. "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report. "The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech." In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth. Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today. Meanwhile, that figure hasn't changed much for everyone else in the S&P 500, lingering around $550,000 for the last seven years. Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else. And across the economy, AI hasn't yet dramatically increased productivity growth as some AI optimists have predicted. Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," Slok said. "That may be harder than it sounds," he added. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

passages: “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.

Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.

AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).

extraction.body: AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch). Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said. Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.” “AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.” Recent studies have also found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains .

Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered “zero financial payoff” to most large U.S. companies outside the tech industry, according to Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management. In a recent note , Slok wrote that AI’s financial benefits remain concentrated in the Magnificent 7 mega-cap tech companies, while the broader S&P 493 is seeing little to no improvement in key metrics. “Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493,” Slok wrote. “Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493.” He added: “And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth.” The findings challenge the growing narrative that AI is already transforming corporate America. According to Slok, mainstream companies are increasingly viewing token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins. With no clear impact on the bottom line, many are pulling back. Venture capital-backed companies continue to spend more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America “does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it,” Slok wrote. As long as agentic AI and token spending remain confined to a small part of the economy, he argues, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be “very limited.” Looking ahead, the key question is whether mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins, even as AI models become commoditized. Slok suggests that may be harder than it sounds. “AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote. Judgment depends on context, he added, and the answer varies depending on which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, Slok says AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness—all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins. “The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector,” Slok wrote. Slok’s charts split the S&P 500 into the seven-company "Mag 7" group and the remaining 493 constituents called the "S&P 493," and he said "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493." Slok also said "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493," and he framed the lack of broad gains as a problem for the economics of AI spending. Apollo’s note added that "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," while its productivity chart tracked output per hour and total factor productivity from January 1985. Reviewed by Codex validator (AI) · 26 Oct 2026

Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, argued in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026 that artificial intelligence has delivered "zero financial payoff" to corporate America outside of tech. Slok’s charts split the S&P 500 into the seven-company "Mag 7" group and the remaining 493 constituents called the "S&P 493," and he said "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493." Slok also said "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493," and he framed the lack of broad gains as a problem for the economics of AI spending.

Apollo’s note added that "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," while its productivity chart tracked output per hour and total factor productivity from January 1985. The Daily Spark note concluded that the AI story would be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and that there was "no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector."

TechCrunch said Slok focused on the S&P 493, finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat and that there was no evidence that AI was improving productivity. Slok argued that it would be tough for corporate America to "turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," and he wrote that "AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness." Startup Fortune reported that Slok’s note landed as a separate AI-financing scare unfolded, after Chamath Palihapitiya flagged that the yield on $1.25 billion of CoreWeave bonds due in 2032 briefly touched 15%.

Startup Fortune said CoreWeave shares fell more than 15% on October 14, and it said yields on its unsecured bonds subsequently remained near 15% as Oracle and other AI infrastructure stocks sold off. Apollo’s Daily Spark note said mainstream corporate America was pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.

TECHi said Apollo’s chief economist argued in an October 24 research note that broad US companies still show little measurable financial payoff from artificial intelligence, and it framed the warning as about the economics of AI buyers. TECHi reported that from September 24 to the October 23 close, its NVDA forecast data showed the same-period FY2027 EPS estimate edging from $9.3071 to $9.3124 while the share price fell from $224.58 to $210.96. TECHi calculated that the implied price-to-estimated-earnings ratio slipped from about 24.13 to 22.65, and it said the compression, rather than a documented collapse in Nvidia profit expectations, was the starting point for its forecast.

Nvidia’s August 26 results provided a counterweight, because Nvidia reported revenue for the quarter ended July 26 of $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, with Data Center revenue at $89.0 billion, up 117%. Nvidia guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, and a 74.0% gross margin, plus or minus 0.5 percentage point, while TECHi noted that Apollo’s S&P 493 comparison did not establish that enterprises buying AI services are themselves earning attractive returns.

extraction.body: Only tech companies are seeing growth from the AI boom, Apollo Global Management says. Apollo says that though some big companies are spending big on AI, they may soon pull back. Corporate America is starting to see AI spending not as a source of growth, but as a cost center. One of the world's largest investment firms says that only tech companies are getting a share of the AI pie . In an economic analysis published on Saturday, Apollo Global Management said that while the Magnificent Seven — a group of established tech companies that includes Nvidia and Meta — are seeing revenue growth during the AI boom, this growth isn't being shared by other industries. "Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Torsten Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, said in the report. "The technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech." In a series of graphs, Slok measured three main metrics that have boomed for tech companies but not for regular companies: revenue per worker, profit margins, and productivity growth. Since 2022, revenue per employee figures have skyrocketed for tech companies — rising from $550,000 to nearly $800,000 today. Meanwhile, that figure hasn't changed much for everyone else in the S&P 500, lingering around $550,000 for the last seven years. Similarly, while profit margins soared among tech companies since 2022, they've stagnated at about 10% for everyone else. And across the economy, AI hasn't yet dramatically increased productivity growth as some AI optimists have predicted. Apollo's research portends a dark shadow over a US economy throwing massive amounts of dough toward AI tools and companies, whose leaders have promised that an " age of abundance ," where people won't have to work as much, will soon be upon us. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," Slok said. "That may be harder than it sounds," he added. If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered “zero financial payoff” to most large U.S. companies outside the tech industry, according to Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management. In a recent note , Slok wrote that AI’s financial benefits remain concentrated in the Magnificent 7 mega-cap tech companies, while the broader S&P 493 is seeing little to no improvement in key metrics. “Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493,” Slok wrote. “Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493.” He added: “And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth.” The findings challenge the growing narrative that AI is already transforming corporate America. According to Slok, mainstream companies are increasingly viewing token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins. With no clear impact on the bottom line, many are pulling back. Venture capital-backed companies continue to spend more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America “does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it,” Slok wrote. As long as agentic AI and token spending remain confined to a small part of the economy, he argues, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be “very limited.” Looking ahead, the key question is whether mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins, even as AI models become commoditized. Slok suggests that may be harder than it sounds. “AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote. Judgment depends on context, he added, and the answer varies depending on which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, Slok says AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness—all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins. “The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector,” Slok wrote. extraction.body: Oct 26 — Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley will provide $63 billion ​in financing to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic, in one of the largest debt deals tied ‌to the AI buildout. Rising AI demand is driving massive investment in computing infrastructure as ⁠technology companies race to secure ​capacity for increasingly complex workloads. The ⁠transaction will be carried out through a newly formed special ‌purpose vehicle that will ‌purchase Broadcom's AI accelerators and networking equipment and lease ⁠them to the Claude maker, the ⁠companies said on Monday. Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley are arranging the first-lien financing, while Blackstone will provide the committed portion of the second-lien financing. Broadcom is providing "residual value support" to senior debt lenders, effectively providing a guarantee to them in ‌the financing structure, agreeing to absorb potential ​declines in the value of the assets up to an amount equal to the first-lien debt, although the release did not disclose the size of this debt. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027 as part of a previously announced strategic compute capacity agreement involving Broadcom, the companies said. Apollo and Blackstone had agreed ​to finance a $35 billion expansion of Anthropic's AI computing capacity under ‌a prior agreement ‌with Broadcom. The ⁠latest deal highlights the growing role of banks and alternative asset managers in financing the infrastructure needed to support rising demand for AI computing capacity. Anthropic filed for a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, ‌even as disclosures of ​steep losses and security concerns threatened ‌to test investor appetite ⁠for the ​AI heavyweight. (Reporting by Aditya Soni and Prakhar Srivastava in Bengaluru; Editing by ​Pooja Desai)

passages: Broadcom is working to arrange more than $50 billion in financing for an AI chip it is developing with OpenAI .
The talks are early, and no deal is expected before the end of the year.
The financing sits on top of a partnership that OpenAI and Broadcom announced in October 2025.
The two companies agreed to collaborate on custom AI accelerators, the specialized chips that train and run large AI models.
The Journal reported the discussions on October 7, 2026.
The terms of the financing are still being negotiated.
That matters, because “over $50 billion” is a target, not a signed check.
Broadcom and OpenAI have already done business at significant scale.

Custom chips promise better performance and more control over costs, but they require enormous upfront commitments that a financing package helps spread out.
The chips come out of OpenAI’s internal program called Nexus .
The first generations are named Jalapeño and Serrano.

The ⁠transaction will be carried out through a newly formed special ‌purpose vehicle that will ‌purchase Broadcom's AI accelerators and networking equipment and lease ⁠them to the Claude maker, the ⁠companies said on Monday. relevantPassages.text: Oct 26 — Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley will provide $63 billion ​in financing to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic, in one of the largest debt deals tied ‌to the AI buildout.
Apollo and Blackstone had agreed ​to finance a $35 billion expansion of Anthropic's AI computing capacity under ‌a prior agreement ‌with Broadcom.
Anthropic filed for a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, ‌even as disclosures of ​steep losses and security concerns threatened ‌to test investor appetite ⁠for the ​AI heavyweight.

sources.title: Broadcom is lining up over $50 billion in financing for OpenAI’s custom AI chips - Crypto Briefing
passages: Broadcom is working to arrange more than $50 billion in financing for an AI chip it is developing with OpenAI .
The talks are early, and no deal is expected before the end of the year.
The financing sits on top of a partnership that OpenAI and Broadcom announced in October 2025.
The two companies agreed to collaborate on custom AI accelerators, the specialized chips that train and run large AI models.
The Journal reported the discussions on October 7, 2026.
The terms of the financing are still being negotiated.
That matters, because “over $50 billion” is a target, not a signed check.
Broadcom and OpenAI have already done business at significant scale.
There have been multiple past orders between the companies worth billions of dollars, though the financial terms have not been disclosed.
This is also not Broadcom’s first lap around this track.
The company previously put together a debt financing package of roughly $60 billion to support Anthropic ’s AI chip needs.
Custom chips promise better performance and more control over costs, but they require enormous upfront commitments that a financing package helps spread out.
The chips come out of OpenAI’s internal program called Nexus .
The first generations are named Jalapeño and Serrano.

The Anthropic package and the OpenAI talks together point to a growing pattern of private lenders funding large-scale AI infrastructure.

sources.title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips, Elon Musk says - CNBC
passages: SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems.

In a post on X on Sunday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said it had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses.

The financing underscores the AI boom's enormous capital requirements, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models.
Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers.

extraction.body: SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems. In a post on X on Sunday, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said it had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses. In a follow-up post , he added that the financing primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, which are expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027. In a regulatory filing Monday, SpaceX said it signed a binding commitment with an Apollo-managed entity for roughly $40 billion in GPU financing. The financing underscores the AI boom's enormous capital requirements, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models. SpaceX has expanded aggressively into artificial intelligence this year, referring to the business as "Super Intelligence," or SI. The segment has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its latest earnings release. Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers. He predicted that more than 200 so-called neocloud companies, which provide cloud computing infrastructure designed for AI and machine-learning workloads, would face widespread failures and consolidation, with only a small number surviving. sources.title: Elon Musk's SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal to buy AI chips, warns of neocloud failures - Moneycontrol.com
passages: Elon Musk announced on Sunday that SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase graphics processing units (GPUs), marking another major investment in artificial intelligence as technology companies race to expand their computing infrastructure.
The expansion also comes with substantial spending commitments.
Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen expects fourth-quarter capital expenditure to reach between $35 billion and $40 billion.
Musk also recently told investors that merging SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea”, citing increasing technological overlap between the two companies.

The developments highlight Musk's broader push into AI computing and semiconductor manufacturing, even as rising infrastructure costs and tightening financing conditions raise questions about the sustainability of the industry's rapid expansion.
Moneycontrol World Desk first published: Oct 26, 2026 06:46 am Discover the latest Business News , Sensex , and Nifty updates.
Obtain Personal Finance insights, tax queries, and expert opinions on Moneycontrol or download the Moneycontrol App to stay updated!
While outlining SpaceX's financing plans, Musk warned that companies relying heavily on AI infrastructure revenue could face mounting financial pressure.
He said debt markets "have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers."
The financing comes as artificial intelligence takes on a larger role in SpaceX's business.
The company's revenue surged 161% year-on-year to $14.58 billion in the quarter ended September 30, while AI revenue jumped nearly tenfold to $7.56 billion.
Musk predicted consolidation and potential failures among neocloud operators, which provide specialised computing infrastructure for AI workloads.
Musk also ruled out SpaceX acquiring neocloud businesses, describing such a move as “pointless.”

extraction.body: A handful of first-hand reports show similar damage, suggesting a bad batch of hinges. Here's what to do if your Duo screen fails. The iPhone Duo started landing in customers’ hands last Friday, and it didn’t take long for the problems to start rolling in. And the most obvious — and urgent — of these teething troubles is a screen damage issue that leaves a block or line of bright pixels on the display. Owners are seeing bright white lines appear on the display, sometimes within a few hours of ownership. And all the damage being reported seems to be the same — one or more bright lines running across the right-hand side of the display about a third of the way up, with a secondary line along the middle. Bottom line: We don’t know, but there are some well-informed guesses out there. There’s been a flurry of activity over the weekend related to what is, rather predictably, being called “Crackgate.” The teardown experts at iFixit have been busy — they completely disassembled a Duo, built a 3D model of the hinge, and identified several ways the hinge mechanism could be damaging the inner display. It could be that the flexible display is coming into contact with a support bar that doesn’t retract properly, or that a rail that moves during folding is brushing against the screen, causing a pressure hotspot. Finally, the damage appears to start where a lot of edges, components, and moving parts converge, and that convergence could be stressing the display more than expected. South Korean YouTuber CuriousHagi 궁금하기 also took apart an iPhone Duo to examine the hinge and posted a very informative video. Another pattern I’ve noticed in reports from affected users is that their Duos initially opened and closed smoothly, but then they began to encounter resistance when opening and closing the handset, and after this, the display would break within a few open/close cycles. The speed with which these damage reports began to appear — some within a few hours — suggests this is a manufacturing or assembly issue, not wear. It’s a complicated hinge made up of more than a hundred components, so there’s a lot of scope for things to go wrong. Because this is a manufacturing or assembly issue, it’s ultimately not down to you. If you can wait, then my advice is to wait. But if you were planning to sell or trade in your existing handset, that would leave you in a bit of a bind. Grabbing a refund and waiting for all this to blow over before buying another one will be the best option for you. Tricky question. What if your Duo is fine right now, but falls victim to “Crackgate” down the line? I’m assuming that most people dropping $1,999 to $3,199 on a handset will have AppleCare or some third-party insurance to fall back on. That’ll give you peace of mind moving forward no matter what Apple’s policy on this ends up being in the long term. Also, if you bought the handset directly from Apple, you have 14 days to return it if this issue has made you lose confidence in the robustness of a folding iPhone. If you bought it from a carrier or third party, you’ll have to check their returns policy (and be aware of any fees). It’s safe to say that any new iPhone launch will see hundreds of thousands, maybe millions, of devices land in the hands of new owners on day one. Despite the hype around “Crackgate,” I’ve read fewer than a dozen firsthand reports of the issue. This, combined with the fact that the damage all seems to be exactly the same, suggests it’s likely a batch of defective hinges that made it into the wild, and it’s an issue that’ll be sorted out going forward. But whether that causes more shortages in the short term remains to be seen. Please accept cookies to view the comments powered by Disqus. © 2026 ZDNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

extraction.body: Apple’s “precision-engineered” hinge is apparently damaging some iPhone Duo screens. The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple’s first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn’t going great. Despite the company’s big talk about its “precision-engineered” hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device’s impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use. The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin. Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo’s screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself. It sounds like most affected devices are failing within about a day of use. But a few unlucky buyers note they only opened and closed the phone a few times , and in some cases, they hadn’t even finished the initial setup process. Some customers have reported success taking their defective phones to Apple stores for replacement, but spares may be in short supply right now. Early iPhone Duo adopters from the U.S. to China and Australia are seeing the same issue crop up, so it doesn't appear limited to any specific market.

They estimated they'd probably opened it less than 20 times so far. YouTuber JerryRigEverything put Apple's foldable phone through its paces in his latest durability test video, and the iPhone Duo failed miserably.

Despite its IP68 rating for dust resistance, dust made its way into the hinge through multiple entry points, overpowering the magnets designed to keep the phone closed. A subsequent bend test resulted in a permanent green line across the inner display, which eventually stopped responding altogether.

The outer display, protected by Ceramic Shield 2, resisted scratches until level 7 on the Mohs hardness scale. The inner screen, however, showed scratches at level 2 with deeper grooves at a level fingernail. "I've been testing these folding phones since the first generation seven years ago – most do survive," said Zack Nelson. "The iPhone Duo did not."

With so many people getting their hands on the iPhone Duo this week, some defective units are to be expected. However, it's unclear how widespread the issue is or whether we'll see more reports of hinge failures trickle in over time. coreStoryFacts.text: The iPhone Duo started landing in customers’ hands last Friday, and it didn’t take long for the problems to start rolling in.
And the most obvious — and urgent — of these teething troubles is a screen damage issue that leaves a block or line of bright pixels on the display.
South Korean YouTuber CuriousHagi 궁금하기 also took apart an iPhone Duo to examine the hinge and posted a very informative video.
© 2026 ZDNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.
A handful of first-hand reports show similar damage, suggesting a bad batch of hinges.
Here's what to do if your Duo screen fails.
Apple’s “precision-engineered” hinge is apparently damaging some iPhone Duo screens.
In the absence of any official explanation, iFixit may be the next best thing.
The site has already torn an iPhone Duo apart and taken a close look at the affected area.
After years of seeing other foldables fail, there are a few suspects to check.
Since foldables need to pass data and power across the hinge, there’s always a cable tucked in there that could press on the screen.
The iPhone Duo has a wide cable with “accordion-like pleats,” according to iFixit, but this doesn’t quite match the accounts of the damage.
For some early buyers, the morning after isn’t going great.

Despite the company’s big talk about its “precision-engineered” hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device’s impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use.
Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect.
When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them.
Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness.
Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black.

After about six hours of use, one Reddit user in Australia said they "heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge." They estimated they'd probably opened it less than 20 times so far.
At first, Apple offered an express replacement over the phone, with the stipulation that the customer would have to place a hold for the full cost of the handset.
Apple also couldn't provide an estimated arrival date for the replacement.

Rather than wait, they went to an Apple Store in person, where staff "apologized and replaced it with a brand-new one on the spot," suggesting Apple may have replacement iPhone Duo units available in-store to handle early hardware failures.
Apple's long-awaited foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, came out this week, and already the cracks are starting to show.
And I mean that literally: Some iPhone Duo early adopters are already running into issues that cause the display to crack along the entire hinge.

Hinge failures from normal use should be covered under the one-year warranty, and customers receiving an ‌iPhone Duo‌ today will also have two weeks to make a return.

extraction.body: A handful of first-hand reports show similar damage, suggesting a bad batch of hinges. Here's what to do if your Duo screen fails. The iPhone Duo started landing in customers’ hands last Friday, and it didn’t take long for the problems to start rolling in. And the most obvious — and urgent — of these teething troubles is a screen damage issue that leaves a block or line of bright pixels on the display. Owners are seeing bright white lines appear on the display, sometimes within a few hours of ownership. And all the damage being reported seems to be the same — one or more bright lines running across the right-hand side of the display about a third of the way up, with a secondary line along the middle. Bottom line: We don’t know, but there are some well-informed guesses out there. There’s been a flurry of activity over the weekend related to what is, rather predictably, being called “Crackgate.” The teardown experts at iFixit have been busy — they completely disassembled a Duo, built a 3D model of the hinge, and identified several ways the hinge mechanism could be damaging the inner display. It could be that the flexible display is coming into contact with a support bar that doesn’t retract properly, or that a rail that moves during folding is brushing against the screen, causing a pressure hotspot. Finally, the damage appears to start where a lot of edges, components, and moving parts converge, and that convergence could be stressing the display more than expected. South Korean YouTuber CuriousHagi 궁금하기 also took apart an iPhone Duo to examine the hinge and posted a very informative video. Another pattern I’ve noticed in reports from affected users is that their Duos initially opened and closed smoothly, but then they began to encounter resistance when opening and closing the handset, and after this, the display would break within a few open/close cycles. The speed with which these damage reports began to appear — some within a few hours — suggests this is a manufacturing or assembly issue, not wear. It’s a complicated hinge made up of more than a hundred components, so there’s a lot of scope for things to go wrong. Because this is a manufacturing or assembly issue, it’s ultimately not down to you. If you can wait, then my advice is to wait. But if you were planning to sell or trade in your existing handset, that would leave you in a bit of a bind. Grabbing a refund and waiting for all this to blow over before buying another one will be the best option for you. Tricky question. What if your Duo is fine right now, but falls victim to “Crackgate” down the line? I’m assuming that most people dropping $1,999 to $3,199 on a handset will have AppleCare or some third-party insurance to fall back on. That’ll give you peace of mind moving forward no matter what Apple’s policy on this ends up being in the long term. Also, if you bought the handset directly from Apple, you have 14 days to return it if this issue has made you lose confidence in the robustness of a folding iPhone. If you bought it from a carrier or third party, you’ll have to check their returns policy (and be aware of any fees). It’s safe to say that any new iPhone launch will see hundreds of thousands, maybe millions, of devices land in the hands of new owners on day one. Despite the hype around “Crackgate,” I’ve read fewer than a dozen firsthand reports of the issue. This, combined with the fact that the damage all seems to be exactly the same, suggests it’s likely a batch of defective hinges that made it into the wild, and it’s an issue that’ll be sorted out going forward. But whether that causes more shortages in the short term remains to be seen. Please accept cookies to view the comments powered by Disqus. © 2026 ZDNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

The iPhone Duo started landing in customers’ hands last Friday, and it didn’t take long for the problems to start rolling in. And the most obvious — and urgent — of these teething troubles is a screen damage issue that leaves a block or line of bright pixels on the display.

Owners are seeing bright white lines appear on the display, sometimes within a few hours of ownership. And all the damage being reported seems to be the same — one or more bright lines running across the right-hand side of the display about a third of the way up, with a secondary line along the middle.
Bottom line: We don’t know, but there are some well-informed guesses out there.

There’s been a flurry of activity over the weekend related to what is, rather predictably, being called “Crackgate.” The teardown experts at iFixit have been busy — they completely disassembled a Duo, built a 3D model of the hinge, and identified several ways the hinge mechanism could be damaging the inner display.

It could be that the flexible display is coming into contact with a support bar that doesn’t retract properly, or that a rail that moves during folding is brushing against the screen, causing a pressure hotspot. Finally, the damage appears to start where a lot of edges, components, and moving parts converge, and that convergence could be stressing the display more than expected.
South Korean YouTuber CuriousHagi 궁금하기 also took apart an iPhone Duo to examine the hinge and posted a very informative video.

Another pattern I’ve noticed in reports from affected users is that their Duos initially opened and closed smoothly, but then they began to encounter resistance when opening and closing the handset, and after this, the display would break within a few open/close cycles.

The speed with which these damage reports began to appear — some within a few hours — suggests this is a manufacturing or assembly issue, not wear. It’s a complicated hinge made up of more than a hundred components, so there’s a lot of scope for things to go wrong.
Because this is a manufacturing or assembly issue, it’s ultimately not down to you.

If you can wait, then my advice is to wait. But if you were planning to sell or trade in your existing handset, that would leave you in a bit of a bind. Grabbing a refund and waiting for all this to blow over before buying another one will be the best option for you.
Tricky question. What if your Duo is fine right now, but falls victim to “Crackgate” down the line?

I’m assuming that most people dropping $1,999 to $3,199 on a handset will have AppleCare or some third-party insurance to fall back on. That’ll give you peace of mind moving forward no matter what Apple’s policy on this ends up being in the long term.

Also, if you bought the handset directly from Apple, you have 14 days to return it if this issue has made you lose confidence in the robustness of a folding iPhone. If you bought it from a carrier or third party, you’ll have to check their returns policy (and be aware of any fees).

It’s safe to say that any new iPhone launch will see hundreds of thousands, maybe millions, of devices land in the hands of new owners on day one. Despite the hype around “Crackgate,” I’ve read fewer than a dozen firsthand reports of the issue.

This, combined with the fact that the damage all seems to be exactly the same, suggests it’s likely a batch of defective hinges that made it into the wild, and it’s an issue that’ll be sorted out going forward. But whether that causes more shortages in the short term remains to be seen.

extraction.body: Apple’s “precision-engineered” hinge is apparently damaging some iPhone Duo screens. The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple’s first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn’t going great. Despite the company’s big talk about its “precision-engineered” hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device’s impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use. The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin. Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo’s screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself. It sounds like most affected devices are failing within about a day of use. But a few unlucky buyers note they only opened and closed the phone a few times , and in some cases, they hadn’t even finished the initial setup process. Some customers have reported success taking their defective phones to Apple stores for replacement, but spares may be in short supply right now. In the absence of any official explanation, iFixit may be the next best thing. The site has already torn an iPhone Duo apart and taken a close look at the affected area. After years of seeing other foldables fail, there are a few suspects to check. Since foldables need to pass data and power across the hinge, there’s always a cable tucked in there that could press on the screen. The iPhone Duo has a wide cable with “accordion-like pleats,” according to iFixit, but this doesn’t quite match the accounts of the damage. People with broken $2,000 iPhones say there’s unusual physical resistance and sometimes even a clicking sound as the device closes. After that, the lines appear. Using CT scans of the phone, iFixit has shown that the point of failure starts below where the ribbon cable passes through the hinge. The width of the supporting hinge mechanism changes in that spot, suggesting a mechanical misalignment. The animation above shows iFixit’s best guess at what’s happening. The support bar in that narrowed section of the hinge may be getting stuck, preventing it from dropping far enough to accommodate the waterdrop bend in the OLED panel when the device closes. This creates stress on the display that ultimately damages the matrix. YouTuber CuriousHagi also zeroed in on that region, identifying a place where the thinner link may be snapping during operation. He speculates the component is physically sticking to the support plate. If this fiddly little hinge piece is the culprit, there’s no way to prevent the OLED on an affected device from failing. It could happen after five minutes or five days, but continuous pressure on an OLED panel will eventually lead to permanent damage. Apple has yet to acknowledge the issue, and it probably won’t have anything to say until the problem is fully investigated. The scale is impossible to know—Apple sells a lot of devices, so even a low failure rate could see a flood of reports on social media. Adding moving parts to a phone will lead to at least some increase in hardware issues. Apple certainly wouldn’t be the first device maker to have problems with its first foldable launch. In 2019, Samsung released the original Galaxy Fold with a much more primitive hinge design. Even before launch, reviewers began seeing OLED damage after a few days of use. The issue in that case was a design with openings that allowed particulates to infiltrate the hinge , where they damaged the screen from underneath. Samsung delayed the release while it re-engineered the hinge. Samsung’s foldables have not been bulletproof by any means, but there have not been widespread reports of defects immediately after unboxing. Other makers of foldable phones move so few units that occasional defects may not make waves online. Apple is just lucky that way.

Apple's long-awaited foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, came out this week, and already the cracks are starting to show. And I mean that literally: Some iPhone Duo early adopters are already running into issues that cause the display to crack along the entire hinge. Photos shared on Reddit show the iPhone Duo's inner display cracking from top to bottom alongside the hinge — exactly where the device folds — less than 24 hours after launch.

It’s still not entirely clear what’s causing the issue, but photos of cracked iPhone Duo displays circulating on social media show a consistent pattern. A large crack appears on the inner display along the hinge, causing a pixel issue that produces a bright white line down the right-hand side of the screen. Early iPhone Duo adopters from the U.S. to China and Australia are seeing the same issue crop up, so it doesn't appear limited to any specific market.

After about six hours of use, one Reddit user in Australia said they "heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge." They estimated they'd probably opened it less than 20 times so far. At first, Apple offered an express replacement over the phone, with the stipulation that the customer would have to place a hold for the full cost of the handset. Apple also couldn't provide an estimated arrival date for the replacement. Rather than wait, they went to an Apple Store in person, where staff "apologized and replaced it with a brand-new one on the spot," suggesting Apple may have replacement iPhone Duo units available in-store to handle early hardware failures.

Early durability tests show the inner display's crease at the hinge becomes more visible the more users fold and unfold the device, something they are want to do considering that's kinda the biggest selling point for Apple's $2,000 handset. YouTuber JerryRigEverything put Apple's foldable phone through its paces in his latest durability test video, and the iPhone Duo failed miserably.

Despite its IP68 rating for dust resistance, dust made its way into the hinge through multiple entry points, overpowering the magnets designed to keep the phone closed. A subsequent bend test resulted in a permanent green line across the inner display, which eventually stopped responding altogether.

The outer display, protected by Ceramic Shield 2, resisted scratches until level 7 on the Mohs hardness scale. The inner screen, however, showed scratches at level 2 with deeper grooves at a level fingernail. Its matte nano-texture coating did offer one clever trick, making marks seemingly "magically disappear," but that wasn't enough to save the phone from failing the durability test.
"I've been testing these folding phones since the first generation seven years ago – most do survive," said Zack Nelson. "The iPhone Duo did not."

With so many people getting their hands on the iPhone Duo this week, some defective units are to be expected. However, it's unclear how widespread the issue is or whether we'll see more reports of hinge failures trickle in over time. Any problems resulting from normal use should be covered by Apple's one-year warranty, and there's also a 14-day window to return your iPhone Duo if need be.

passages: The macOS Golden Gate 27.2 offers some of the same things: contextual memory for Siri, the same additional Siri AI languages, and miscellaneous unspecified bug fixes.
It adds a memory feature to Siri, so it can “recall your past conversations” and reference them when chatting with you.
It also expands what data sources Siri can access when giving responses to include voicemails, Messages attachments, and more.
Today, Apple rolled out the 27.2 updates for its operating systems, including iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and so on.
Apple’s own iOS and macOS update notes are below.
This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context.
It also introduces Suggestions in Messages that help you take quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders based on context from your conversation.
This release includes additional features, bug fixes, and security updates for your Mac.

Also, as previously discovered in the beta releases of macOS 27.2, there are some references to new gesture recognition capabilities in applications like Photos, Notes, and Safari—which may be related to unconfirmed reports of touch support on the next MacBook Pro refresh, which may be revealed at a scheduled public briefing this Wednesday.
Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

On the flip side, there is now an “Excluded Apps” option that allows you to “choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access.” Further, Siri AI is now available in five more languages beyond English, as previously announced: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish—though Siri AI remains unavailable in Europe (and mainland China).

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max) - Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week - Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List - Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting - Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need - Siri AI is available in more languages, with support tor French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. This update also introduces Suggestions in Messages that help you take quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders based on context from your conversation. coreStoryFacts.text: iOS 27.2 beta 2 arrived today , and so far seems to have minimal user-facing changes.
Describe a Shortcut could soon support actions from third-party developers.
Currently, the feature only supports Apple-developed actions.
To enable: sudo mkdir -p… pic.twitter.com/sR6OJMwADy
Today’s beta 2 has more descriptive language on this addition—now called “Extended Erase”—as discovered by Aaron Perris.
For example, X user pdfu discovered that Apple Music will soon add live countdowns for new album releases.
But perhaps the addition of new theming features means Apple is about to expand support to another automaker.

Whenever Apple releases new beta software, we tend to discover changes in two ways: through user-facing features active in the software, as well as underlying code changes that point to forthcoming changes.
Check out 9to5Mac on YouTube for more Apple news:
The macOS Golden Gate 27.2 offers some of the same things: contextual memory for Siri, the same additional Siri AI languages, and miscellaneous unspecified bug fixes.
It adds a memory feature to Siri, so it can “recall your past conversations” and reference them when chatting with you.
It also expands what data sources Siri can access when giving responses to include voicemails, Messages attachments, and more.
Today, Apple rolled out the 27.2 updates for its operating systems, including iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and so on.
Apple’s own iOS and macOS update notes are below.
This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context.
It also introduces Suggestions in Messages that help you take quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders based on context from your conversation.
This release includes additional features, bug fixes, and security updates for your Mac.

Also, as previously discovered in the beta releases of macOS 27.2, there are some references to new gesture recognition capabilities in applications like Photos, Notes, and Safari—which may be related to unconfirmed reports of touch support on the next MacBook Pro refresh, which may be revealed at a scheduled public briefing this Wednesday.
Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

On the flip side, there is now an “Excluded Apps” option that allows you to “choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access.” Further, Siri AI is now available in five more languages beyond English, as previously announced: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish—though Siri AI remains unavailable in Europe (and mainland China).
The iOS 27.2 update expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.
It also adds profiles for the Apple TV app, a new icon and branding for Apple Music , and support for AI suggestions in the Messages app for taking quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders.
In the European Union, it introduces an alternative expanded prompt for App Tracking Transparency.
Apple also released iOS 26.7.2 with security updates.

With iOS 27.2, there were a variety of new features available for testing from day one, like the all-new Health app , user profiles in Apple TV , Siri AI expansions , and more.
But users skilled at examining the underlying code found even more changes in the works.
For example, X user pdfu discovered that Apple Music will soon add live countdowns for new album releases.

Shortcuts’ new ‘Describe a Shortcut’ feature looks like it will soon gain support for including actions from third-party apps.

Today, Apple rolled out the 27.2 updates for its operating systems, including iOS, macOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, and so on.
Apple’s own iOS and macOS update notes are below.
This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context.

This release includes additional features, bug fixes, and security updates for your Mac.

Also, as previously discovered in the beta releases of macOS 27.2, there are some references to new gesture recognition capabilities in applications like Photos, Notes, and Safari—which may be related to unconfirmed reports of touch support on the next MacBook Pro refresh, which may be revealed at a scheduled public briefing this Wednesday.

extraction.body: Apple today released iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2, the first major updates to the iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 operating systems that came out in September. iOS 27.2 is available for all iPhones able to run ‌iOS 27‌, including the iPhone Duo , while iPadOS 27.2 is available for all iPads able to run ‌iPadOS 27‌, including the newly announced OLED iPad mini . The iOS 27.2 update expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. It also adds profiles for the Apple TV app, a new icon and branding for Apple Music , and support for AI suggestions in the Messages app for taking quick actions in apps like Calendar and Reminders. In the European Union, it introduces an alternative expanded prompt for App Tracking Transparency. Apple's release notes for iOS 27.2 are below. Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max) - Siri AI can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week - Siri AI can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List - Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting - Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need - Siri AI is available in more languages, with support tor French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Siri AI is not available in the EU or mainland China Other - Suggestions in Messages help you take action based on the context of your conversations, like adding a Calendar invite for a dinner - Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos - Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground - The Home tab in the Podcasts app offers two separate sections for New Episodes and Continue Playing, letting you find the latest updates from your shows and then pick up where you left off - Friends tab in the Games app provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends' player pages - Simple Profiles in the Apple TV app lets everyone in your household have their own profile, with recommendations that fit what they like to watch - FaceTime supports adding a third party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call Apple has separate release notes for the ‌iPhone Duo‌: This update provides enhancements to Siri AI with the ability to retain useful context from previous Siri interactions as well as draw from a wider range of personal context. iPhone Duo gets support for Apple Pencil, as well as Edge Light to illuminate your face during video calls. sources.title: Apple Debuts $699 Water-Resistant iPad Mini With OLED Screen - Bloomberg.com
passages: Apple Inc. on Monday unveiled a revamped iPad mini with an OLED display, water-resistant design and faster chip, kicking off a week of product launches.
The tablet, priced at $699, features an 8.5-inch OLED, or organic light-emitting diode, screen that delivers deeper blacks, brighter whites and improved contrast.
Apple has increased the display size from the previous 8.3 inches by slimming down the bezels around the panel.

The redesigned device also includes a new “Acoustic Display” audio system that places the speakers beneath the display, helping to make this the first iPad with an IP67 dust and water resistance rating.

extraction.body: Just as rumors last week suggested, the redesigned 8th-generation iPad Mini (2026) has arrived ahead of Apple's "Pro and Tell" event on Wednesday, October 28th. The refreshed pint-sized tablet features a larger 8.5-inch OLED display, the A20 Pro chip, an improved front-facing camera, and, for the first time on any iPad, IP67 water and dust resistance. The redesigned pint-sized tablet also features a less thick 5.4mm design and 24% thinner bezels. On the display front, the new 8.5-inch OLED screen offers 2x higher peak brightness at 1,200 nits (along with 1 nit minimum brightness), plus a nano-texture display option similar to recent iPad Pro releases. However, the new iPad Mini still doesn't feature a 120Hz ProMotion display and is locked to 60Hz. The 2024-released 7th-generation iPad Mini featured an 8.3-inch LCD screen with relatively thick bezels. The larger OLED panel should deliver deeper blacks, improved contrast, and more vibrant colors. At the same time, the tablet might also have worse battery life, since OLED panel technology consumes more power, though efficiency improvements in the A20 Pro could offset that. In the press release, Apple says that the new iPad Mini can hit 10 hours of battery life while watching videos or browsing the web on Wi-Fi. Regarding the A20 Pro specifically, the chip features a 5-core CPU with two super cores and three efficiency cores, making it compatible with Apple's new Siri AI features, including the assistant's more expressive voice. It also has a 7-core GPU that delivers up to 2.7x faster graphics performance. Lastly, the 512GB model features a 6-core CPU. The tablet's front-facing camera has been upgraded to a 12-megapixel Center Stage shooter that sits on its landscape bezel edge. Other upgrades include the Acoustic Display, which Apple says features "specially designed woofers" that are "paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume." Lastly, the tablet features Apple's C2 cellular modem (if you opt for the cellular version), alongside its N1 wireless chip. Apple says the new iPad Mini will be available to pre-order on Wednesday, October 28th, starting at $700, with availability launching on November 6th. While the 8th-gen iPad Mini seems like a solid all-around upgrade thanks to the A20 Pro chip and the new OLED panel, it's a bit crazy that it starts at $700, especially since the last refresh in 2024 launched at $500 (which already felt pretty expensive). Later this week, Apple is expected to reveal a touch-screen MacBook Pro and the M6-powered MacBook Pro and iPad. New features include more accurate health tracking and longer battery life.

Leading up to its "pro and tell" event later this week, Apple kicked off its latest round of announcements by revealing the new iPad mini . The 8th-generation small tablet now comes with an 8.5-inch OLED display, a longstanding wish list item for many mini fans. The new tablet also gains an updated A20 Pro processor, a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and a nano-texture option for the display. It starts at $699, $100 more than the previous version, and will be available for pre-order on Oct. 28. Apple has been slow to update the iPad mini over the years, much to the chagrin of its niche yet vocal fanbase . The previous generation came out in 2024, adding more storage, Apple Pencil support and a processor upgrade. The version before that came out in 2021 and finally removed the aging Home button from the tiny tablet. Apple has spent more time updating other iPad models, including the entry-level iPad and iPad Pro lineup. The latter received OLED screens in 2024, so the inclusion of that technology on the latest iPad mini now is noteworthy. Why are fans so keen on an OLED iPad mini? OLED displays offer better contrast and deeper blacks, resulting in higher-quality images overall. Flagship smartphones like the iPhone 18 Pro and Samsung Galaxy S26 use OLED screens too, so updating the iPad mini to have the same technology will make it look and feel more modern. But most popular smartphones also have 120Hz refresh rates, which makes scrolling feel quicker and smoother. Apple appears to have skipped this on the new iPad mini (no refresh rate is listed in the new iPad mini's specs; we've reached out to Apple to confirm) and that will likely be a deal breaker for some who find the standard 60Hz to feel too sluggish in comparison. There's also the argument that one could simply get an iPhone Duo now, which has similar dimensions to the iPad mini when unfolded, along with an OLED screen and a 120Hz refresh rate. But the iPhone Duo costs $2,000, and it seems to be having some unique issues of its own at the moment, just days after its official launch. The new iPad mini's A20 Pro processor should give it a decent performance boost, while the 12MP Center Stage camera on its landscape edge should make it more convenient to make FaceTime video calls. The nano-texture display option appears similar to that of the iPhone Duo's inner display, which is designed to reduce glare. Note, though, that this feature is optional on the iPad mini, is only available on the 256GB and 512GB storage options and bumps up the final price by an additional $100. Pre-orders open for the new iPad mini on Oct. 28, and it will be widely available starting Nov. 6.

The new iPad mini has roughly the same footprint as the 2024 release, but the display is slightly larger thanks to a 24 percent reduction in bezel thickness. The 7th-Gen iPad mini didn’t have any official IP rating. The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR display (up from 8.3 inches) moves on from the IPS technology of the last-gen device to adopt OLED. That means dapper blacks and a much higher peak brightness—1,200 nits versus just 500 nits for the previous mini. It can also manage 1-nit minimum brightness so as not to sear your retinas in a dark room. There will also be a nano-textured matte display option. The display experience on the new mini should be much more in line with what we’ve come to expect from Apple’s Pro-level devices. The 2-nanometer A20 Pro chip was a noticeable upgrade in the iPhone 18 Pro , and it will be even more significant in this tablet. The previous model had a 3-nanometer A17 Pro chip, which was already a year old when it appeared in the iPad mini. In the iPhone 18 Pro, we found the A20 Pro significantly improved graphics performance thanks in part to a 50 percent increase in memory bandwidth. Higher memory speed also helps with on-device AI applications, but the Neural Engine is the primary factor. Unfortunately, not all versions of the new iPad mini will be equally capable. Apple notes the 512GB configuration will have the dual 16-core Neural Engine we saw in the iPhone 18 Pro, but the 128GB and 256GB versions will have a single 16-core NPU. These versions will also have a slightly different CPU configuration, with five cores instead of six. Apple has retained the 12 MP cameras for the front and back of the tablet, but the front-facing one has changed location. Rather than being on the short edge for portrait-orientation video calls, it’s now on the long edge. That might take a little getting used to for those who frequently use their tablets for FaceTime. The $699 base price gets you 128GB of storage and Wi-Fi connectivity. It’s $100 more for 256GB and $300 more for 512GB. The nano-texture display is also a $100 upsell, but it’s only available for the 256GB and 512GB versions. The step up to cellular will cost $849 for the 128GB model. Pricing is, sadly, not eye-popping for 2026, but it marks yet another price increase for Apple. The 7th-gen iPad mini launched for $499 in 2024, but it has since risen to $599. The new model adds $100, but it does have some nice upgrades. Preorders for the new iPad mini begin at 10:10 am PT on October 28 (Wednesday), and devices will arrive on doorsteps and in stores on November 6. The refreshed pint-sized tablet features a larger 8.5-inch OLED display, the A20 Pro chip, an improved front-facing camera, and, for the first time on any iPad, IP67 water and dust resistance.
However, the new iPad Mini still doesn't feature a 120Hz ProMotion display and is locked to 60Hz.
The larger OLED panel should deliver deeper blacks, improved contrast, and more vibrant colors.
It also has a 7-core GPU that delivers up to 2.7x faster graphics performance.
Lastly, the 512GB model features a 6-core CPU.
Later this week, Apple is expected to reveal a touch-screen MacBook Pro and the M6-powered MacBook Pro and iPad.

extraction.body: Just as rumors last week suggested, the redesigned 8th-generation iPad Mini (2026) has arrived ahead of Apple's "Pro and Tell" event on Wednesday, October 28th. The refreshed pint-sized tablet features a larger 8.5-inch OLED display, the A20 Pro chip, an improved front-facing camera, and, for the first time on any iPad, IP67 water and dust resistance. The redesigned pint-sized tablet also features a less thick 5.4mm design and 24% thinner bezels. On the display front, the new 8.5-inch OLED screen offers 2x higher peak brightness at 1,200 nits (along with 1 nit minimum brightness), plus a nano-texture display option similar to recent iPad Pro releases. However, the new iPad Mini still doesn't feature a 120Hz ProMotion display and is locked to 60Hz. The 2024-released 7th-generation iPad Mini featured an 8.3-inch LCD screen with relatively thick bezels. The larger OLED panel should deliver deeper blacks, improved contrast, and more vibrant colors. At the same time, the tablet might also have worse battery life, since OLED panel technology consumes more power, though efficiency improvements in the A20 Pro could offset that. In the press release, Apple says that the new iPad Mini can hit 10 hours of battery life while watching videos or browsing the web on Wi-Fi. Regarding the A20 Pro specifically, the chip features a 5-core CPU with two super cores and three efficiency cores, making it compatible with Apple's new Siri AI features, including the assistant's more expressive voice. It also has a 7-core GPU that delivers up to 2.7x faster graphics performance. Lastly, the 512GB model features a 6-core CPU. The tablet's front-facing camera has been upgraded to a 12-megapixel Center Stage shooter that sits on its landscape bezel edge. Other upgrades include the Acoustic Display, which Apple says features "specially designed woofers" that are "paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume." Lastly, the tablet features Apple's C2 cellular modem (if you opt for the cellular version), alongside its N1 wireless chip. Apple says the new iPad Mini will be available to pre-order on Wednesday, October 28th, starting at $700, with availability launching on November 6th. While the 8th-gen iPad Mini seems like a solid all-around upgrade thanks to the A20 Pro chip and the new OLED panel, it's a bit crazy that it starts at $700, especially since the last refresh in 2024 launched at $500 (which already felt pretty expensive). Later this week, Apple is expected to reveal a touch-screen MacBook Pro and the M6-powered MacBook Pro and iPad. New features include more accurate health tracking and longer battery life.

sources.title: Apple’s new iPad mini finally gets an OLED screen — and a $100 price increase - Yahoo Tech
passages: Apple has been slow to update the iPad mini over the years, much to the chagrin of its niche yet vocal fanbase .
The previous generation came out in 2024, adding more storage, Apple Pencil support and a processor upgrade.
Apple has spent more time updating other iPad models, including the entry-level iPad and iPad Pro lineup.
The latter received OLED screens in 2024, so the inclusion of that technology on the latest iPad mini now is noteworthy.
Leading up to its "pro and tell" event later this week, Apple kicked off its latest round of announcements by revealing the new iPad mini .
The 8th-generation small tablet now comes with an 8.5-inch OLED display, a longstanding wish list item for many mini fans.
The new tablet also gains an updated A20 Pro processor, a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and a nano-texture option for the display.
It starts at $699, $100 more than the previous version, and will be available for pre-order on Oct.
But the iPhone Duo costs $2,000, and it seems to be having some unique issues of its own at the moment, just days after its official launch.
OLED displays offer better contrast and deeper blacks, resulting in higher-quality images overall.
But most popular smartphones also have 120Hz refresh rates, which makes scrolling feel quicker and smoother.

Leading up to its "pro and tell" event later this week, Apple kicked off its latest round of announcements by revealing the new iPad mini . The 8th-generation small tablet now comes with an 8.5-inch OLED display, a longstanding wish list item for many mini fans. The new tablet also gains an updated A20 Pro processor, a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and a nano-texture option for the display. It starts at $699, $100 more than the previous version, and will be available for pre-order on Oct. 28. Apple has been slow to update the iPad mini over the years, much to the chagrin of its niche yet vocal fanbase . The previous generation came out in 2024, adding more storage, Apple Pencil support and a processor upgrade. The version before that came out in 2021 and finally removed the aging Home button from the tiny tablet. Apple has spent more time updating other iPad models, including the entry-level iPad and iPad Pro lineup. The latter received OLED screens in 2024, so the inclusion of that technology on the latest iPad mini now is noteworthy. Why are fans so keen on an OLED iPad mini? OLED displays offer better contrast and deeper blacks, resulting in higher-quality images overall. Flagship smartphones like the iPhone 18 Pro and Samsung Galaxy S26 use OLED screens too, so updating the iPad mini to have the same technology will make it look and feel more modern. But most popular smartphones also have 120Hz refresh rates, which makes scrolling feel quicker and smoother. Apple appears to have skipped this on the new iPad mini (no refresh rate is listed in the new iPad mini's specs; we've reached out to Apple to confirm) and that will likely be a deal breaker for some who find the standard 60Hz to feel too sluggish in comparison. There's also the argument that one could simply get an iPhone Duo now, which has similar dimensions to the iPad mini when unfolded, along with an OLED screen and a 120Hz refresh rate. But the iPhone Duo costs $2,000, and it seems to be having some unique issues of its own at the moment, just days after its official launch. The new iPad mini's A20 Pro processor should give it a decent performance boost, while the 12MP Center Stage camera on its landscape edge should make it more convenient to make FaceTime video calls. The nano-texture display option appears similar to that of the iPhone Duo's inner display, which is designed to reduce glare. Note, though, that this feature is optional on the iPad mini, is only available on the 256GB and 512GB storage options and bumps up the final price by an additional $100. Pre-orders open for the new iPad mini on Oct. 28, and it will be widely available starting Nov. 6.

sources.title: SpaceX Secures Record $40 Billion GPU Lease Deal With Apollo - Yahoo Finance
passages: Apollo confirmed the financing will support Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX's terrestrial compute expansion.

The hardware is intended to run Grok, AI services for enterprise and consumer users, and SpaceX's existing and future cloud customers, according to reporting by Yahoo Finance citing the Apollo announcement.

A $40 billion committed deployment channel may provide Nvidia with meaningful demand visibility for hardware that has not yet shipped at scale, though the ultimate commercial impact depends on delivery speed, utilization, and customer demand.
Rather than purchasing hardware outright, SpaceX will rely on an Apollo-managed entity to acquire the GPUs and data-center equipment.
That entity then leases the hardware back to SpaceX under a master finance lease structure.
Forty billion dollars is not a rounding error.

The deal reflects a broader shift in how AI infrastructure capital is moving: toward operators with diversified, creditworthy revenue and, analysts suggest, away from companies that depend almost entirely on GPU rental.
The $40 billion commitment represents a binding financing arrangement, not completed funding: the transaction remained subject to closing conditions as of the announcement.

What determines whether the deal justifies its scale is execution, specifically delivery speed, hardware utilization, the pace of AI and cloud revenue growth, and whether SpaceX can manage lease obligations as GPU generations continue to evolve.

Equipment lease financing at this scale could become a template for other large AI infrastructure operators, but only if the installed capacity generates the returns that make the payment schedule sustainable.
SpaceX's case for its financing advantage rests on its business mix: revenue from Starlink subscriptions and rocket launch operations is independent of AI data center performance.
The binding commitment establishes scale and intent; what follows depends on how quickly SpaceX can bring the hardware online and generate returns against a five-year lease clock.
Apollo and Goldman Sachs led the financing effort.

sources.title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo
passages: SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday .
In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing” .
Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”

SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.
SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.
The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.
The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
