Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing. SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive. The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets. “This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services. Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.” The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses. The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business . SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined. Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone. The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits. While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals. Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads. “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X . “Some will make it through, but not many.” Buy One Pass, Get a Second Free Cover more ground at TechCrunch’s ultimate founder bootcamp of the year by bringing your co-founder or partner for free Book before the BOGO deal expires Grok releases the first seven minutes of its AI-generated ‘Odyssey’ Anthony Ha The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it Lauren Forristal Warhound raises $200M to engineer war dogs and arm them with Anduril gear Dominic-Madori Davis Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work Lucas Ropek

CFO Bret Johnsen had said SpaceX still expects fourth-quarter capital expenditure of $35 billion to $40 billion. Reuters reported earlier this month that SpaceX was in talks with banks and asset managers to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips. coreStoryFacts.text: Apollo confirmed the financing will support Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX's terrestrial compute expansion.

The hardware is intended to run Grok, AI services for enterprise and consumer users, and SpaceX's existing and future cloud customers, according to reporting by Yahoo Finance citing the Apollo announcement.

A $40 billion committed deployment channel may provide Nvidia with meaningful demand visibility for hardware that has not yet shipped at scale, though the ultimate commercial impact depends on delivery speed, utilization, and customer demand.
Rather than purchasing hardware outright, SpaceX will rely on an Apollo-managed entity to acquire the GPUs and data-center equipment.
That entity then leases the hardware back to SpaceX under a master finance lease structure.
Forty billion dollars is not a rounding error.

The deal reflects a broader shift in how AI infrastructure capital is moving: toward operators with diversified, creditworthy revenue and, analysts suggest, away from companies that depend almost entirely on GPU rental.
The $40 billion commitment represents a binding financing arrangement, not completed funding: the transaction remained subject to closing conditions as of the announcement.

What determines whether the deal justifies its scale is execution, specifically delivery speed, hardware utilization, the pace of AI and cloud revenue growth, and whether SpaceX can manage lease obligations as GPU generations continue to evolve.

Equipment lease financing at this scale could become a template for other large AI infrastructure operators, but only if the installed capacity generates the returns that make the payment schedule sustainable.
SpaceX's case for its financing advantage rests on its business mix: revenue from Starlink subscriptions and rocket launch operations is independent of AI data center performance.
The binding commitment establishes scale and intent; what follows depends on how quickly SpaceX can bring the hardware online and generate returns against a five-year lease clock.

extraction.body: Oct 26 (Reuters) - SpaceX said on Monday an affiliate of Apollo Global Management will buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them to the rockets-to-AI firm, in a deal with total principal payments of about $40 billion. Each lease will run a little over five years from the day the equipment arrives, according to a regulatory filing. The deal highlights SpaceX's heavy spending, as it tries to capitalize on surging demand for computing power to help bankroll its Moon and Mars ambitions. The company aims to finalize the deal by the end of the year. The leases are expected to start in the first half of 2027, once the chips are delivered. On Sunday, CEO Elon Musk said on X that SpaceX had "closed" $40 billion in debt financing for graphics processing units. Musk said the funding mainly targeted chips arriving in the first and second quarters and would not be "a major factor this quarter." CFO Bret Johnsen had said SpaceX still expects fourth-quarter capital expenditure of $35 billion to $40 billion. Reuters reported earlier this month that SpaceX was in talks with banks and asset managers to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips. (Reporting by Akash Sriram in Bengaluru; Editing by Shilpi Majumdar and Sriraj Kalluvila)

extraction.body: Apple has just released iOS 27.2, bringing Apple Pencil support to the iPhone Duo. The software update also includes an “Edge Light” feature for the iPhone Duo that’s intended to illuminate your face during video calls. Apple previously said the iPhone Duo would add support for the Apple Pencil “later this year.” The company’s first foldable comes with revamped iOS 27 controls designed to work across the device’s 7.6-inch inner display and 5.4-inch outer screen. Many major apps, like Netflix, Prime Video, and Microsoft Outlook, already support the Duo’s extra screen real estate, but some still need some work. The iOS 27.2 update also allows Siri AI to take suggested actions in Messages, while adding support for Siri AI in more languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Apple is rolling out support for Google’s SynthID AI watermark in Photos and Image Playground, too, according to 9to5Mac. Other smaller but notable updates include user profiles on the Apple TV app on iPhone. The Apple Podcasts app is also replacing its “Up Next” queue with a list of “New Episodes,” along with a “Continue Playing” section just beneath it. And group calls on FaceTime now support dual capture so you can show both what’s visible from your selfie cam and your back cameras. Apple also released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, watchOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, and HomePod 27.2.

extraction.body: Apple has just released iOS 27.2, bringing Apple Pencil support to the iPhone Duo. The software update also includes an “Edge Light” feature for the iPhone Duo that’s intended to illuminate your face during video calls. Apple previously said the iPhone Duo would add support for the Apple Pencil “later this year.” The company’s first foldable comes with revamped iOS 27 controls designed to work across the device’s 7.6-inch inner display and 5.4-inch outer screen. Many major apps, like Netflix, Prime Video, and Microsoft Outlook, already support the Duo’s extra screen real estate, but some still need some work. The iOS 27.2 update also allows Siri AI to take suggested actions in Messages, while adding support for Siri AI in more languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Apple is rolling out support for Google’s SynthID AI watermark in Photos and Image Playground, too, according to 9to5Mac. Other smaller but notable updates include user profiles on the Apple TV app on iPhone. The Apple Podcasts app is also replacing its “Up Next” queue with a list of “New Episodes,” along with a “Continue Playing” section just beneath it. And group calls on FaceTime now support dual capture so you can show both what’s visible from your selfie cam and your back cameras. Apple also released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, watchOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, and HomePod 27.2.

extraction.body: Ukraine says Starshield back to normal, denies misuse of Starlink commercial service. Musk said Ukraine used the Starlink commercial service for offensive drone strikes. Musk’s comment on Saturday came after SpaceX imposed a restriction preventing Ukraine from using the satellite technology on drones flying above certain speeds. One current and one former Ukraine official denied Musk’s accusation and said previous limits imposed by SpaceX already prevented Ukraine’s military from using Starlink in the way Musk described. Ukraine officials have accused Musk of throttling their use of Starshield, the military variant of Starlink that Ukraine has access to through a deal with the US government. Meanwhile, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said over the weekend that the new satellite restrictions have been lifted, possibly ending a controversy that began almost two weeks ago . Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, denied the allegation in a Telegram post on Sunday . Beskrestnov wrote that all Starlink terminals located over Ukrainian territory, including territories occupied by Russia, were already subject to a movement speed limit of 70 to 90 kilometers per hour. He added that Starlink does not function over the territory of Russia. “Consequently, it is PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE for us to use commercial Starlink for deep-strike or medium-range strike operations,” Beskrestnov wrote . He called it “very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine.” The Starlink and Starshield names are often used interchangeably by government officials discussing military use, making it difficult to determine whether certain statements refer to the civilian or military version of the technology. Zelenskyy and other Ukraine officials this month referred to both Starlink and Starshield when they complained that military drones lost satellite connectivity when traveling above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). Ukraine officials say the restriction imposed earlier this month has been lifted. “Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again,” according to The Kyiv Independent . Zelenskyy wrote on Saturday , “Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored to the speeds we had before the restrictions. The speeds are now where they need to be. The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient. This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Serhii Sternenko, who served as an advisor for the Ukraine Ministry of Defense earlier this year and now runs an organization that supplies drones to the Ukraine military, wrote that “Ukraine did not violate the terms of use.” “Elon Musk claims that Ukraine allegedly violated Starlink’s terms of use and used the system on combat drones. As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true,” Sternenko wrote. “In February of this year, whitelists were introduced. Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work. In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” Musk added that “Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action,” but did not at first accuse Ukraine of violating that restriction. President Trump denied making the decision to limit Ukraine’s satellite connectivity and reportedly called Musk to ask him to lift the restrictions. SpaceX’s Starlink and its military-focused Starshield service are critical to Ukraine’s wartime connectivity. Officials said the so-called speed caps were lifted on Saturday, and the service was restored. Still, questions have persisted about who ordered the interruptions to satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks. Writing on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that drones operated via the civilian Starlink system had a speed restriction of 70–90 kmh (43-56 mph) within Ukraine and did not work in Russia. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” he said. Musk acknowledged on Saturday that SpaceX had throttled Starlink in Ukraine. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote. That loophole was closed last week.” But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. President Donald Trump has maintained that he didn't make that call, while Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk. Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the Ukrainian military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions. They also added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by Trump’s reported deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia that Ukraine viewed as a betrayal. The US is making new efforts to end the war The restoration of Starlink service followed a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on Western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors. “This week alone, Russia has launched about 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, and almost 2,300 strike drones at Ukraine,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post. He said the attacks — many of them deadly — had affected nine regions of the country, damaging power plants, grain stores, civilian homes and commercial facilities.

coreStoryFacts.text: Musk initially responded to the controversy by stating that, unlike the Starlink commercial service, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.
“Elon Musk claims that Ukraine allegedly violated Starlink’s terms of use and used the system on combat drones.
As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true,” Sternenko wrote.
“In February of this year, whitelists were introduced.
Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians.
But for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system.
Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work.
In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible.
All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.”
Musk’s comment on Saturday came after SpaceX imposed a restriction preventing Ukraine from using the satellite technology on drones flying above certain speeds.
In May 2026, Musk said that US military suicide drones set up by a contractor incorrectly used Starlink instead of Starshield.

He called it “very strange that Elon Musk is unaware of the operational limitations of Starlink in Ukraine.”

extraction.body: Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said long-standing restrictions on the civilian system in Ukraine made such offensive use impossible. “It’s very strange that Elon Musk doesn’t know about the restrictions on Starlink’s operation in Ukraine,” he wrote in an online post. SpaceX’s Starlink and its military-focused Starshield service are critical to Ukraine’s wartime connectivity. Officials said the so-called speed caps were lifted on Saturday, and the service was restored. Still, questions have persisted about who ordered the interruptions to satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks. Writing on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that drones operated via the civilian Starlink system had a speed restriction of 70–90 kmh (43-56 mph) within Ukraine and did not work in Russia. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” he said. Musk acknowledged on Saturday that SpaceX had throttled Starlink in Ukraine. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote. That loophole was closed last week.” But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. President Donald Trump has maintained that he didn't make that call, while Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk. Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the Ukrainian military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions. They also added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by Trump’s reported deal with Moscow to import diesel from Russia that Ukraine viewed as a betrayal. The US is making new efforts to end the war The restoration of Starlink service followed a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week, renewing his call on Western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors. “This week alone, Russia has launched about 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, and almost 2,300 strike drones at Ukraine,” Zelenskyy wrote in an online post. He said the attacks — many of them deadly — had affected nine regions of the country, damaging power plants, grain stores, civilian homes and commercial facilities.

sources.title: Apple unveils new iPad mini with OLED display and faster A20 Pro chip
passages: Apple on Monday announced a new iPad mini with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display.
The tablet features a thinner and lighter design than its predecessor and is powered by an A20 Pro chip.
The tech giant revealed the new device just days before its “Pro and Tell” event that’s scheduled to take place on Wednesday.
Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, the iPad mini has up to 4.5-times faster AI performance than the previous generation, according to Apple.
It also features an “Acoustic Display” that Apple says enhances the audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content.
Specially designed woofers integrated into the display deliver deeper bass and higher volume for richer sound, per the company.
The Super Retina XDR display uses OLED technology for pixel-level lighting control, delivering deeper blacks, richer contrast, and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vibrant colors.

The updated tablet now also features a 12-megapixel center stage front camera, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support. Specially designed woofers integrated into the display deliver deeper bass and higher volume for richer sound, per the company. The new iPad mini launches with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions, and understand what’s on their screen. Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, the iPad mini has up to 4.5-times faster AI performance than the previous generation, according to Apple. The A20 Pro also features a 6-core CPU, delivering up to 60% faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks such as photo editing and multitasking across apps. The device can be preordered on October 28, with availability beginning November 6. extraction.body: For small businesses that need a full-featured computer without adding another bulky laptop to the travel bag, Apple is positioning its redesigned iPad mini as a mobile work tool rather than simply a compact tablet. Apple announced the new iPad mini on October 26, saying the device delivers its largest update yet. The company highlighted an 8.5-inch OLED display, a thinner and lighter design, the A20 Pro processor, faster wireless connectivity, water and dust resistance, and new artificial intelligence capabilities through iPadOS 27. Customers can pre-order the device beginning October 28, with shipments and retail availability starting November 6. Prices start at $699 for the Wi-Fi model and $849 for the Wi-Fi + Cellular version in the United States. Apple says the new model measures 5.4 millimeters thick and weighs less than its predecessor. Its IP67 rating means it can withstand dust and immersion in up to one meter of water for as long as 30 minutes under controlled laboratory conditions. That could benefit contractors checking plans outdoors, restaurant managers moving between locations, or shop owners using a tablet near sinks and work counters. However, the rating does not make the iPad mini waterproof for everyday business purposes. Apple warns that resistance can decline with normal wear and that users should not charge a wet device. Liquid damage is not covered under warranty, an important consideration for companies working in unpredictable environments. The display represents one of the more visible upgrades. Apple says the OLED panel produces deeper blacks, a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and peak brightness of up to 1,200 nits. A new nano-texture option reduces glare in bright surroundings. For a photographer, designer, architect, or field technician, that could make reviewing images, diagrams, and documents easier outdoors. The nano-texture version may carry additional cost, however, and business owners should confirm pricing before budgeting for multiple employees. Performance could matter more for businesses using demanding applications. Apple claims the A20 Pro can accelerate on-device AI, local language models, photo editing, graphics work, and 3D rendering. The 512GB configuration includes a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which Apple says doubles the processing power of the previous generation for certain AI workloads. Those claims come from Apple’s own testing, conducted in September 2026. Actual performance will depend on the software, workload, storage configuration, and whether an application processes data on the device or through the cloud. Businesses should test their core applications before replacing existing laptops or tablets across a team. The iPad mini also adds a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera positioned on the landscape edge. That arrangement could improve video calls when the tablet sits in a stand or connects to a keyboard. The rear camera supports 4K video and an Adaptive True Tone flash, which may help employees scan documents, capture inventory, record job progress, or create social media content. “iPad mini is beloved for its fantastic portability, performance, and display by a wide range of users, from creators and small business owners to doctors, field service workers, and gamers,” said Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With a remarkably thinner and lighter design, a stunning new OLED display, the incredibly powerful A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance, the new iPad mini is a huge leap forward for users who love having the full iPad experience in the palm of their hand.” Connectivity could make the cellular version attractive to mobile businesses. Apple says its C2 modem supports up to 50 percent faster cellular data speeds than the prior model, while the N1 wireless chip enables Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. Cellular connectivity could help salespeople, inspectors, delivery operators, and service technicians stay connected away from office networks. It also adds a recurring data-plan expense, and speeds will vary by carrier, location, and network conditions. Apple’s most consequential software pitch involves artificial intelligence. Siri AI, which rolls out in beta with iPadOS 27, can use personal context, interpret onscreen information, and answer questions. Apple Intelligence also includes upgraded photo tools, Image Playground, systemwide dictation improvements, and Safari notifications for changes such as product restocks or price drops. For small businesses, those tools could reduce time spent searching through messages, rewriting notes, editing images, and monitoring web pages. Privacy may appeal to companies handling sensitive information: Apple says many requests use on-device processing or Private Cloud Compute, and that data handled through Private Cloud Compute is not stored or made accessible to Apple. Still, AI should not be treated as a substitute for review. Siri AI remains in beta, some features are unavailable in certain regions or languages, and Apple says server-based tools may face daily usage limits. Owners should also establish policies for confidential customer, employee, and financial information before allowing staff to use AI features. The tablet supports Apple Pencil USB-C for $79 and Apple Pencil Pro for $129, while the new Smart Folio costs $79. Those extras can quickly raise the total cost of ownership. A Wi-Fi model with the Pencil Pro and folio reaches $907 before taxes, and a cellular model with the same accessories reaches $1,057. Apple offers trade-in credits, installment plans, leasing, and AppleCare options. Financing can reduce the immediate cash burden, but eligibility requirements, credit approval, carrier conditions, and lease termination charges apply. Apple announced the new iPad mini on October 26, saying the device delivers its largest update yet. The company highlighted an 8.5-inch OLED display, a thinner and lighter design, the A20 Pro processor, faster wireless connectivity, water and dust resistance, and new artificial intelligence capabilities through iPadOS 27.

Customers can pre-order the device beginning October 28, with shipments and retail availability starting November 6. Prices start at $699 for the Wi-Fi model and $849 for the Wi-Fi + Cellular version in the United States.

Apple says the new model measures 5.4 millimeters thick and weighs less than its predecessor. Its IP67 rating means it can withstand dust and immersion in up to one meter of water for as long as 30 minutes under controlled laboratory conditions. That could benefit contractors checking plans outdoors, restaurant managers moving between locations, or shop owners using a tablet near sinks and work counters.

However, the rating does not make the iPad mini waterproof for everyday business purposes. Apple warns that resistance can decline with normal wear and that users should not charge a wet device. Liquid damage is not covered under warranty, an important consideration for companies working in unpredictable environments.

The display represents one of the more visible upgrades. Apple says the OLED panel produces deeper blacks, a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and peak brightness of up to 1,200 nits. A new nano-texture option reduces glare in bright surroundings. For a photographer, designer, architect, or field technician, that could make reviewing images, diagrams, and documents easier outdoors. The nano-texture version may carry additional cost, however, and business owners should confirm pricing before budgeting for multiple employees.

Performance could matter more for businesses using demanding applications. Apple claims the A20 Pro can accelerate on-device AI, local language models, photo editing, graphics work, and 3D rendering. The 512GB configuration includes a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which Apple says doubles the processing power of the previous generation for certain AI workloads.

Those claims come from Apple’s own testing, conducted in September 2026. Actual performance will depend on the software, workload, storage configuration, and whether an application processes data on the device or through the cloud. Businesses should test their core applications before replacing existing laptops or tablets across a team.

The iPad mini also adds a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera positioned on the landscape edge. That arrangement could improve video calls when the tablet sits in a stand or connects to a keyboard. The rear camera supports 4K video and an Adaptive True Tone flash, which may help employees scan documents, capture inventory, record job progress, or create social media content.

“iPad mini is beloved for its fantastic portability, performance, and display by a wide range of users, from creators and small business owners to doctors, field service workers, and gamers,” said Dave Pakula, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With a remarkably thinner and lighter design, a stunning new OLED display, the incredibly powerful A20 Pro, and water and dust resistance, the new iPad mini is a huge leap forward for users who love having the full iPad experience in the palm of their hand.”

Connectivity could make the cellular version attractive to mobile businesses. Apple says its C2 modem supports up to 50 percent faster cellular data speeds than the prior model, while the N1 wireless chip enables Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. Cellular connectivity could help salespeople, inspectors, delivery operators, and service technicians stay connected away from office networks. It also adds a recurring data-plan expense, and speeds will vary by carrier, location, and network conditions.

Apple’s most consequential software pitch involves artificial intelligence. Siri AI, which rolls out in beta with iPadOS 27, can use personal context, interpret onscreen information, and answer questions. Apple Intelligence also includes upgraded photo tools, Image Playground, systemwide dictation improvements, and Safari notifications for changes such as product restocks or price drops.

For small businesses, those tools could reduce time spent searching through messages, rewriting notes, editing images, and monitoring web pages. Privacy may appeal to companies handling sensitive information: Apple says many requests use on-device processing or Private Cloud Compute, and that data handled through Private Cloud Compute is not stored or made accessible to Apple.

Still, AI should not be treated as a substitute for review. Siri AI remains in beta, some features are unavailable in certain regions or languages, and Apple says server-based tools may face daily usage limits. Owners should also establish policies for confidential customer, employee, and financial information before allowing staff to use AI features.

The tablet supports Apple Pencil USB-C for $79 and Apple Pencil Pro for $129, while the new Smart Folio costs $79. Those extras can quickly raise the total cost of ownership. A Wi-Fi model with the Pencil Pro and folio reaches $907 before taxes, and a cellular model with the same accessories reaches $1,057.

sources.title: Bitcoin dips below US$80,000 as AI-related market selloff deepens - The Business Times
passages: BITCOIN retreated below US$80,000 on Monday (Oct 26) as broader risk-off sentiment ahead of a Federal Reserve meeting and concerns over the artificial intelligence trade weighed on cryptocurrencies.
Smaller tokens including Ether, XRP and Solana also declined.

The moves came after investors pulled US$772.4 million from US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Thursday and Friday, a sharp reversal from more than US$1 billion of net inflows earlier in the week.
“Bitcoin has so far been relatively resilient to the AI debt concerns that are weighing on all risk assets,” said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets.
“The market focus is now on the Fed meeting, followed by US midterm elections .”
Bitcoin remains in the risk-off basket for many systematic funds and algorithmic traders, leaving it vulnerable to deteriorating sentiment, said Pratik Kala, portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto.

The largest digital asset fell as much as 1.4 per cent to under US$79,300 before paring some losses to trade around US$80,000 in afternoon trading in Asia. Smaller tokens including Ether, XRP and Solana also declined. The moves came after investors pulled US$772.4 million from US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds on Thursday and Friday, a sharp reversal from more than US$1 billion of net inflows earlier in the week. The declines accompanied a broader market slump that extended from last week as investors questioned massive spending on AI and looked toward this week’s earnings reports from tech giants for clues about the outlook. The Kospi Index in South Korea — a bellwether for the AI trade — fell 0.2 per cent and chip-related stocks were among the biggest decliners in Japan’s Nikkei. “Bitcoin has so far been relatively resilient to the AI debt concerns that are weighing on all risk assets,” said Caroline Mauron, co-founder of Orbit Markets. “The market focus is now on the Fed meeting, followed by US midterm elections .” Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines. Bitcoin remains in the risk-off basket for many systematic funds and algorithmic traders, leaving it vulnerable to deteriorating sentiment, said Pratik Kala, portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto. Kala pointed to online discussions about AI, including comments from SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk about potential consolidation next year, as contributing to market strain. Advances in AI have also exacerbated potential security risks for crypto, making some investors skittish, he added. BLOOMBERG

sources.title: Will the real Anthropic please stand up
passages: As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post : “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry.
And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”
After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus.
The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.

Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology.
“I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said.
We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”
Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said.
Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.
Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience.
When so little seems certain, what Anthropic (and its fellow frontier AI companies) say is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship.
I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this. (That’s for another day.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum.
Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us.
But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra.
In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.
It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic?
It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think.

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation.
Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked ).
But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that.
As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free.

Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because of their egos.

extraction.body: The company has been masterful at storytelling for years. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask or lean deeper into the myth-making? This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. In fact, its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture. Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here. Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers. Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation. And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience. The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?) Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.” Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. extraction.body: Get unlimited access to everything VICE has to offer. For the last five years, Mac DeMarco has been trying to show his real side. Some artists create a character and run with it, or see themselves splintering off into Medusa-like multiples. But DeMarco’s persona – if that’s what you want to call it – was mostly created without his doing. “Maybe I painted some kind of weird picture,” he’ll tell me when we meet later in east London, considering how that persona may have come about. “But it’s something you’ve gotta accept, because it’s out of your hands. It’s like making music. The songs come out and they aren’t yours anymore.” It’s hard to tell when the Canadian lo-fi singer-songwriter’s reputation left his control in the first place. Like a cartoon character, the DeMarco of side jibes, fart jokes and general goofiness has been partly exaggerated. Not that he doesn’t bring the reputation on himself. For proof that DeMarco really is a pin-up for inane humour, his presenting job for MTV’s Weird Vibes is evidence enough – it’s all faux British accents, inside jokes and the sort of awkwardly blunt conversations you might expect from a professional television host. And in the rare case that you’re a naturally funny person, people expect you to perform. This is a guy who made a sketch pretending to be a guy called Dave Fuck , spending his life showing cars how to reverse into parking spaces. What’s essentially schoolboy humour somehow doesn’t come across as crude or stupid – it’s hilarious. But there’s a separation between the meme-friendly Mac and the sincere guy you hear on record. Up until now, it’s been hard to decipher between the two. Just when he’ll look to settle into a groove of honest, no-frills songwriting, he’ll throw in healthy dose of tongue-in-cheek satire. Take 2014’s “ Passing Out The Pieces ” – a song about not being every stranger’s property, a 24/7 jester, that also happened to be accompanied by a video where he kills his friends and gives birth in a bath of cabbages. It’s a style of warped humour he can’t seem to resist. With the 5 May release of his latest record This Old Dog however, the playful side simmers down to a low cool. For a large portion of the record DeMarco is essentially talking to himself, staring at a mirror image, prodding away and seeing what’s inside his head. The album itself is rooted in an honest account of family and, specifically, DeMarco’s father, who recently became gravely ill. Not that you’d pick up on Mac’s heartfelt, deep-thinking side from the build-up surrounding this record. In one session video for This Old Dog ‘s title track, he can be seen performing in the middle of a dog grooming parlour. “You may be asking yourself, ‘Why is Mac in Groom Dog City? Why?’” he says, introducing the song. “Well,” he sighs, “probably because the next song I’m gonna play is called ‘This Old Dog’… And while I may not be speaking about a real dog in the song, this is what my press will probably look like for the next two years.” It’s a joke veiled in serious jadedness. He goes along with it, seeing the funny side, but there’s also a sense he’s getting tired of the schtick. He’s been the funny guy for half a decade – perhaps that’s long enough. The very day this session is being filmed, he sits in the middle of Brick Lane’s Beigel Bake with me, chewing on what turns out to be his third salt beef bagel in 24 hours. He’s also being shown the footage of #Bagelgate, a beautifully brutal encapsulation of British culture that he doesn’t quite seem to understand. This is my fault. It’s been two days since #Bagelgate swept the nation, and because we’re in a bagel shop ( geddit?! ), I’ve decided Funny Guy Mac will love this video. “Eight pieces of bread in one little nugget? That’s going to do crazy things to your stomach and your mind,” he says, offering some explanation of what he’s being made to watch. But it’s clear he’d rather steer the topic towards his music. At an acoustic show later that night in east London, he happily tells the crowd how he’s spent the day doing press, which he hates. It’s easy to see why, when instead of being asked about his records, an average promo day consists of dog parlours and viral bagel-throwing videos, for the lols . It’s very tempting to go into a Mac DeMarco interview thinking he’ll be your best mate by the end of it. He’s personable like that. And in fairness, his personality is part and parcel of why he’s so huge, selling out a venue like south London’s 4,900-capacity Brixton Academy in minutes. But – press notwithstanding – he’s long attempted to break the myth of being that two-dimensional, fun-time, up-for-everything guy. Up until last year, Mac lived in the Far Rockaways neighbourhood of Queens, New York. On 2015 mini-album Another One , he chose to share his address with fans. “Stop on by, I’ll make you a cup of coffee. See you later,” he says on “ My House On The Water “. This might seem like a strange move from a guy already idolised by countless flannel shirt-sporting, baseball-cap wearing, Viceroy-smoking kids. Surely by making himself accessible at all times, he’d be expected to live up to his persona 24/7. “There were times when it was like, ‘Are you fucking kidding me right now?’” he admits. His invitation for a cup of coffee was approached broadly by fans, who’d show up to his place drunk at 2AM. “I never regretted doing it, though. It was cool meeting so many people, and nothing bad or sketchy happened.” Like every fan encounter he has, Mac was himself: chilled out, unfussed, not quite the on-call jester you might expect from his online reputation. This was partly the point of giving out his address – to dispel the myth. This Old Dog does a similar job of demystifying the weird hurrah around DeMarco. Lyrically, he’s not performing backflips. Most of the themes being addressed are approached in a direct way, but with enough ambiguity that they’re not rammed down your throat. Of everything DeMarco tackles, the feeling of growing older keeps cropping up. It’s like a nagging thought that can’t be erased. “Dreams From Yesterday” is the sound of a young kid hitting the jackpot, only to find himself in limbo. “Once your life set to settle down / Take a look around you, no more dreaming to be found,” he sings. “My Old Man” even refers directly to a reputation preceding him. “There’s a price tag hanging off of all that fun,” he goes, like two split personalities having a private conversation. In truth, DeMarco has most definitely grown up. But not in a boring, fun-sapping way. Those previously loose guitar parts have tightened up, and these are neatly-bundled songs with a perfect flow. That’s not to say there isn’t a sense of youth racing through the album too, because there is – it’s just staring the threat of old age directly in the face, jostling to get the upper hand. He’s been sincere before – 2012’s “ Still Together ” is an earnest ode to childhood sweetheart Kiera “Kiki” McNally, who he’s still with today, while 2014’s “ Let My Baby Stay ” grapples with the thought that she might be kicked out the U.S. due to immigration laws. It’s rare, however, for his songs to be so direct and autobiographical. “I’m not a great lyricist, so I can’t go Bob Dylan style without looking like a jackass,” he insists. “I’m not like, ‘Chicagoooo, in October !’” he adds, just a shade away from a funny Sun Kil Moon impression. So – besides wanting to offer up a more honest portrayal of himself – what’s the reason for DeMarco’s new direction? Part of the new approach is down to his 2016 move to Los Angeles, where he put music to one side while readjusting to a new place. “I had three or four months of getting settled,” he remembers. “Because I had more peace in that sense, I was released from the party-guy-drunk-on-tour-every-night thing. Getting a big chunk of away time changed how I was thinking about things. I usually have a month off, and you don’t have a chance to decompress and think about things, or realise, ‘Oh yeah, I have a family!’ But when you get a lot of time off, you step back and look at what’s happening in your life. You’ve become a little older without really noticing.” Writing on-and-off in 2016 between New York and LA coincided with news of his father’s illness, which at the time was taking a turn for the worse. It’s documented in “Watching Him Fade Away”, the new record’s closing track, and its most striking moment. DeMarco’s father was rarely in his life, prone to drug and alcohol abuse, appearing every so often as his son grew up, but never as a central part of his upbringing. Mac’s songs have related this before, but “This Old Dog”, and “Watching Him Fade Away” in particular, grapple with the idea of saying goodbye to someone who was seldom there in the first place. “And even though you barely know each other, it still hurts, watching him fade away” he sings, torn between his dad’s bedside and the exit door. It makes for DeMarco’s most generously honest, gut-wrenching song to date. “The funny thing is he’s now recovered,” he says, awkwardly laughing. “I didn’t think he was going to hear these songs, regardless of everyone else hearing it. But he’s going to! I’ll probably get an interesting phone call at some point.” The real Mac, warts and all, is a constant presence on this record. Both sides are bookended by short-lived, earnest songs. “Watching Him Fade Away” ends the second half, while “Sister” – a touching tribute to his half-sister Holly – closes the first. There’s also “Moonlight on the River”, a vast expanse of a song that seems to burrow down inside his psyche. Lasting seven minutes, its second half is pretty much just the sound of DeMarco screaming into an amplifier, creating a wall of maddening feedback. “That was at like 4 in the morning, me in my studio alone, smoking and laughing like a jackass. It’s a weird scene.” He cites laughter, but the song’s second half sounds like a musician climbing up the walls. Sticking to his honesty-first policy, he considers the bagel he’s just consumed. “It’s not the best one I’ve ever had, but it’s pretty good,” he says, wiping mustard off his face. “I think the bagel was a little less salted than regular. Which is, y’know… It’s in the name – you need the salt. Usually I eat these when I’m really drunk, after a show. So there’s that style. Today I’m completely sober. You know what? I enjoyed it. Now I understand the nuances of the beef.” He’s still performing slightly, because that’s what comes naturally. Less a defence mechanism and more a default, this persona hasn’t plagued DeMarco, but it’s threatened to. He only gets approached once mid-interview by a fan, and the conversation is typical – there’s no expectation of him delivering a gag or pulling a funny face for a selfie. As we exit the bagel shop, he starts up a conversation with a homeless man outside, handing him a £10 note once he’s ruffled around his pockets for change, before piling his acoustic guitar into a cab for tonight’s show. “On this one I just wanted to keep it real,” he says, circuiting back to the record. “That’s that. It feels right to me, so maybe other people will like it. These songs are personal to me, but if someone listening to it doesn’t know my backstory, they wouldn’t pick up on it. It’s vague enough that they might not know what I’m talking about, but they could connect to it in other ways. That’s another philosophy of mine with songwriting – keep it simple, stupid.” Mac DeMarco plays Primavera Sound festival on Friday 2 June at Parc del Fòrum, and is on tour from May. You’ve become a little older without really noticing.”

Writing on-and-off in 2016 between New York and LA coincided with news of his father’s illness, which at the time was taking a turn for the worse. It’s documented in “Watching Him Fade Away”, the new record’s closing track, and its most striking moment. DeMarco’s father was rarely in his life, prone to drug and alcohol abuse, appearing every so often as his son grew up, but never as a central part of his upbringing. Mac’s songs have related this before, but “This Old Dog”, and “Watching Him Fade Away” in particular, grapple with the idea of saying goodbye to someone who was seldom there in the first place.

“And even though you barely know each other, it still hurts, watching him fade away” he sings, torn between his dad’s bedside and the exit door. It makes for DeMarco’s most generously honest, gut-wrenching song to date. “The funny thing is he’s now recovered,” he says, awkwardly laughing. “I didn’t think he was going to hear these songs, regardless of everyone else hearing it. But he’s going to! I’ll probably get an interesting phone call at some point.”

The real Mac, warts and all, is a constant presence on this record. Both sides are bookended by short-lived, earnest songs. “Watching Him Fade Away” ends the second half, while “Sister” – a touching tribute to his half-sister Holly – closes the first. There’s also “Moonlight on the River”, a vast expanse of a song that seems to burrow down inside his psyche. Lasting seven minutes, its second half is pretty much just the sound of DeMarco screaming into an amplifier, creating a wall of maddening feedback.

“That was at like 4 in the morning, me in my studio alone, smoking and laughing like a jackass. It’s a weird scene.” He cites laughter, but the song’s second half sounds like a musician climbing up the walls. Sticking to his honesty-first policy, he considers the bagel he’s just consumed. “It’s not the best one I’ve ever had, but it’s pretty good,” he says, wiping mustard off his face. “I think the bagel was a little less salted than regular. Which is, y’know… It’s in the name – you need the salt. Usually I eat these when I’m really drunk, after a show. So there’s that style. Today I’m completely sober. You know what? I enjoyed it. Now I understand the nuances of the beef.”

He’s still performing slightly, because that’s what comes naturally. Less a defence mechanism and more a default, this persona hasn’t plagued DeMarco, but it’s threatened to. He only gets approached once mid-interview by a fan, and the conversation is typical – there’s no expectation of him delivering a gag or pulling a funny face for a selfie.

As we exit the bagel shop, he starts up a conversation with a homeless man outside, handing him a £10 note once he’s ruffled around his pockets for change, before piling his acoustic guitar into a cab for tonight’s show. “On this one I just wanted to keep it real,” he says, circuiting back to the record. “That’s that. It feels right to me, so maybe other people will like it. These songs are personal to me, but if someone listening to it doesn’t know my backstory, they wouldn’t pick up on it. It’s vague enough that they might not know what I’m talking about, but they could connect to it in other ways. That’s another philosophy of mine with songwriting – keep it simple, stupid.”
Mac DeMarco plays Primavera Sound festival on Friday 2 June at Parc del Fòrum, and is on tour from May.

Before it was heard in concert halls and wrestling rings, the name echoed around Capitol Hill as moniker of John Nance Garner. He was a whiskey-guzzling, cowboy-hat-wearing politician from Texas who spent more than 30 years in the U.S. House of Representatives. After, he went on to become the 32nd Vice President under Franklin D. Roosevelt. It has been awhile since Cactus Jack was a household name, a name he earned for suggesting that the prickly pear cactus would make a better state flower than the bluebonnet – although he lost that battle. passages: By Laura Rice February 12, 2016 3:06 pm Arts & Culture , Government & Politics , History Image via Flickr/FDR Presidential Library (Public Domain)
John Nance Garner, known as Cactus Jack, on campaign trail with FDR during his first Presidential run in 1932.
It is a name that is part of Texas lore, a name known far and wide and as big as Texas itself: Cactus Jack.

Before it was heard in concert halls and wrestling rings, the name echoed around Capitol Hill as moniker of John Nance Garner. He was a whiskey-guzzling, cowboy-hat-wearing politician from Texas who spent more than 30 years in the U.S. House of Representatives. After, he went on to become the 32nd Vice President under Franklin D. Roosevelt.

It has been awhile since Cactus Jack was a household name, a name he earned for suggesting that the prickly pear cactus would make a better state flower than the bluebonnet – although he lost that battle.

A new documentary plans to set the record straight about who the “real” Cactus Jack might be. It’s airing on PBS stations across the country just in time for President’s Day and is directed by Nancy Schiesari , a professor at the University of Texas at Austin. Don Carleton , executive director of UT’s Briscoe Center, produced the film.

Schiesari says she didn’t know anything about Cactus Jack before starting on the documentary about him until folks from the Briscoe Center approached her. His story starts in small-town Texas in Red River County.
“We told the story chronologically, onto his movement to Washington,” she says. “We have incredible storytellers in the film, like Don, who give that whole history life.”

Carleton says they’ve been looking how to “rescue” Cactus Jack from obscurity. “He’s bascially been lost to history,” he says, “and he’s just way too important a historical character to have been lost like that.”

coreStoryFacts.text: As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post : “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry.
And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”
After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus.
The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.

Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology.
“I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said.
We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”
Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said.
Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.
Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience.
When so little seems certain, what Anthropic (and its fellow frontier AI companies) say is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship.
I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this. (That’s for another day.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum.
Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us.
But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra.
In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.
It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic?
It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think.

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation.
Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked ).
But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that.
As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free.

Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because of their egos.
For the last five years, Mac DeMarco has been trying to show his real side.

extraction.body: Get unlimited access to everything VICE has to offer. For the last five years, Mac DeMarco has been trying to show his real side. Some artists create a character and run with it, or see themselves splintering off into Medusa-like multiples. But DeMarco’s persona – if that’s what you want to call it – was mostly created without his doing. “Maybe I painted some kind of weird picture,” he’ll tell me when we meet later in east London, considering how that persona may have come about. “But it’s something you’ve gotta accept, because it’s out of your hands. It’s like making music. The songs come out and they aren’t yours anymore.” It’s hard to tell when the Canadian lo-fi singer-songwriter’s reputation left his control in the first place. Like a cartoon character, the DeMarco of side jibes, fart jokes and general goofiness has been partly exaggerated. Not that he doesn’t bring the reputation on himself. For proof that DeMarco really is a pin-up for inane humour, his presenting job for MTV’s Weird Vibes is evidence enough – it’s all faux British accents, inside jokes and the sort of awkwardly blunt conversations you might expect from a professional television host. And in the rare case that you’re a naturally funny person, people expect you to perform. This is a guy who made a sketch pretending to be a guy called Dave Fuck , spending his life showing cars how to reverse into parking spaces. What’s essentially schoolboy humour somehow doesn’t come across as crude or stupid – it’s hilarious. But there’s a separation between the meme-friendly Mac and the sincere guy you hear on record. Up until now, it’s been hard to decipher between the two. Just when he’ll look to settle into a groove of honest, no-frills songwriting, he’ll throw in healthy dose of tongue-in-cheek satire. Take 2014’s “ Passing Out The Pieces ” – a song about not being every stranger’s property, a 24/7 jester, that also happened to be accompanied by a video where he kills his friends and gives birth in a bath of cabbages. It’s a style of warped humour he can’t seem to resist. With the 5 May release of his latest record This Old Dog however, the playful side simmers down to a low cool. For a large portion of the record DeMarco is essentially talking to himself, staring at a mirror image, prodding away and seeing what’s inside his head. The album itself is rooted in an honest account of family and, specifically, DeMarco’s father, who recently became gravely ill. Not that you’d pick up on Mac’s heartfelt, deep-thinking side from the build-up surrounding this record. In one session video for This Old Dog ‘s title track, he can be seen performing in the middle of a dog grooming parlour. “You may be asking yourself, ‘Why is Mac in Groom Dog City? Why?’” he says, introducing the song. “Well,” he sighs, “probably because the next song I’m gonna play is called ‘This Old Dog’… And while I may not be speaking about a real dog in the song, this is what my press will probably look like for the next two years.” It’s a joke veiled in serious jadedness. He goes along with it, seeing the funny side, but there’s also a sense he’s getting tired of the schtick. He’s been the funny guy for half a decade – perhaps that’s long enough. The very day this session is being filmed, he sits in the middle of Brick Lane’s Beigel Bake with me, chewing on what turns out to be his third salt beef bagel in 24 hours. He’s also being shown the footage of #Bagelgate, a beautifully brutal encapsulation of British culture that he doesn’t quite seem to understand. This is my fault. It’s been two days since #Bagelgate swept the nation, and because we’re in a bagel shop ( geddit?! ), I’ve decided Funny Guy Mac will love this video. “Eight pieces of bread in one little nugget? That’s going to do crazy things to your stomach and your mind,” he says, offering some explanation of what he’s being made to watch. But it’s clear he’d rather steer the topic towards his music. At an acoustic show later that night in east London, he happily tells the crowd how he’s spent the day doing press, which he hates. It’s easy to see why, when instead of being asked about his records, an average promo day consists of dog parlours and viral bagel-throwing videos, for the lols . It’s very tempting to go into a Mac DeMarco interview thinking he’ll be your best mate by the end of it. He’s personable like that. And in fairness, his personality is part and parcel of why he’s so huge, selling out a venue like south London’s 4,900-capacity Brixton Academy in minutes. But – press notwithstanding – he’s long attempted to break the myth of being that two-dimensional, fun-time, up-for-everything guy. Up until last year, Mac lived in the Far Rockaways neighbourhood of Queens, New York. On 2015 mini-album Another One , he chose to share his address with fans. “Stop on by, I’ll make you a cup of coffee. See you later,” he says on “ My House On The Water “. This might seem like a strange move from a guy already idolised by countless flannel shirt-sporting, baseball-cap wearing, Viceroy-smoking kids. Surely by making himself accessible at all times, he’d be expected to live up to his persona 24/7. “There were times when it was like, ‘Are you fucking kidding me right now?’” he admits. His invitation for a cup of coffee was approached broadly by fans, who’d show up to his place drunk at 2AM. “I never regretted doing it, though. It was cool meeting so many people, and nothing bad or sketchy happened.” Like every fan encounter he has, Mac was himself: chilled out, unfussed, not quite the on-call jester you might expect from his online reputation. This was partly the point of giving out his address – to dispel the myth. This Old Dog does a similar job of demystifying the weird hurrah around DeMarco. Lyrically, he’s not performing backflips. Most of the themes being addressed are approached in a direct way, but with enough ambiguity that they’re not rammed down your throat. Of everything DeMarco tackles, the feeling of growing older keeps cropping up. It’s like a nagging thought that can’t be erased. “Dreams From Yesterday” is the sound of a young kid hitting the jackpot, only to find himself in limbo. “Once your life set to settle down / Take a look around you, no more dreaming to be found,” he sings. “My Old Man” even refers directly to a reputation preceding him. “There’s a price tag hanging off of all that fun,” he goes, like two split personalities having a private conversation. In truth, DeMarco has most definitely grown up. But not in a boring, fun-sapping way. Those previously loose guitar parts have tightened up, and these are neatly-bundled songs with a perfect flow. That’s not to say there isn’t a sense of youth racing through the album too, because there is – it’s just staring the threat of old age directly in the face, jostling to get the upper hand. He’s been sincere before – 2012’s “ Still Together ” is an earnest ode to childhood sweetheart Kiera “Kiki” McNally, who he’s still with today, while 2014’s “ Let My Baby Stay ” grapples with the thought that she might be kicked out the U.S. due to immigration laws. It’s rare, however, for his songs to be so direct and autobiographical. “I’m not a great lyricist, so I can’t go Bob Dylan style without looking like a jackass,” he insists. “I’m not like, ‘Chicagoooo, in October !’” he adds, just a shade away from a funny Sun Kil Moon impression. So – besides wanting to offer up a more honest portrayal of himself – what’s the reason for DeMarco’s new direction? Part of the new approach is down to his 2016 move to Los Angeles, where he put music to one side while readjusting to a new place. “I had three or four months of getting settled,” he remembers. “Because I had more peace in that sense, I was released from the party-guy-drunk-on-tour-every-night thing. Getting a big chunk of away time changed how I was thinking about things. I usually have a month off, and you don’t have a chance to decompress and think about things, or realise, ‘Oh yeah, I have a family!’ But when you get a lot of time off, you step back and look at what’s happening in your life. You’ve become a little older without really noticing.” Writing on-and-off in 2016 between New York and LA coincided with news of his father’s illness, which at the time was taking a turn for the worse. It’s documented in “Watching Him Fade Away”, the new record’s closing track, and its most striking moment. DeMarco’s father was rarely in his life, prone to drug and alcohol abuse, appearing every so often as his son grew up, but never as a central part of his upbringing. Mac’s songs have related this before, but “This Old Dog”, and “Watching Him Fade Away” in particular, grapple with the idea of saying goodbye to someone who was seldom there in the first place. “And even though you barely know each other, it still hurts, watching him fade away” he sings, torn between his dad’s bedside and the exit door. It makes for DeMarco’s most generously honest, gut-wrenching song to date. “The funny thing is he’s now recovered,” he says, awkwardly laughing. “I didn’t think he was going to hear these songs, regardless of everyone else hearing it. But he’s going to! I’ll probably get an interesting phone call at some point.” The real Mac, warts and all, is a constant presence on this record. Both sides are bookended by short-lived, earnest songs. “Watching Him Fade Away” ends the second half, while “Sister” – a touching tribute to his half-sister Holly – closes the first. There’s also “Moonlight on the River”, a vast expanse of a song that seems to burrow down inside his psyche. Lasting seven minutes, its second half is pretty much just the sound of DeMarco screaming into an amplifier, creating a wall of maddening feedback. “That was at like 4 in the morning, me in my studio alone, smoking and laughing like a jackass. It’s a weird scene.” He cites laughter, but the song’s second half sounds like a musician climbing up the walls. Sticking to his honesty-first policy, he considers the bagel he’s just consumed. “It’s not the best one I’ve ever had, but it’s pretty good,” he says, wiping mustard off his face. “I think the bagel was a little less salted than regular. Which is, y’know… It’s in the name – you need the salt. Usually I eat these when I’m really drunk, after a show. So there’s that style. Today I’m completely sober. You know what? I enjoyed it. Now I understand the nuances of the beef.” He’s still performing slightly, because that’s what comes naturally. Less a defence mechanism and more a default, this persona hasn’t plagued DeMarco, but it’s threatened to. He only gets approached once mid-interview by a fan, and the conversation is typical – there’s no expectation of him delivering a gag or pulling a funny face for a selfie. As we exit the bagel shop, he starts up a conversation with a homeless man outside, handing him a £10 note once he’s ruffled around his pockets for change, before piling his acoustic guitar into a cab for tonight’s show. “On this one I just wanted to keep it real,” he says, circuiting back to the record. “That’s that. It feels right to me, so maybe other people will like it. These songs are personal to me, but if someone listening to it doesn’t know my backstory, they wouldn’t pick up on it. It’s vague enough that they might not know what I’m talking about, but they could connect to it in other ways. That’s another philosophy of mine with songwriting – keep it simple, stupid.” Mac DeMarco plays Primavera Sound festival on Friday 2 June at Parc del Fòrum, and is on tour from May.
