It’s easy to see why, when instead of being asked about his records, an average promo day consists of dog parlours and viral bagel-throwing videos, for the lols . It’s very tempting to go into a Mac DeMarco interview thinking he’ll be your best mate by the end of it. He’s personable like that. And in fairness, his personality is part and parcel of why he’s so huge, selling out a venue like south London’s 4,900-capacity Brixton Academy in minutes. But – press notwithstanding – he’s long attempted to break the myth of being that two-dimensional, fun-time, up-for-everything guy.

Up until last year, Mac lived in the Far Rockaways neighbourhood of Queens, New York. On 2015 mini-album Another One , he chose to share his address with fans. “Stop on by, I’ll make you a cup of coffee. See you later,” he says on “ My House On The Water “. This might seem like a strange move from a guy already idolised by countless flannel shirt-sporting, baseball-cap wearing, Viceroy-smoking kids. Surely by making himself accessible at all times, he’d be expected to live up to his persona 24/7. “There were times when it was like, ‘Are you fucking kidding me right now?’” he admits. His invitation for a cup of coffee was approached broadly by fans, who’d show up to his place drunk at 2AM. “I never regretted doing it, though. It was cool meeting so many people, and nothing bad or sketchy happened.” Like every fan encounter he has, Mac was himself: chilled out, unfussed, not quite the on-call jester you might expect from his online reputation. This was partly the point of giving out his address – to dispel the myth.

This Old Dog does a similar job of demystifying the weird hurrah around DeMarco. Lyrically, he’s not performing backflips. Most of the themes being addressed are approached in a direct way, but with enough ambiguity that they’re not rammed down your throat. Of everything DeMarco tackles, the feeling of growing older keeps cropping up. It’s like a nagging thought that can’t be erased. “Dreams From Yesterday” is the sound of a young kid hitting the jackpot, only to find himself in limbo. “Once your life set to settle down / Take a look around you, no more dreaming to be found,” he sings. “My Old Man” even refers directly to a reputation preceding him. “There’s a price tag hanging off of all that fun,” he goes, like two split personalities having a private conversation. In truth, DeMarco has most definitely grown up. But not in a boring, fun-sapping way. Those previously loose guitar parts have tightened up, and these are neatly-bundled songs with a perfect flow. That’s not to say there isn’t a sense of youth racing through the album too, because there is – it’s just staring the threat of old age directly in the face, jostling to get the upper hand.

He’s been sincere before – 2012’s “ Still Together ” is an earnest ode to childhood sweetheart Kiera “Kiki” McNally, who he’s still with today, while 2014’s “ Let My Baby Stay ” grapples with the thought that she might be kicked out the U.S. due to immigration laws. It’s rare, however, for his songs to be so direct and autobiographical. “I’m not a great lyricist, so I can’t go Bob Dylan style without looking like a jackass,” he insists. “I’m not like, ‘Chicagoooo, in October !’” he adds, just a shade away from a funny Sun Kil Moon impression. So – besides wanting to offer up a more honest portrayal of himself – what’s the reason for DeMarco’s new direction?

Part of the new approach is down to his 2016 move to Los Angeles, where he put music to one side while readjusting to a new place. “I had three or four months of getting settled,” he remembers. “Because I had more peace in that sense, I was released from the party-guy-drunk-on-tour-every-night thing. Getting a big chunk of away time changed how I was thinking about things. I usually have a month off, and you don’t have a chance to decompress and think about things, or realise, ‘Oh yeah, I have a family!’ But when you get a lot of time off, you step back and look at what’s happening in your life. You’ve become a little older without really noticing.”

Writing on-and-off in 2016 between New York and LA coincided with news of his father’s illness, which at the time was taking a turn for the worse. It’s documented in “Watching Him Fade Away”, the new record’s closing track, and its most striking moment. DeMarco’s father was rarely in his life, prone to drug and alcohol abuse, appearing every so often as his son grew up, but never as a central part of his upbringing. Mac’s songs have related this before, but “This Old Dog”, and “Watching Him Fade Away” in particular, grapple with the idea of saying goodbye to someone who was seldom there in the first place.

“And even though you barely know each other, it still hurts, watching him fade away” he sings, torn between his dad’s bedside and the exit door. It makes for DeMarco’s most generously honest, gut-wrenching song to date. “The funny thing is he’s now recovered,” he says, awkwardly laughing. “I didn’t think he was going to hear these songs, regardless of everyone else hearing it. But he’s going to! I’ll probably get an interesting phone call at some point.”

The real Mac, warts and all, is a constant presence on this record. Both sides are bookended by short-lived, earnest songs. “Watching Him Fade Away” ends the second half, while “Sister” – a touching tribute to his half-sister Holly – closes the first. There’s also “Moonlight on the River”, a vast expanse of a song that seems to burrow down inside his psyche. Lasting seven minutes, its second half is pretty much just the sound of DeMarco screaming into an amplifier, creating a wall of maddening feedback.

“That was at like 4 in the morning, me in my studio alone, smoking and laughing like a jackass. It’s a weird scene.” He cites laughter, but the song’s second half sounds like a musician climbing up the walls. Sticking to his honesty-first policy, he considers the bagel he’s just consumed. “It’s not the best one I’ve ever had, but it’s pretty good,” he says, wiping mustard off his face. “I think the bagel was a little less salted than regular. Which is, y’know… It’s in the name – you need the salt. Usually I eat these when I’m really drunk, after a show. So there’s that style. Today I’m completely sober. You know what? I enjoyed it. Now I understand the nuances of the beef.”

He’s still performing slightly, because that’s what comes naturally. Less a defence mechanism and more a default, this persona hasn’t plagued DeMarco, but it’s threatened to. He only gets approached once mid-interview by a fan, and the conversation is typical – there’s no expectation of him delivering a gag or pulling a funny face for a selfie.

As we exit the bagel shop, he starts up a conversation with a homeless man outside, handing him a £10 note once he’s ruffled around his pockets for change, before piling his acoustic guitar into a cab for tonight’s show. “On this one I just wanted to keep it real,” he says, circuiting back to the record. “That’s that. It feels right to me, so maybe other people will like it. These songs are personal to me, but if someone listening to it doesn’t know my backstory, they wouldn’t pick up on it. It’s vague enough that they might not know what I’m talking about, but they could connect to it in other ways. That’s another philosophy of mine with songwriting – keep it simple, stupid.”
Mac DeMarco plays Primavera Sound festival on Friday 2 June at Parc del Fòrum, and is on tour from May.

It is a name that is part of Texas lore, a name known far and wide and as big as Texas itself: Cactus Jack. Before it was heard in concert halls and wrestling rings, the name echoed around Capitol Hill as moniker of John Nance Garner. He was a whiskey-guzzling, cowboy-hat-wearing politician from Texas who spent more than 30 years in the U.S. House of Representatives. After, he went on to become the 32nd Vice President under Franklin D. Roosevelt. It has been awhile since Cactus Jack was a household name, a name he earned for suggesting that the prickly pear cactus would make a better state flower than the bluebonnet – although he lost that battle. A new documentary plans to set the record straight about who the “real” Cactus Jack might be. It’s airing on PBS stations across the country just in time for President’s Day and is directed by Nancy Schiesari , a professor at the University of Texas at Austin. Don Carleton , executive director of UT’s Briscoe Center, produced the film. Schiesari says she didn’t know anything about Cactus Jack before starting on the documentary about him until folks from the Briscoe Center approached her. His story starts in small-town Texas in Red River County. “We told the story chronologically, onto his movement to Washington,” she says. “We have incredible storytellers in the film, like Don, who give that whole history life.” Carleton says they’ve been looking how to “rescue” Cactus Jack from obscurity. “He’s bascially been lost to history,” he says, “and he’s just way too important a historical character to have been lost like that.” Listen to the full interview in the audio player above. {date} "},"theme":{"name":""}} NO MATTER WHERE YOU ARE, YOU’RE ON TEXAS STANDARD TIME Statewide support provided by --> The Texas Standard is a partnership of ©2026 Texas Standard. passages: By Laura Rice February 12, 2016 3:06 pm Arts & Culture , Government & Politics , History Image via Flickr/FDR Presidential Library (Public Domain)
John Nance Garner, known as Cactus Jack, on campaign trail with FDR during his first Presidential run in 1932.
It is a name that is part of Texas lore, a name known far and wide and as big as Texas itself: Cactus Jack.

Before it was heard in concert halls and wrestling rings, the name echoed around Capitol Hill as moniker of John Nance Garner. He was a whiskey-guzzling, cowboy-hat-wearing politician from Texas who spent more than 30 years in the U.S. House of Representatives. After, he went on to become the 32nd Vice President under Franklin D. Roosevelt.

It has been awhile since Cactus Jack was a household name, a name he earned for suggesting that the prickly pear cactus would make a better state flower than the bluebonnet – although he lost that battle.

A new documentary plans to set the record straight about who the “real” Cactus Jack might be. It’s airing on PBS stations across the country just in time for President’s Day and is directed by Nancy Schiesari , a professor at the University of Texas at Austin. Don Carleton , executive director of UT’s Briscoe Center, produced the film.

Schiesari says she didn’t know anything about Cactus Jack before starting on the documentary about him until folks from the Briscoe Center approached her. His story starts in small-town Texas in Red River County.
“We told the story chronologically, onto his movement to Washington,” she says. “We have incredible storytellers in the film, like Don, who give that whole history life.”

Carleton says they’ve been looking how to “rescue” Cactus Jack from obscurity. “He’s bascially been lost to history,” he says, “and he’s just way too important a historical character to have been lost like that.”

passages: A hacker has successfully breached a vulnerable server, claiming a prize pot worth $2,021.22 in Bitcoin after exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, a posting on the Steal My Bitcoin website has shown.
The challenge's creator confirmed the win on October 25, ending an experiment designed to test claims that exploiting critical software vulnerabilities is becoming easier.
A Bitcoin hacking challenge is daring security researchers to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities and steal the cryptocurrency, putting claims about real-world exploitability to the test.
Bitcoin recovery efforts have previously involved reverse-engineering software rather than exploiting a live server.

In 2024, hardware hacker Joe Grand, known as ‘Kingpin”, and researcher Bruno recovered access to 43.6 BTC belonging to an owner identified as Michael, who had forgotten a 20-character wallet password.
The flaws received critical severity ratings, and fixes were released on October 21.
Turning the vulnerabilities into a reliable attack, however, requires more than simply running a publicly available exploit against an arbitrary server.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
The challenge, hosted on the website a day earlier and announced through a forum post , initially offered approximately $502 worth of Bitcoin.
PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP’s request-handling and memory-management processes.
Under vulnerable configurations, an attacker could potentially exploit these flaws to execute code with the privileges of the web server account.
The latest event comes as security teams face pressure to patch PHP installations following the public disclosure of PHP2Shell.
A separate report on the vulnerability disclosure controversy detailed how premature publication disrupted the coordinated release process.
That said, for now, evidence of the latest successful attack suggests that exploiting these PHP vulnerabilities may not be that hard after all.

The winner, ‘KillaBoi’, published a proof of concept on GitHub describing the attack against the live challenge and providing a local test environment.

The exploit took advantage of PHP's handling of multipart uploads and session data, where, by pushing a PHP worker beyond its memory limit, the attacker could leave internal state in an inconsistent condition.
The researchers reverse-engineered an older version of RoboForm's password generator and identified a flaw that made the password predictable.
They recovered the wallet in November 2023, when the Bitcoin was worth approximately $1.6 million.
Its value had climbed to nearly $3 million by the time the recovery was reported in May 2024.
The backup contained the keys needed to access the Bitcoin.
Notably, the attacker used those addresses to construct a forged PHP data structure that triggered command execution during cleanup.
The final request returned evidence that the command had run inside the PHP process.
Although the server was successfully compromised, the recovered private key did not match the advertised prize address.
However, on-chain data shows the funds were subsequently sent to an address “bc1qr4…lk7a9” , labeled as a Kraken cold wallet.

coreStoryFacts.text: A hacker has successfully breached a vulnerable server, claiming a prize pot worth $2,021.22 in Bitcoin after exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, a posting on the Steal My Bitcoin website has shown.
The challenge's creator confirmed the win on October 25, ending an experiment designed to test claims that exploiting critical software vulnerabilities is becoming easier.
A Bitcoin hacking challenge is daring security researchers to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities and steal the cryptocurrency, putting claims about real-world exploitability to the test.
Bitcoin recovery efforts have previously involved reverse-engineering software rather than exploiting a live server.

In 2024, hardware hacker Joe Grand, known as ‘Kingpin”, and researcher Bruno recovered access to 43.6 BTC belonging to an owner identified as Michael, who had forgotten a 20-character wallet password.
The flaws received critical severity ratings, and fixes were released on October 21.
Turning the vulnerabilities into a reliable attack, however, requires more than simply running a publicly available exploit against an arbitrary server.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
The challenge, hosted on the website a day earlier and announced through a forum post , initially offered approximately $502 worth of Bitcoin.
PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP’s request-handling and memory-management processes.
Under vulnerable configurations, an attacker could potentially exploit these flaws to execute code with the privileges of the web server account.
The latest event comes as security teams face pressure to patch PHP installations following the public disclosure of PHP2Shell.
A separate report on the vulnerability disclosure controversy detailed how premature publication disrupted the coordinated release process.
That said, for now, evidence of the latest successful attack suggests that exploiting these PHP vulnerabilities may not be that hard after all.

The winner, ‘KillaBoi’, published a proof of concept on GitHub describing the attack against the live challenge and providing a local test environment.

The exploit took advantage of PHP's handling of multipart uploads and session data, where, by pushing a PHP worker beyond its memory limit, the attacker could leave internal state in an inconsistent condition.
The researchers reverse-engineered an older version of RoboForm's password generator and identified a flaw that made the password predictable.
They recovered the wallet in November 2023, when the Bitcoin was worth approximately $1.6 million.
Its value had climbed to nearly $3 million by the time the recovery was reported in May 2024.
The backup contained the keys needed to access the Bitcoin.
Notably, the attacker used those addresses to construct a forged PHP data structure that triggered command execution during cleanup.
The final request returned evidence that the command had run inside the PHP process.
Although the server was successfully compromised, the recovered private key did not match the advertised prize address.
However, on-chain data shows the funds were subsequently sent to an address “bc1qr4…lk7a9” , labeled as a Kraken cold wallet.

A security researcher was able to exploit an intentionally unpatched PHP server and claim its Bitcoin bounty in just over 19 hours.
The page reads: “For now, there are no bitcoin on this server,” adding that more challenges may follow.
The experiment came days after a scramble over two critical bugs in PHP.
Details of the vulnerabilities leaked online, prompting PHP’s maintainers to ship emergency fixes on October 21, a day ahead of schedule, as Cryptopolitan reported.
Stealmybitcoin.com, the site where the game was hosted, verified the bounty had been claimed.
Its results page shows the Bitcoin was taken after 19.28 hours, with the win being logged at 15:47 UTC on Sunday, October 25.

Randa holds a degree in Electrical and Electronics Engineering from the University of Bradford.
The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and dubbed PHP2Shell, both received a severity score of 9.2 out of 10 and enable remote code execution on unpatched servers.
The public stunt was a test to see if the recent PHP2Shell flaws are as dangerous as they are said to be.

coreFacts.text: A hacker has successfully breached a vulnerable server, claiming a prize pot worth $2,021.22 in Bitcoin after exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, a posting on the Steal My Bitcoin website has shown.
The challenge's creator confirmed the win on October 25, ending an experiment designed to test claims that exploiting critical software vulnerabilities is becoming easier.
A Bitcoin hacking challenge is daring security researchers to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities and steal the cryptocurrency, putting claims about real-world exploitability to the test.
Bitcoin recovery efforts have previously involved reverse-engineering software rather than exploiting a live server.

In 2024, hardware hacker Joe Grand, known as ‘Kingpin”, and researcher Bruno recovered access to 43.6 BTC belonging to an owner identified as Michael, who had forgotten a 20-character wallet password.
The flaws received critical severity ratings, and fixes were released on October 21.
Turning the vulnerabilities into a reliable attack, however, requires more than simply running a publicly available exploit against an arbitrary server.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
The challenge, hosted on the website a day earlier and announced through a forum post , initially offered approximately $502 worth of Bitcoin.
PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP’s request-handling and memory-management processes.
Under vulnerable configurations, an attacker could potentially exploit these flaws to execute code with the privileges of the web server account.
The latest event comes as security teams face pressure to patch PHP installations following the public disclosure of PHP2Shell.
A separate report on the vulnerability disclosure controversy detailed how premature publication disrupted the coordinated release process.
That said, for now, evidence of the latest successful attack suggests that exploiting these PHP vulnerabilities may not be that hard after all.

extraction.body: A security researcher was able to exploit an intentionally unpatched PHP server and claim its Bitcoin bounty in just over 19 hours. The public stunt was a test to see if the recent PHP2Shell flaws are as dangerous as they are said to be. Stealmybitcoin.com, the site where the game was hosted, verified the bounty had been claimed. Its results page shows the Bitcoin was taken after 19.28 hours, with the win being logged at 15:47 UTC on Sunday, October 25. The prize pot was 0.02511679 BTC, worth $2,021.22 at that time. The page reads: “For now, there are no bitcoin on this server,” adding that more challenges may follow. The winner, who goes by the handle KillaBoi, posted a proof-of-concept write-up to GitHub . The target was running PHP 8.4.26. The write-up says that the one private key it recovered did not derive the prize address shown on the homepage. It calls this a mistake by the creator, acknowledged via email, and the site still lists the challenge as won. The contest was also seen by more people through the @hackerfantastic account, which is connected to the company hacker.house. In a post on October 25, the account explained how the challenge worked. The experiment came days after a scramble over two critical bugs in PHP. Details of the vulnerabilities leaked online, prompting PHP’s maintainers to ship emergency fixes on October 21, a day ahead of schedule, as Cryptopolitan reported. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and dubbed PHP2Shell, both received a severity score of 9.2 out of 10 and enable remote code execution on unpatched servers. PHP is used by about 70% of sites that have a known server-side language, and many sites shut down as a precaution. Finland, the Netherlands and France all temporarily pulled government websites offline. Cloudflare said it saw millions of what it called exploitation attempts in the hours after the bugs were made public. Two months were given to a coalition that included OpenAI to make fixes. OpenAI said that the same AI tools that found the flaws could also help attackers quickly make exploits. sources.title: Mars colony and Grok warnings: five strange details in SpaceX’s pitch to investors - The Guardian
passages: The sci-fi rhetoric is not theoretical; it bears financial stakes.
Musk will receive an award of 1bn shares in the company if SpaceX achieves “the establishment of a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants”.
The interplanetary ambitions of SpaceX’s central mission also result in some warnings to investors.
Reaching such unusual business goals as understanding the “true nature of the universe” may prove difficult, the company advises.

Throughout the investor prospectus, SpaceX reiterates that its ultimate goal is to establish colonies on the moon and Mars that will usher in human civilization’s next evolution and expand humanity’s presence in the universe.
Several of these relate to xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company that SpaceX acquired in February.
SpaceX’s filing shows that it has funneled increasing amounts of money in recent years to Musk’s security firm, with expenses of $2m in 2023, $3m in 2024 and $4m last year related to the company.
It also stated that it spent $1m during the first three months of 2026 on its services.
As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing.
The bot itself disclosed that it had generated images of “minors in minimal clothing”.
Several people, including minors, have filed lawsuits since alleging the company profited off of sexual predation and child sexual abuse material.
Although much of that money – $506m to Tesla in 2025 and $191m in 2024 – went to purchasing Tesla’s Megapack battery product, SpaceX also spent lavishly on Cybertrucks.

The prospectus discloses that in 2025 SpaceX obtained $131m worth of Cybertrucks at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, which ranges between about $69,900 and $99,900, depending on the options.
While outlining risk factors, SpaceX includes several large caveats surrounding its products and plans.
Such disclosures accounting for potential future risks and the uncertainty of guaranteed revenue are standard in IPO filings.
At one point, the prospectus includes what appears to be an AI-generated rendering of life on Mars .
The image shows a family on Mars looking out at a rocket launch amid a field of geodesic domes and rows of solar panels.
Elsewhere in the filing, SpaceX disclaims that, in order to make its vision successful, it will have to continue to pour more money into experimental and unproven technologies.

These big swings, core to its business, may simply not work out: “Many of the innovative products and services described elsewhere in this prospectus may ultimately be unsuccessful and may require great expense.”

extraction.body: IPO filing from Elon Musk’s company reveals closer look at finances, cosmic ambitions and tech empire’s quirks IPO filing from Elon Musk’s company reveals closer look at finances, cosmic ambitions and tech empire’s quirks SpaceX publicly released an investor prospectus on Wednesday as part of its plan for a $1.75tn debut on the US stock market next month, revealing unseen details about the finances and future plans of Elon Musk ’s flagship company. In addition to new information on operating costs and revenue, the filing also included trademark Muskian sweeping proclamations about the universe and insights into some of the quirks of his tech empire. Scattered throughout the 300-plus-page prospectus are several disclosures and risk warnings that show the eccentricities of Musk’s company and its cosmic ambitions. Other financial details in the document highlight how interdependent Musk’s various businesses have become and the risks that they carry. As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing. SpaceX appears to have done extensive business with Tesla , spending hundreds of millions of dollars with Musk’s electric car company in recent years. Although much of that money – $506m to Tesla in 2025 and $191m in 2024 – went to purchasing Tesla’s Megapack battery product, SpaceX also spent lavishly on Cybertrucks. The prospectus discloses that in 2025 SpaceX obtained $131m worth of Cybertrucks at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, which ranges between about $69,900 and $99,900, depending on the options. At that price, SpaceX would have acquired at least 1,300 vehicles. Tesla only sold a total of 20,237 Cybertrucks last year, according to auto industry sales reports , meaning that SpaceX’s purchases made up a significant portion of its overall sales. Throughout the investor prospectus, SpaceX reiterates that its ultimate goal is to establish colonies on the moon and Mars that will usher in human civilization’s next evolution and expand humanity’s presence in the universe. “By moving beyond the only home we have ever known, we ensure species-level redundancy and that the light of consciousness will not be tied to a single planet subject to the inevitable hazards of a harsh and vast universe,” the prospectus says. “We do not want humans to have the same fate as dinosaurs.” At one point, the prospectus includes what appears to be an AI-generated rendering of life on Mars . The image shows a family on Mars looking out at a rocket launch amid a field of geodesic domes and rows of solar panels. The sci-fi rhetoric is not theoretical; it bears financial stakes. Musk will receive an award of 1bn shares in the company if SpaceX achieves “the establishment of a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants”. The interplanetary ambitions of SpaceX’s central mission also result in some warnings to investors. Reaching such unusual business goals as understanding the “true nature of the universe” may prove difficult, the company advises. “We face a number of challenges relating to our business and growth strategy and, ultimately, the achievement of our mission to make life multiplanetary, understand the true nature of the universe, and extend the light of consciousness to the stars,” the prospectus reads. The section of SpaceX’s filing that outlines risks to investors contains an array of legal and regulatory issues that reference various investigations, lawsuits and scandals involving Musk. Several of these relate to xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company that SpaceX acquired in February. One passage in the prospectus discloses that xAI’s Grok chatbot, especially its “spicy” and “unhinged” modes, present a heightened risk of creating numerous harms including “the generation of potentially explicit content and misinformation or deceptive outputs, potential nonconsensual or exploitative imagery, intellectual property infringement, or content that could be viewed as exploitative, harmful, harassing, abusive, or discriminatory”. The prospectus also states that the company is the subject of numerous domestic and international law enforcement investigations and inquiries related to allegations of Grok creating nonconsensual images. Grok generated more than 3m sexualized images in the span of just 11 days earlier this year before the company increased some restrictions on its output, according to an estimate from the Center for Countering Digital Hate. The bot itself disclosed that it had generated images of “minors in minimal clothing”. Several people, including minors, have filed lawsuits since alleging the company profited off of sexual predation and child sexual abuse material. Musk has long expressed public concern about his personal safety and threats to his security. Through his private foundation and one of his top lieutenants, Musk has registered security companies in both California and Texas to provide him protection. SpaceX’s filing shows that it has funneled increasing amounts of money in recent years to Musk’s security firm, with expenses of $2m in 2023, $3m in 2024 and $4m last year related to the company. It also stated that it spent $1m during the first three months of 2026 on its services. Musk has repeatedly claimed that he frequently faces death threats and risks to his safety, especially during the period when he became the face of his “department of government efficiency” effort to gut federal agencies and humanitarian aid. IPO filing from Elon Musk’s company reveals closer look at finances, cosmic ambitions and tech empire’s quirks

SpaceX publicly released an investor prospectus on Wednesday as part of its plan for a $1.75tn debut on the US stock market next month, revealing unseen details about the finances and future plans of Elon Musk ’s flagship company. In addition to new information on operating costs and revenue, the filing also included trademark Muskian sweeping proclamations about the universe and insights into some of the quirks of his tech empire.

Scattered throughout the 300-plus-page prospectus are several disclosures and risk warnings that show the eccentricities of Musk’s company and its cosmic ambitions. Other financial details in the document highlight how interdependent Musk’s various businesses have become and the risks that they carry.
As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing.

SpaceX appears to have done extensive business with Tesla , spending hundreds of millions of dollars with Musk’s electric car company in recent years. Although much of that money – $506m to Tesla in 2025 and $191m in 2024 – went to purchasing Tesla’s Megapack battery product, SpaceX also spent lavishly on Cybertrucks.

The prospectus discloses that in 2025 SpaceX obtained $131m worth of Cybertrucks at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, which ranges between about $69,900 and $99,900, depending on the options. At that price, SpaceX would have acquired at least 1,300 vehicles.
Tesla only sold a total of 20,237 Cybertrucks last year, according to auto industry sales reports , meaning that SpaceX’s purchases made up a significant portion of its overall sales.

Throughout the investor prospectus, SpaceX reiterates that its ultimate goal is to establish colonies on the moon and Mars that will usher in human civilization’s next evolution and expand humanity’s presence in the universe.

“By moving beyond the only home we have ever known, we ensure species-level redundancy and that the light of consciousness will not be tied to a single planet subject to the inevitable hazards of a harsh and vast universe,” the prospectus says. “We do not want humans to have the same fate as dinosaurs.”

At one point, the prospectus includes what appears to be an AI-generated rendering of life on Mars . The image shows a family on Mars looking out at a rocket launch amid a field of geodesic domes and rows of solar panels.

The sci-fi rhetoric is not theoretical; it bears financial stakes. Musk will receive an award of 1bn shares in the company if SpaceX achieves “the establishment of a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants”.

The interplanetary ambitions of SpaceX’s central mission also result in some warnings to investors. Reaching such unusual business goals as understanding the “true nature of the universe” may prove difficult, the company advises.

“We face a number of challenges relating to our business and growth strategy and, ultimately, the achievement of our mission to make life multiplanetary, understand the true nature of the universe, and extend the light of consciousness to the stars,” the prospectus reads.

The section of SpaceX’s filing that outlines risks to investors contains an array of legal and regulatory issues that reference various investigations, lawsuits and scandals involving Musk. Several of these relate to xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company that SpaceX acquired in February.

One passage in the prospectus discloses that xAI’s Grok chatbot, especially its “spicy” and “unhinged” modes, present a heightened risk of creating numerous harms including “the generation of potentially explicit content and misinformation or deceptive outputs, potential nonconsensual or exploitative imagery, intellectual property infringement, or content that could be viewed as exploitative, harmful, harassing, abusive, or discriminatory”.

The prospectus also states that the company is the subject of numerous domestic and international law enforcement investigations and inquiries related to allegations of Grok creating nonconsensual images.

The bot itself disclosed that it had generated images of “minors in minimal clothing”. Several people, including minors, have filed lawsuits since alleging the company profited off of sexual predation and child sexual abuse material.

SpaceX’s filing shows that it has funneled increasing amounts of money in recent years to Musk’s security firm, with expenses of $2m in 2023, $3m in 2024 and $4m last year related to the company. It also stated that it spent $1m during the first three months of 2026 on its services.

extraction.body: Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions. At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055. The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company. It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US. It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development. Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.

IPO filing from Elon Musk’s company reveals closer look at finances, cosmic ambitions and tech empire’s quirks

SpaceX publicly released an investor prospectus on Wednesday as part of its plan for a $1.75tn debut on the US stock market next month, revealing unseen details about the finances and future plans of Elon Musk ’s flagship company. In addition to new information on operating costs and revenue, the filing also included trademark Muskian sweeping proclamations about the universe and insights into some of the quirks of his tech empire.

Scattered throughout the 300-plus-page prospectus are several disclosures and risk warnings that show the eccentricities of Musk’s company and its cosmic ambitions. Other financial details in the document highlight how interdependent Musk’s various businesses have become and the risks that they carry.
As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing.

SpaceX appears to have done extensive business with Tesla , spending hundreds of millions of dollars with Musk’s electric car company in recent years. Although much of that money – $506m to Tesla in 2025 and $191m in 2024 – went to purchasing Tesla’s Megapack battery product, SpaceX also spent lavishly on Cybertrucks.

The prospectus discloses that in 2025 SpaceX obtained $131m worth of Cybertrucks at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, which ranges between about $69,900 and $99,900, depending on the options. At that price, SpaceX would have acquired at least 1,300 vehicles.
Tesla only sold a total of 20,237 Cybertrucks last year, according to auto industry sales reports , meaning that SpaceX’s purchases made up a significant portion of its overall sales.

Throughout the investor prospectus, SpaceX reiterates that its ultimate goal is to establish colonies on the moon and Mars that will usher in human civilization’s next evolution and expand humanity’s presence in the universe.

“By moving beyond the only home we have ever known, we ensure species-level redundancy and that the light of consciousness will not be tied to a single planet subject to the inevitable hazards of a harsh and vast universe,” the prospectus says. “We do not want humans to have the same fate as dinosaurs.”

At one point, the prospectus includes what appears to be an AI-generated rendering of life on Mars . The image shows a family on Mars looking out at a rocket launch amid a field of geodesic domes and rows of solar panels.

The sci-fi rhetoric is not theoretical; it bears financial stakes. Musk will receive an award of 1bn shares in the company if SpaceX achieves “the establishment of a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants”.

The interplanetary ambitions of SpaceX’s central mission also result in some warnings to investors. Reaching such unusual business goals as understanding the “true nature of the universe” may prove difficult, the company advises.

“We face a number of challenges relating to our business and growth strategy and, ultimately, the achievement of our mission to make life multiplanetary, understand the true nature of the universe, and extend the light of consciousness to the stars,” the prospectus reads.

The section of SpaceX’s filing that outlines risks to investors contains an array of legal and regulatory issues that reference various investigations, lawsuits and scandals involving Musk. Several of these relate to xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company that SpaceX acquired in February.

One passage in the prospectus discloses that xAI’s Grok chatbot, especially its “spicy” and “unhinged” modes, present a heightened risk of creating numerous harms including “the generation of potentially explicit content and misinformation or deceptive outputs, potential nonconsensual or exploitative imagery, intellectual property infringement, or content that could be viewed as exploitative, harmful, harassing, abusive, or discriminatory”.

The prospectus also states that the company is the subject of numerous domestic and international law enforcement investigations and inquiries related to allegations of Grok creating nonconsensual images.

Grok generated more than 3m sexualized images in the span of just 11 days earlier this year before the company increased some restrictions on its output, according to an estimate from the Center for Countering Digital Hate. The bot itself disclosed that it had generated images of “minors in minimal clothing”. Several people, including minors, have filed lawsuits since alleging the company profited off of sexual predation and child sexual abuse material.

Musk has long expressed public concern about his personal safety and threats to his security. Through his private foundation and one of his top lieutenants, Musk has registered security companies in both California and Texas to provide him protection.

SpaceX’s filing shows that it has funneled increasing amounts of money in recent years to Musk’s security firm, with expenses of $2m in 2023, $3m in 2024 and $4m last year related to the company. It also stated that it spent $1m during the first three months of 2026 on its services.

Musk has repeatedly claimed that he frequently faces death threats and risks to his safety, especially during the period when he became the face of his “department of government efficiency” effort to gut federal agencies and humanitarian aid.

While outlining risk factors, SpaceX includes several large caveats surrounding its products and plans. The company disclosed that its massive amounts of spending have resulted in huge losses, including $4.9bn in 2025 and $4.3bn in the first quarter of this year alone. Such disclosures accounting for potential future risks and the uncertainty of guaranteed revenue are standard in IPO filings.
“We have a history of net losses and may not achieve profitability in the future,” the prospectus states.

Elsewhere in the filing, SpaceX disclaims that, in order to make its vision successful, it will have to continue to pour more money into experimental and unproven technologies. These big swings, core to its business, may simply not work out: “Many of the innovative products and services described elsewhere in this prospectus may ultimately be unsuccessful and may require great expense.”

extraction.body: Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions. At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055. The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company. It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US. It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development. Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.

At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported.

Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing.
Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards.
President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million.
Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela.
Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055.
The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission.
Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong.

For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges.
There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company.
It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering.

The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029.
Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years.
Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US.
It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation.
But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public.
Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters.
Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development.
Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.
extraction.headline: Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing
extraction.description: From conscious AI and ‘catastrophic’ risk to unusual corporate structures and executive perks.

AI delivers zero financial payoff outside the technology sector. Magnificent Seven show rising revenue per worker and margins. These headlines repeat or cite Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok’s conclusion that his measures show no AI payoff outside tech. The pattern reflects one analyst’s interpretation and its coverage, not independent proof that every non-tech company has had zero return. Five news headlines report or paraphrase a conclusion from Slok’s October Daily Spark note, and Apollo’s own page is the source. The note compares revenue per worker, profit margins and productivity measures for the S&P 493 and Mag 7. This grouping captures coverage of one analyst’s interpretation; the headlines do not establish causation or that every non-tech company has had no return. Reviewed by Codex validator (AI) · 26 Oct 2026 Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, argued in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026 that artificial intelligence has delivered "zero financial payoff" to corporate America outside of tech. Slok’s charts split the S&P 500 into the seven-company "Mag 7" group and the remaining 493 constituents called the "S&P 493," and he said "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493." Slok also said "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493," and he framed the lack of broad gains as a problem for the economics of AI spending. Apollo’s note added that "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," while its productivity chart tracked output per hour and total factor productivity from January 1985. The Daily Spark note concluded that the AI story would be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and that there was "no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector." TechCrunch said Slok focused on the S&P 493, finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat and that there was no evidence that AI was improving productivity. Slok argued that it would be tough for corporate America to "turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," and he wrote that "AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness." Startup Fortune reported that Slok’s note landed as a separate AI-financing scare unfolded, after Chamath Palihapitiya flagged that the yield on $1.25 billion of CoreWeave bonds due in 2032 briefly touched 15%. Startup Fortune said CoreWeave shares fell more than 15% on October 14, and it said yields on its unsecured bonds subsequently remained near 15% as Oracle and other AI infrastructure stocks sold off. Apollo’s Daily Spark note said mainstream corporate America was pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins. TECHi said Apollo’s chief economist argued in an October 24 research note that broad US companies still show little measurable financial payoff from artificial intelligence, and it framed the warning as about the economics of AI buyers. TECHi reported that from September 24 to the October 23 close, its NVDA forecast data showed the same-period FY2027 EPS estimate edging from $9.3071 to $9.3124 while the share price fell from $224.58 to $210.96. TECHi calculated that the implied price-to-estimated-earnings ratio slipped from about 24.13 to 22.65, and it said the compression, rather than a documented collapse in Nvidia profit expectations, was the starting point for its forecast. Nvidia’s August 26 results provided a counterweight, because Nvidia reported revenue for the quarter ended July 26 of $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, with Data Center revenue at $89.0 billion, up 117%. Nvidia guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, and a 74.0% gross margin, plus or minus 0.5 percentage point, while TECHi noted that Apollo’s S&P 493 comparison did not establish that enterprises buying AI services are themselves earning attractive returns. whether the story is macro payoff gap or Nvidia valuation Techi reframes the Apollo note around Nvidia valuation timing, while others stress economy-wide profit and productivity gaps. passages: What: A Daily Spark note arguing that AI has delivered "zero financial payoff" to US companies outside tech.

Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen for the Magnificent 7 but stayed flat for the S&P 493, productivity growth shows no AI effect, the top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of model serving and inference spend in Ramp data, and 80.4% of the top 1% of AI spenders are venture-backed.
The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015.
These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note.
Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data.
The October 24 note is the latest in a run of Daily Spark entries in which Slok has tracked the gap between AI investment and returns outside technology.
The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side.
Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets.
When their margins are flat, marketing budgets come under the same scrutiny Slok describes for token spending.
Many of the AI features built into ad platforms - automated bidding, generated creative, agentic AI tools that run campaigns - are sold to these buyers on the promise of efficiency.
The charts show correlation in time, not cause.

Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI.
The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits.
The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data.
The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist.
Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins?
A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are.
This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it.
For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies.
Ray Dalio said earlier this month that his bubble indicator puts AI level with 1929 and 2000 .

Analyst Ed Zitron argued in August, citing UBS estimates, that OpenAI and Anthropic could make up more than 48% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027 - a concentration risk that echoes the Ramp data in Slok's note.
When: Published October 24, 2026, following related Apollo notes on June 30 and August 9, 2026.
Where: The United States, with the analysis centred on S&P 500 companies and Ramp's business spending data.

extraction.body: Top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of AI inference spend in Ramp data cited by Apollo. Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins? Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. Its conclusion is blunt. "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok wrote. A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are. This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it. For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies. The note's central device is a division of the S&P 500 into two unequal parts. The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side. The remaining 493 constituents, which Slok calls the "S&P 493," sit on the other. Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets. "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493," Slok wrote. "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493." The first chart, titled "Revenue per worker moving up for tech but not for the rest of the economy," tracks inflation-adjusted revenue per employee, in thousands of dollars at 2019 fourth-quarter prices, from the first quarter of 2019. On PPC Land's reading of the chart, the Magnificent 7 started the period at roughly $695,000 per employee, fell to a trough of about $565,000 around the turn of 2022 and 2023, and then climbed steadily to roughly $780,000 in the most recent quarter shown, with the sharpest jump at the very end of the series. The S&P 493 line moves within a much narrower band: about $495,000 in early 2019, a low near $465,000 in 2021, a peak around $548,000 in late 2022, and roughly $527,000 in the latest reading. Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data. The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015. Reading from Apollo's chart, the Magnificent 7 profit margin rose from around 11% in 2015 to about 22% in early 2022, dropped to roughly 14% in 2023, and has since risen to close to 30%. The S&P 493 margin stood at about 8.5% in 2015, dipped to around 6.5% during the pandemic, peaked near 11.7% in early 2022, and has hovered between 9% and 10% since 2023. These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note. The shape matters as much as the level. For the largest technology companies, both revenue per worker and margins have accelerated in the period that coincides with heavy AI investment. For the rest of the index, the lines are close to flat over the same years. The third chart widens the lens from corporate accounts to the whole economy. Titled "No signs of AI boosting productivity growth," it plots two measures of year-over-year productivity growth from January 1985: labour output per hour from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and total factor productivity, or TFP. The TFP series is the utilisation-adjusted measure maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald, 2014), which corrects for cyclical swings in how intensively capital and labour are used. On the chart, output per hour spiked to around 7% during the 2020 pandemic, when lower-productivity jobs disappeared first, and then dipped below zero. In the most recent readings, output per hour growth runs at roughly 2% to 2.5%, while TFP growth has slipped to around zero and appears slightly negative at the end of the series. Neither line shows the kind of sustained step up that would mark a technology-driven productivity boom. "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," Slok wrote. TFP is the measure economists usually watch for the effect of a general-purpose technology, because it captures output growth that cannot be explained by adding more workers or more machines. A flat or falling TFP line, set against record AI capital spending, is the core of Slok's case. The note goes further than describing flat lines. It makes a claim about corporate behaviour. "With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Slok wrote. Token spending refers to the fees companies pay to AI providers for processing text and data, measured in tokens . The note does not quantify the pullback it describes, and it does not cite a survey for the shift in attitude. Other recent data points in the same direction. A KPMG survey of 2,145 senior leaders found that 49% had scaled back, narrowed, delayed or paused AI agent rollouts after costs began to outweigh value, while only 7% reported established return on investment. An August TransUnion study found that 53% of enterprise marketers reported meaningful ROI from AI, with most gains so far coming from time savings rather than revenue. Slok also draws a line between who buys AI and who does not. "VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it," he wrote. "As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited." The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data. The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist. It shows the share of spending in each category that comes from the top 10% of firms versus the bottom 90%. The note does not explain how the top 10% is defined - whether by total spend, category spend or company size - or what period the table covers. The most AI-specific categories are the most concentrated. Spending on model serving and inference cost - the computing bill for running AI models once they are trained - is almost entirely in the hands of the top tenth of firms, at 99.5%. Neoclouds, the specialist GPU cloud providers that rent computing capacity outside the large hyperscaler platforms, draw 99% of their spend from the same group. Direct payments to OpenAI and Anthropic, the two leading model developers, are 95.6% concentrated. Yet concentration is not unique to AI. Paid advertising, at 91.9%, is about as concentrated as conventional software-as-a-service spending, at 91.8%. CRM software is the least concentrated category in the table, with the bottom 90% of firms accounting for 15.8% of spend. The comparison suggests that the top tenth of firms dominates business spending in general, and AI spending more so. The chart's title links that finding to a wider debate about circular financing in the AI industry, in which investors fund AI start-ups that then spend much of that money on cloud computing and model access from companies tied to the same investors. Slok's note does not spell out the mechanism. Its data shows only that the heaviest token buyers are overwhelmingly funded by venture capital, while the typical business buying AI is not. The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits. That is not the same as demand from mainstream companies paying for AI out of improved margins - the outcome the S&P 493 charts say has not yet arrived. Slok frames the open question as whether falling prices change the picture. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," he wrote. "That may be harder than it sounds." His reasoning is qualitative. "AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment," Slok wrote. "Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask." He added that "AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins." The note closes on a single sentence that summarises the argument: "The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector." The charts show correlation in time, not cause. Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI. The flat S&P 493 lines do not prove AI has no effect at company level; gains in some firms or sectors could be offset by losses elsewhere, or could take longer to show up in aggregate figures. The note's claim that mainstream companies are "pulling back" on token spending is not backed by a specific data series in the note itself. The Ramp figures also come with limits. They reflect businesses that use Ramp's cards and expense software, not the economy as a whole, and they are not the same population as the S&P 493 in the first two charts. The note does not state the sample size, time period or definition of the top 10%. The October 24 note is the latest in a run of Daily Spark entries in which Slok has tracked the gap between AI investment and returns outside technology. On June 30, 2026, he argued in a note titled "AI: The ROI Runway Could Be Long Outside the Tech Sector" that sectors such as health care, banking and energy face longer timelines to productivity gains than software companies, and that AI company valuations depend on margins eventually rising in the S&P 493. On August 9, 2026, in "The Buyers of AI Are Still Waiting for the Payoff" , he broke S&P 493 margins down by sector and argued that the capital spending boom was showing up in the margins of AI sellers, not buyers. The October note adds the revenue-per-worker comparison, the productivity series and the Ramp spending data. The advertising market sits on both sides of Slok's divide. Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft are among the Magnificent 7 and earn much of their revenue from advertising, which in turn funds their AI infrastructure. Alphabet guided to $175 billion to $185 billion in 2026 capital expenditure when it reported fourth-quarter 2025 results in February. Microsoft said in April that its AI business had passed a $37 billion annual revenue run rate , up 123% year over year, with quarterly capital spending of $31.9 billion. Google said this month that Gemini 4 Argon processed almost 25 trillion tokens in its first 72 hours , and that the company remains capacity constrained. The advertisers on the other side of those platforms are, for the most part, S&P 493 companies and smaller businesses. When their margins are flat, marketing budgets come under the same scrutiny Slok describes for token spending.
