Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. Its conclusion is blunt. "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok wrote.

A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are. This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it. For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies.

The note's central device is a division of the S&P 500 into two unequal parts. The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side. The remaining 493 constituents, which Slok calls the "S&P 493," sit on the other. Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets.
"Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493," Slok wrote. "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493."

The first chart, titled "Revenue per worker moving up for tech but not for the rest of the economy," tracks inflation-adjusted revenue per employee, in thousands of dollars at 2019 fourth-quarter prices, from the first quarter of 2019. On PPC Land's reading of the chart, the Magnificent 7 started the period at roughly $695,000 per employee, fell to a trough of about $565,000 around the turn of 2022 and 2023, and then climbed steadily to roughly $780,000 in the most recent quarter shown, with the sharpest jump at the very end of the series. The S&P 493 line moves within a much narrower band: about $495,000 in early 2019, a low near $465,000 in 2021, a peak around $548,000 in late 2022, and roughly $527,000 in the latest reading. Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data.

The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015. Reading from Apollo's chart, the Magnificent 7 profit margin rose from around 11% in 2015 to about 22% in early 2022, dropped to roughly 14% in 2023, and has since risen to close to 30%. The S&P 493 margin stood at about 8.5% in 2015, dipped to around 6.5% during the pandemic, peaked near 11.7% in early 2022, and has hovered between 9% and 10% since 2023. These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note.

The shape matters as much as the level. For the largest technology companies, both revenue per worker and margins have accelerated in the period that coincides with heavy AI investment. For the rest of the index, the lines are close to flat over the same years.

The third chart widens the lens from corporate accounts to the whole economy. Titled "No signs of AI boosting productivity growth," it plots two measures of year-over-year productivity growth from January 1985: labour output per hour from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and total factor productivity, or TFP. The TFP series is the utilisation-adjusted measure maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald, 2014), which corrects for cyclical swings in how intensively capital and labour are used.

On the chart, output per hour spiked to around 7% during the 2020 pandemic, when lower-productivity jobs disappeared first, and then dipped below zero. In the most recent readings, output per hour growth runs at roughly 2% to 2.5%, while TFP growth has slipped to around zero and appears slightly negative at the end of the series. Neither line shows the kind of sustained step up that would mark a technology-driven productivity boom. "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," Slok wrote.

TFP is the measure economists usually watch for the effect of a general-purpose technology, because it captures output growth that cannot be explained by adding more workers or more machines. A flat or falling TFP line, set against record AI capital spending, is the core of Slok's case.

The note goes further than describing flat lines. It makes a claim about corporate behaviour. "With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Slok wrote.

Token spending refers to the fees companies pay to AI providers for processing text and data, measured in tokens . The note does not quantify the pullback it describes, and it does not cite a survey for the shift in attitude. Other recent data points in the same direction. A KPMG survey of 2,145 senior leaders found that 49% had scaled back, narrowed, delayed or paused AI agent rollouts after costs began to outweigh value, while only 7% reported established return on investment. An August TransUnion study found that 53% of enterprise marketers reported meaningful ROI from AI, with most gains so far coming from time savings rather than revenue.

Slok also draws a line between who buys AI and who does not. "VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it," he wrote. "As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited."

The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data. The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist. It shows the share of spending in each category that comes from the top 10% of firms versus the bottom 90%. The note does not explain how the top 10% is defined - whether by total spend, category spend or company size - or what period the table covers.

The most AI-specific categories are the most concentrated. Spending on model serving and inference cost - the computing bill for running AI models once they are trained - is almost entirely in the hands of the top tenth of firms, at 99.5%. Neoclouds, the specialist GPU cloud providers that rent computing capacity outside the large hyperscaler platforms, draw 99% of their spend from the same group. Direct payments to OpenAI and Anthropic, the two leading model developers, are 95.6% concentrated.

Yet concentration is not unique to AI. Paid advertising, at 91.9%, is about as concentrated as conventional software-as-a-service spending, at 91.8%. CRM software is the least concentrated category in the table, with the bottom 90% of firms accounting for 15.8% of spend. The comparison suggests that the top tenth of firms dominates business spending in general, and AI spending more so.

The chart's title links that finding to a wider debate about circular financing in the AI industry, in which investors fund AI start-ups that then spend much of that money on cloud computing and model access from companies tied to the same investors. Slok's note does not spell out the mechanism. Its data shows only that the heaviest token buyers are overwhelmingly funded by venture capital, while the typical business buying AI is not.

The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits. That is not the same as demand from mainstream companies paying for AI out of improved margins - the outcome the S&P 493 charts say has not yet arrived.

Slok frames the open question as whether falling prices change the picture. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," he wrote. "That may be harder than it sounds."

His reasoning is qualitative. "AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment," Slok wrote. "Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask." He added that "AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins."

The note closes on a single sentence that summarises the argument: "The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector."

The charts show correlation in time, not cause. Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI. The flat S&P 493 lines do not prove AI has no effect at company level; gains in some firms or sectors could be offset by losses elsewhere, or could take longer to show up in aggregate figures. The note's claim that mainstream companies are "pulling back" on token spending is not backed by a specific data series in the note itself.

The Ramp figures also come with limits. They reflect businesses that use Ramp's cards and expense software, not the economy as a whole, and they are not the same population as the S&P 493 in the first two charts. The note does not state the sample size, time period or definition of the top 10%.

The October 24 note is the latest in a run of Daily Spark entries in which Slok has tracked the gap between AI investment and returns outside technology. On June 30, 2026, he argued in a note titled "AI: The ROI Runway Could Be Long Outside the Tech Sector" that sectors such as health care, banking and energy face longer timelines to productivity gains than software companies, and that AI company valuations depend on margins eventually rising in the S&P 493. On August 9, 2026, in "The Buyers of AI Are Still Waiting for the Payoff" , he broke S&P 493 margins down by sector and argued that the capital spending boom was showing up in the margins of AI sellers, not buyers. The October note adds the revenue-per-worker comparison, the productivity series and the Ramp spending data.

The advertising market sits on both sides of Slok's divide. Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft are among the Magnificent 7 and earn much of their revenue from advertising, which in turn funds their AI infrastructure. Alphabet guided to $175 billion to $185 billion in 2026 capital expenditure when it reported fourth-quarter 2025 results in February. Microsoft said in April that its AI business had passed a $37 billion annual revenue run rate , up 123% year over year, with quarterly capital spending of $31.9 billion. Google said this month that Gemini 4 Argon processed almost 25 trillion tokens in its first 72 hours , and that the company remains capacity constrained.

The advertisers on the other side of those platforms are, for the most part, S&P 493 companies and smaller businesses. When their margins are flat, marketing budgets come under the same scrutiny Slok describes for token spending. Many of the AI features built into ad platforms - automated bidding, generated creative, agentic AI tools that run campaigns - are sold to these buyers on the promise of efficiency. Whether that efficiency reaches their own profit and loss accounts is the question Apollo's charts say has not yet been answered.

Measurement on the buyer side remains thin. A Basis survey published on October 19 found that only 6.5% of 184 organisations measured AI returns against defined benchmarks, even as 88.6% paid for premium AI tools. Survey-based studies tend to show more optimism than the aggregate data: Meta's YouGov survey of 3,983 Asia-Pacific small business owners found 76% reporting a productivity gain, though those were owners' own assessments rather than measured outcomes. Google's AI and Economy ATLAS report found AI usage in 68% of occupations but a median of 21% of tasks within those jobs.

The broader market debate has sharpened too. Ray Dalio said earlier this month that his bubble indicator puts AI level with 1929 and 2000 . Analyst Ed Zitron argued in August, citing UBS estimates, that OpenAI and Anthropic could make up more than 48% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027 - a concentration risk that echoes the Ramp data in Slok's note. Apollo's chief economist adds a different kind of evidence to that debate: not valuations or financing, but the plain accounts of the companies that are supposed to be AI's customers.

AI delivers zero financial payoff outside the technology sector. Magnificent Seven show rising revenue per worker and margins. These headlines repeat or cite Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok’s conclusion that his measures show no AI payoff outside tech. The pattern reflects one analyst’s interpretation and its coverage, not independent proof that every non-tech company has had zero return. Five news headlines report or paraphrase a conclusion from Slok’s October Daily Spark note, and Apollo’s own page is the source. The note compares revenue per worker, profit margins and productivity measures for the S&P 493 and Mag 7. This grouping captures coverage of one analyst’s interpretation; the headlines do not establish causation or that every non-tech company has had no return. Reviewed by Codex validator (AI) · 26 Oct 2026 Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, argued in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026 that artificial intelligence has delivered "zero financial payoff" to corporate America outside of tech. Slok’s charts split the S&P 500 into the seven-company "Mag 7" group and the remaining 493 constituents called the "S&P 493," and he said "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493." Slok also said "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493," and he framed the lack of broad gains as a problem for the economics of AI spending. Apollo’s note added that "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," while its productivity chart tracked output per hour and total factor productivity from January 1985. The Daily Spark note concluded that the AI story would be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and that there was "no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector." TechCrunch said Slok focused on the S&P 493, finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat and that there was no evidence that AI was improving productivity. Slok argued that it would be tough for corporate America to "turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," and he wrote that "AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness." Startup Fortune reported that Slok’s note landed as a separate AI-financing scare unfolded, after Chamath Palihapitiya flagged that the yield on $1.25 billion of CoreWeave bonds due in 2032 briefly touched 15%. Startup Fortune said CoreWeave shares fell more than 15% on October 14, and it said yields on its unsecured bonds subsequently remained near 15% as Oracle and other AI infrastructure stocks sold off. Apollo’s Daily Spark note said mainstream corporate America was pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins. TECHi said Apollo’s chief economist argued in an October 24 research note that broad US companies still show little measurable financial payoff from artificial intelligence, and it framed the warning as about the economics of AI buyers. TECHi reported that from September 24 to the October 23 close, its NVDA forecast data showed the same-period FY2027 EPS estimate edging from $9.3071 to $9.3124 while the share price fell from $224.58 to $210.96. TECHi calculated that the implied price-to-estimated-earnings ratio slipped from about 24.13 to 22.65, and it said the compression, rather than a documented collapse in Nvidia profit expectations, was the starting point for its forecast. Nvidia’s August 26 results provided a counterweight, because Nvidia reported revenue for the quarter ended July 26 of $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, with Data Center revenue at $89.0 billion, up 117%. Nvidia guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, and a 74.0% gross margin, plus or minus 0.5 percentage point, while TECHi noted that Apollo’s S&P 493 comparison did not establish that enterprises buying AI services are themselves earning attractive returns. whether the story is macro payoff gap or Nvidia valuation Techi reframes the Apollo note around Nvidia valuation timing, while others stress economy-wide profit and productivity gaps. extraction.body: Top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of AI inference spend in Ramp data cited by Apollo. Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins? Artificial intelligence has delivered no measurable financial return to US companies outside the technology sector, according to Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a Daily Spark note published on October 24, 2026. The note, titled No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector , sets five charts side by side: revenue per worker, profit margins, productivity growth, the concentration of AI spending and the financial backing of the heaviest AI buyers. Its conclusion is blunt. "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech," Slok wrote. A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are. This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it. For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies. The note's central device is a division of the S&P 500 into two unequal parts. The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side. The remaining 493 constituents, which Slok calls the "S&P 493," sit on the other. Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets. "Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493," Slok wrote. "Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493." The first chart, titled "Revenue per worker moving up for tech but not for the rest of the economy," tracks inflation-adjusted revenue per employee, in thousands of dollars at 2019 fourth-quarter prices, from the first quarter of 2019. On PPC Land's reading of the chart, the Magnificent 7 started the period at roughly $695,000 per employee, fell to a trough of about $565,000 around the turn of 2022 and 2023, and then climbed steadily to roughly $780,000 in the most recent quarter shown, with the sharpest jump at the very end of the series. The S&P 493 line moves within a much narrower band: about $495,000 in early 2019, a low near $465,000 in 2021, a peak around $548,000 in late 2022, and roughly $527,000 in the latest reading. Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data. The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015. Reading from Apollo's chart, the Magnificent 7 profit margin rose from around 11% in 2015 to about 22% in early 2022, dropped to roughly 14% in 2023, and has since risen to close to 30%. The S&P 493 margin stood at about 8.5% in 2015, dipped to around 6.5% during the pandemic, peaked near 11.7% in early 2022, and has hovered between 9% and 10% since 2023. These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note. The shape matters as much as the level. For the largest technology companies, both revenue per worker and margins have accelerated in the period that coincides with heavy AI investment. For the rest of the index, the lines are close to flat over the same years. The third chart widens the lens from corporate accounts to the whole economy. Titled "No signs of AI boosting productivity growth," it plots two measures of year-over-year productivity growth from January 1985: labour output per hour from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, and total factor productivity, or TFP. The TFP series is the utilisation-adjusted measure maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Fernald, 2014), which corrects for cyclical swings in how intensively capital and labour are used. On the chart, output per hour spiked to around 7% during the 2020 pandemic, when lower-productivity jobs disappeared first, and then dipped below zero. In the most recent readings, output per hour growth runs at roughly 2% to 2.5%, while TFP growth has slipped to around zero and appears slightly negative at the end of the series. Neither line shows the kind of sustained step up that would mark a technology-driven productivity boom. "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth," Slok wrote. TFP is the measure economists usually watch for the effect of a general-purpose technology, because it captures output growth that cannot be explained by adding more workers or more machines. A flat or falling TFP line, set against record AI capital spending, is the core of Slok's case. The note goes further than describing flat lines. It makes a claim about corporate behaviour. "With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins," Slok wrote. Token spending refers to the fees companies pay to AI providers for processing text and data, measured in tokens . The note does not quantify the pullback it describes, and it does not cite a survey for the shift in attitude. Other recent data points in the same direction. A KPMG survey of 2,145 senior leaders found that 49% had scaled back, narrowed, delayed or paused AI agent rollouts after costs began to outweigh value, while only 7% reported established return on investment. An August TransUnion study found that 53% of enterprise marketers reported meaningful ROI from AI, with most gains so far coming from time savings rather than revenue. Slok also draws a line between who buys AI and who does not. "VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it," he wrote. "As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited." The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data. The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist. It shows the share of spending in each category that comes from the top 10% of firms versus the bottom 90%. The note does not explain how the top 10% is defined - whether by total spend, category spend or company size - or what period the table covers. The most AI-specific categories are the most concentrated. Spending on model serving and inference cost - the computing bill for running AI models once they are trained - is almost entirely in the hands of the top tenth of firms, at 99.5%. Neoclouds, the specialist GPU cloud providers that rent computing capacity outside the large hyperscaler platforms, draw 99% of their spend from the same group. Direct payments to OpenAI and Anthropic, the two leading model developers, are 95.6% concentrated. Yet concentration is not unique to AI. Paid advertising, at 91.9%, is about as concentrated as conventional software-as-a-service spending, at 91.8%. CRM software is the least concentrated category in the table, with the bottom 90% of firms accounting for 15.8% of spend. The comparison suggests that the top tenth of firms dominates business spending in general, and AI spending more so. The chart's title links that finding to a wider debate about circular financing in the AI industry, in which investors fund AI start-ups that then spend much of that money on cloud computing and model access from companies tied to the same investors. Slok's note does not spell out the mechanism. Its data shows only that the heaviest token buyers are overwhelmingly funded by venture capital, while the typical business buying AI is not. The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits. That is not the same as demand from mainstream companies paying for AI out of improved margins - the outcome the S&P 493 charts say has not yet arrived. Slok frames the open question as whether falling prices change the picture. "The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins," he wrote. "That may be harder than it sounds." His reasoning is qualitative. "AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment," Slok wrote. "Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask." He added that "AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins." The note closes on a single sentence that summarises the argument: "The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector." The charts show correlation in time, not cause. Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI. The flat S&P 493 lines do not prove AI has no effect at company level; gains in some firms or sectors could be offset by losses elsewhere, or could take longer to show up in aggregate figures. The note's claim that mainstream companies are "pulling back" on token spending is not backed by a specific data series in the note itself. The Ramp figures also come with limits. They reflect businesses that use Ramp's cards and expense software, not the economy as a whole, and they are not the same population as the S&P 493 in the first two charts. The note does not state the sample size, time period or definition of the top 10%. The October 24 note is the latest in a run of Daily Spark entries in which Slok has tracked the gap between AI investment and returns outside technology. On June 30, 2026, he argued in a note titled "AI: The ROI Runway Could Be Long Outside the Tech Sector" that sectors such as health care, banking and energy face longer timelines to productivity gains than software companies, and that AI company valuations depend on margins eventually rising in the S&P 493. On August 9, 2026, in "The Buyers of AI Are Still Waiting for the Payoff" , he broke S&P 493 margins down by sector and argued that the capital spending boom was showing up in the margins of AI sellers, not buyers. The October note adds the revenue-per-worker comparison, the productivity series and the Ramp spending data. The advertising market sits on both sides of Slok's divide. Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft are among the Magnificent 7 and earn much of their revenue from advertising, which in turn funds their AI infrastructure. Alphabet guided to $175 billion to $185 billion in 2026 capital expenditure when it reported fourth-quarter 2025 results in February. Microsoft said in April that its AI business had passed a $37 billion annual revenue run rate , up 123% year over year, with quarterly capital spending of $31.9 billion. Google said this month that Gemini 4 Argon processed almost 25 trillion tokens in its first 72 hours , and that the company remains capacity constrained. The advertisers on the other side of those platforms are, for the most part, S&P 493 companies and smaller businesses. When their margins are flat, marketing budgets come under the same scrutiny Slok describes for token spending. Many of the AI features built into ad platforms - automated bidding, generated creative, agentic AI tools that run campaigns - are sold to these buyers on the promise of efficiency. Whether that efficiency reaches their own profit and loss accounts is the question Apollo's charts say has not yet been answered. Measurement on the buyer side remains thin. A Basis survey published on October 19 found that only 6.5% of 184 organisations measured AI returns against defined benchmarks, even as 88.6% paid for premium AI tools. Survey-based studies tend to show more optimism than the aggregate data: Meta's YouGov survey of 3,983 Asia-Pacific small business owners found 76% reporting a productivity gain, though those were owners' own assessments rather than measured outcomes. Google's AI and Economy ATLAS report found AI usage in 68% of occupations but a median of 21% of tasks within those jobs. The broader market debate has sharpened too. Ray Dalio said earlier this month that his bubble indicator puts AI level with 1929 and 2000 . Analyst Ed Zitron argued in August, citing UBS estimates, that OpenAI and Anthropic could make up more than 48% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027 - a concentration risk that echoes the Ramp data in Slok's note. Apollo's chief economist adds a different kind of evidence to that debate: not valuations or financing, but the plain accounts of the companies that are supposed to be AI's customers. Who: Torsten Slok, partner and chief economist at Apollo Global Management, using data from Bloomberg, Macrobond, the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics and Ramp, including Ramp chief economist Ara Kharazian. What: A Daily Spark note arguing that AI has delivered "zero financial payoff" to US companies outside tech. Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen for the Magnificent 7 but stayed flat for the S&P 493, productivity growth shows no AI effect, the top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of model serving and inference spend in Ramp data, and 80.4% of the top 1% of AI spenders are venture-backed. When: Published October 24, 2026, following related Apollo notes on June 30 and August 9, 2026. Where: The United States, with the analysis centred on S&P 500 companies and Ramp's business spending data. Why: The returns on AI investment depend on mainstream companies turning AI into higher revenue and margins. Slok argues that this has not happened yet, and that while AI spending stays concentrated among a small group of mostly venture-backed firms, its effect on the wider economy will remain limited. For advertisers and the platforms that sell to them, the question is whether AI-driven efficiency will reach buyers' own profit and loss accounts. Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen for the Magnificent 7 but stayed flat for the S&P 493, productivity growth shows no AI effect, the top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of model serving and inference spend in Ramp data, and 80.4% of the top 1% of AI spenders are venture-backed.
The second chart, "No signs of profit margins going up outside the tech sector," goes back further, to the first quarter of 2015.
These figures are approximations taken from the plotted lines; Apollo did not publish the underlying values in the note.
Apollo credits Bloomberg, Macrobond and its own chief economist's office for the data.
The October 24 note is the latest in a run of Daily Spark entries in which Slok has tracked the gap between AI investment and returns outside technology.
The "Mag 7" - the seven largest US technology companies, usually counted as Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla - sit on one side.
Apollo's note does not list the seven names; the grouping is the conventional one used across financial markets.
When their margins are flat, marketing budgets come under the same scrutiny Slok describes for token spending.
Many of the AI features built into ad platforms - automated bidding, generated creative, agentic AI tools that run campaigns - are sold to these buyers on the promise of efficiency.
The charts show correlation in time, not cause.

Rising Magnificent 7 margins could reflect AI-driven sales of cloud capacity, chips and advertising, but they also reflect cost cutting, layoffs, pricing power and cyclical factors that predate the current wave of generative AI.
The implication is that a large share of measured AI demand comes from companies whose spending depends on fresh capital rather than on operating profits.
The fourth and fifth charts carry that argument with spending data from Ramp, the corporate card and expense management company, which publishes the Ramp AI Index based on business transaction data.
The fourth chart, titled "AI spending is extremely concentrated in a small number of firms," is a table credited to Ara Kharazian, chief economist at Ramp, and Apollo's chief economist.
Can the rest of corporate America turn cheap tokens into higher margins?
A top economist at the investment firm Apollo looked at whether ordinary big US companies, not the tech giants, are making more money because of AI, and found no sign that they are.
This matters because the huge sums being poured into AI chips, data centres and models only make sense if the thousands of companies buying AI eventually earn more from it.
For now, the data shows the gains staying with the biggest tech firms, while spending on AI services sits with a small group of mostly venture-backed companies.
Ray Dalio said earlier this month that his bubble indicator puts AI level with 1929 and 2000 .

Analyst Ed Zitron argued in August, citing UBS estimates, that OpenAI and Anthropic could make up more than 48% of Google Cloud revenue in 2027 - a concentration risk that echoes the Ramp data in Slok's note.

extraction.body: In recent days, President Trump has publicly criticized and made demands of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy while declining to call longtime U.S. antagonist Russian President Vladimir Putin a dictator. Vice President Vance told European leaders at the Munich Security Conference last week that the real threat is not coming from Russia but from within their own countries. Foreign policy experts have told NPR that Trump’s alienation of U.S. allies in Europe is radical and that in the long run, the move won’t benefit the U.S . But what the president and his administration are actually doing is recognizing that post-World War II alliances, including NATO, are outdated, said Victoria Coates, a deputy national security adviser in the first Trump administration. “A war between Germany and France is not our number one national security problem,” Coates said. “[Trump] is looking at the world and saying, OK, there is a war in Europe, but this is the Ukraine-Russia war. It’s been going on for three years. There’s been no diplomacy to proceed to a conclusion of the war.” In an interview with Morning Edition ‘s Steve Inskeep, she said she wonders if it isn’t NATO allies falling short of expectations with the U.S. instead of the other way around. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Steve Inskeep: There has been this world order, particularly in Europe, ever since World War II. The U.S. leads its European allies when necessary against Russia. That was the form in the early years of the war in Ukraine. Do you believe President Trump has upended the world order or switched sides? Victoria Coates: No, I don’t think so. What President Trump is doing is acknowledging that 80 years on the reason that some of the structures were put in place after World War II, which was actually largely to prevent another inter-Europe war, are no longer in place. A war between Germany and France is not our number one national security problem. He is looking at the world and saying, OK, there is a war in Europe, but this is the Ukraine-Russia war. It’s been going on for three years. There’s been no diplomacy to proceed to a conclusion of the war. We’ve had a lot of maximalist rhetoric. We’ve had a lot of sort of displays of support for Ukraine and declarations that Ukraine is a democracy and this is an existential threat to the West. But we’ve also had hundreds of thousands dead and a lot of destruction. He is trying to change that paradigm also. Inskeep: You mentioned that a lot of the structures were put together to avoid an inter-European war. I think that’s correct. But NATO specifically was an alliance against the expansion of what was then the Soviet Union, what is now Russia, which does seem to literally be the problem right now. It’s not just a war between Ukraine and Russia. Russia invaded Ukraine. Coates: Well, it is. We’ll be welcoming the prime minister, Prime Minister Keir Starmer to Washington this week. We’ve already had President Emmanuel Macron. We will have President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. So that hardly looks to me like a Washington that is rejecting Europe. At the NATO summit last year here in Washington, the NATO countries collectively agreed on a series of war plans that we would execute in the event of an additional kinetic action by an enemy. And those war plans require NATO to be investing collectively at 3.5%, which is where the United States is. The UK announced this week with great fanfare they were going to try to get to 2.5%. That math just doesn’t add up. If three years into a war in Europe, you don’t have the major European economies getting to the level of defense expenditure they need to get to in order to sustain what NATO has agreed to, then I have to wonder if it’s not the United States that’s turning its back on NATO, it’s these other NATO members who aren’t investing. Inskeep: I want to ask about the concessions that the United States has offered to Russia’s Vladimir Putin as the president tries to end this war. Michael McFaul, a critic of Trump and former U.S. ambassador there, notes that the U.S. has already publicly said that Ukraine has to give up territory to Russia, that Ukraine can’t join NATO, that the U.S. won’t send peacekeeping troops, that the U.S. will reduce the number of soldiers in Europe, and that Zelensky, the Ukrainian president, has to hold elections before there are peace negotiations and other concessions. And in McFaul’s view, the United States hasn’t demanded anything of Russia. Is that how you see it? Coates: Not at all. I mean, I think what has been offered to Russia has largely been rhetorical. None of this has cost the president anything. I would add the United Nations General Assembly resolution to that list, because off the top of my head, I can’t think of anything more useless than one of those resolutions. Inskeep: You think you think it doesn’t matter that this resolution with the wording that few people other than the United States agreed with passed . Go on. Coates: Yeah, this has largely been rhetorical and what we’ve offered Ukraine, on the other hand, which will be signed at the White House on Friday, is a material economic deal that will invest the United States in Ukraine and Ukraine’s security. So I would see that as a much more serious offer than, you know, rhetoric. Inskeep: Do you think that deal would commit the United States to defend Ukraine against Russia? Coates: I think it gives the United States a vested interest in Ukraine, which is something we have not had before. So we will see what that results. Editor’s note: Zelenskyy is expected to meet with Trump in Washington on Friday to sign an deal to provide critical raw materials used for items like electric vehicle batteries and cancer drugs. The deal could lead to some security guarantees for Ukraine from the U.S. Known for interviews with presidents and Congressional leaders, Inskeep has a passion for stories of the less famous: Pennsylvania truck drivers, Kentucky coal miners, U.S.-Mexico border detainees, Yemeni refugees, California firefighters, American soldiers. Since joining Morning Edition in 2004, Inskeep has hosted the program from New Orleans, Detroit, San Francisco, Cairo, and Beijing; investigated Iraqi police in Baghdad; and received a Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award for "The Price of African Oil," on conflict in Nigeria. He has taken listeners on a 2,428-mile journey along the U.S.-Mexico border, and 2,700 miles across North Africa. He is a repeat visitor to Iran and has covered wars in Syria and Yemen. Inskeep says Morning Edition works to "slow down the news," making sense of fast-moving events. A prime example came during the 2008 Presidential campaign, when Inskeep and NPR's Michele Norris conducted "The York Project," groundbreaking conversations about race, which received an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University Silver Baton for excellence. Inskeep was hired by NPR in 1996. His first full-time assignment was the 1996 presidential primary in New Hampshire. He went on to cover the Pentagon, the Senate, and the 2000 presidential campaign of George W. Bush. After the Sept. 11 attacks, he covered the war in Afghanistan, turmoil in Pakistan, and the war in Iraq. In 2003, he received a National Headliner Award for investigating a military raid gone wrong in Afghanistan. He has twice been part of NPR News teams awarded the Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University Silver Baton for coverage of Iraq. On days of bad news, Inskeep is inspired by the Langston Hughes book, Laughing to Keep From Crying . Of hosting Morning Edition during the 2008 financial crisis and Great Recession, he told Nuvo magazine when "the whole world seemed to be falling apart, it was especially important for me ... to be amused, even if I had to be cynically amused, about the things that were going wrong. Laughter is a sign that you're not defeated." Inskeep is the author of Instant City: Life and Death in Karachi , a 2011 book on one of the world's great megacities. He is also author of Jacksonland , a history of President Andrew Jackson's long-running conflict with John Ross, a Cherokee chief who resisted the removal of Indians from the eastern United States in the 1830s. He has been a guest on numerous TV programs including ABC's This Week, NBC's Meet the Press, MSNBC's Andrea Mitchell Reports, CNN's Inside Politics and the PBS Newshour . He has written for publications including The New York Times , Washington Post , the Wall Street Journal , and The Atlantic .

extraction.body: The Justice Department has charged a suspected Iranian operative for allegedly plotting to assassinate former Trump national security adviser John Bolton. Shahram Poursafi offered to pay contacts in the U.S. up to $300,000 to murder Bolton, according to court papers unsealed Wednesday . The Justice Department says the plot was likely in retaliation for the U.S. killing of top Iranian commander Qassem Soleimani in January 2020. Bolton, an Iran-hawk who served as former President Donald Trump's national security adviser from 2018 to 2019, thanked the Justice Department and FBI for uncovering and foiling the alleged plot. "While much cannot be said publicly right now, one point is indisputable: Iran's rulers are liars, terrorists, and enemies of the United States," he said. "Their radical anti-American objectives are unchanged; the commitments are worthless; and their global threat is growing." Poursafi, who is 45 and believed to be in Iran, was charged by criminal complaint with two counts: use of interstate commerce in the commission of murder for hire; and providing material support to a transnational murder plot. The court papers provide a wealth of details into Poursafi's alleged efforts to arrange the assassination from afar. In October 2021 he first contacted a person only identified as Individual A over social media and asked them to take photographs of Bolton for a book Poursafi was writing, according to prosecutors. That person put Poursafi in touch with a second individual, identified as a government confidential human source, or CHS, who could take the pictures. A few weeks later, Poursafi asked the CHS on an encrypted messaging app if they could hire someone for $200,000 to "eliminate someone." He then provided Bolton's name and made clear that he was the target. Court papers say that Poursafi and the CHS negotiated potential payments, and the price tag eventually rose to $300,000 to compensate the CHS as well as the person the CHS was hiring to carry out the murder. Poursafi allegedly instructed the CHS to open a cryptocurrency account for eventual payment, but he stressed that "his group" would only pay for completed work. Court papers say Poursafi then provided the CHS with Bolton's office address in Washington, D.C., including the name and contact details for someone in the office. In mid-November, the CHS told Poursafi that arrangements had been made with an individual who would carry out the murder. A few days later, the CHS traveled from Texas to Washington, went to Bolton's office, and sent Poursafi two photos of the building. Poursafi said the facility's parking garage would be a good place to carry out the hit. On Dec. 2, the CHS said the person hired to kill Bolton was at Bolton's home taking pictures. Poursafi appeared to be growing concerned that the plot might not come to fruition, and told the CHS that if one took too much time planning something, the window of opportunity could pass. "The CHS thanked Poursafi for his advice and said he/she had no experience in the spy world or any training in killing people," court papers said. By mid-January, the CHS told Poursafi that they'd acquired three vans as well as weapons, silencers and ammunition. But later that month said there was a problem and security concerns. Poursafi pushed for the CHS to "finish the job," and dangled more work in the future. The two sides stayed in touch through April, although no action was ultimately taken against Bolton. "The Justice Department has the solemn duty to defend our citizens from hostile governments who seek to hurt or kill them," said Assistant Attorney General Matthew G. Olsen, who leads the Justice Department's National Security Division. "This is not the first time we have uncovered Iranian plots to exact revenge against individuals on U.S. soil and we will work tirelessly to expose and disrupt every one of these efforts."

In an interview with Morning Edition ‘s Steve Inskeep, she said she wonders if it isn’t NATO allies falling short of expectations with the U.S. instead of the other way around.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Steve Inskeep: There has been this world order, particularly in Europe, ever since World War II. The U.S. leads its European allies when necessary against Russia. That was the form in the early years of the war in Ukraine. Do you believe President Trump has upended the world order or switched sides?

Victoria Coates: No, I don’t think so. What President Trump is doing is acknowledging that 80 years on the reason that some of the structures were put in place after World War II, which was actually largely to prevent another inter-Europe war, are no longer in place. A war between Germany and France is not our number one national security problem. He is looking at the world and saying, OK, there is a war in Europe, but this is the Ukraine-Russia war. It’s been going on for three years. There’s been no diplomacy to proceed to a conclusion of the war. We’ve had a lot of maximalist rhetoric. We’ve had a lot of sort of displays of support for Ukraine and declarations that Ukraine is a democracy and this is an existential threat to the West. But we’ve also had hundreds of thousands dead and a lot of destruction. He is trying to change that paradigm also.

Inskeep: You mentioned that a lot of the structures were put together to avoid an inter-European war. I think that’s correct. But NATO specifically was an alliance against the expansion of what was then the Soviet Union, what is now Russia, which does seem to literally be the problem right now. It’s not just a war between Ukraine and Russia. Russia invaded Ukraine.

Coates: Well, it is. We’ll be welcoming the prime minister, Prime Minister Keir Starmer to Washington this week. We’ve already had President Emmanuel Macron. We will have President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. So that hardly looks to me like a Washington that is rejecting Europe.

At the NATO summit last year here in Washington, the NATO countries collectively agreed on a series of war plans that we would execute in the event of an additional kinetic action by an enemy. And those war plans require NATO to be investing collectively at 3.5%, which is where the United States is. The UK announced this week with great fanfare they were going to try to get to 2.5%. That math just doesn’t add up. If three years into a war in Europe, you don’t have the major European economies getting to the level of defense expenditure they need to get to in order to sustain what NATO has agreed to, then I have to wonder if it’s not the United States that’s turning its back on NATO, it’s these other NATO members who aren’t investing.

Inskeep: I want to ask about the concessions that the United States has offered to Russia’s Vladimir Putin as the president tries to end this war. Michael McFaul, a critic of Trump and former U.S. ambassador there, notes that the U.S. has already publicly said that Ukraine has to give up territory to Russia, that Ukraine can’t join NATO, that the U.S. won’t send peacekeeping troops, that the U.S. will reduce the number of soldiers in Europe, and that Zelensky, the Ukrainian president, has to hold elections before there are peace negotiations and other concessions. And in McFaul’s view, the United States hasn’t demanded anything of Russia. Is that how you see it?

Coates: Not at all. I mean, I think what has been offered to Russia has largely been rhetorical. None of this has cost the president anything. I would add the United Nations General Assembly resolution to that list, because off the top of my head, I can’t think of anything more useless than one of those resolutions.
Inskeep: You think you think it doesn’t matter that this resolution with the wording that few people other than the United States agreed with passed . Go on.

Coates: Yeah, this has largely been rhetorical and what we’ve offered Ukraine, on the other hand, which will be signed at the White House on Friday, is a material economic deal that will invest the United States in Ukraine and Ukraine’s security. So I would see that as a much more serious offer than, you know, rhetoric.
Inskeep: Do you think that deal would commit the United States to defend Ukraine against Russia?
Coates: I think it gives the United States a vested interest in Ukraine, which is something we have not had before. So we will see what that results.

Editor’s note: Zelenskyy is expected to meet with Trump in Washington on Friday to sign an deal to provide critical raw materials used for items like electric vehicle batteries and cancer drugs. The deal could lead to some security guarantees for Ukraine from the U.S.

Known for interviews with presidents and Congressional leaders, Inskeep has a passion for stories of the less famous: Pennsylvania truck drivers, Kentucky coal miners, U.S.-Mexico border detainees, Yemeni refugees, California firefighters, American soldiers.

Since joining Morning Edition in 2004, Inskeep has hosted the program from New Orleans, Detroit, San Francisco, Cairo, and Beijing; investigated Iraqi police in Baghdad; and received a Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Award for "The Price of African Oil," on conflict in Nigeria. He has taken listeners on a 2,428-mile journey along the U.S.-Mexico border, and 2,700 miles across North Africa. He is a repeat visitor to Iran and has covered wars in Syria and Yemen.

Inskeep says Morning Edition works to "slow down the news," making sense of fast-moving events. A prime example came during the 2008 Presidential campaign, when Inskeep and NPR's Michele Norris conducted "The York Project," groundbreaking conversations about race, which received an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University Silver Baton for excellence.

Inskeep was hired by NPR in 1996. His first full-time assignment was the 1996 presidential primary in New Hampshire. He went on to cover the Pentagon, the Senate, and the 2000 presidential campaign of George W. Bush. After the Sept. 11 attacks, he covered the war in Afghanistan, turmoil in Pakistan, and the war in Iraq. In 2003, he received a National Headliner Award for investigating a military raid gone wrong in Afghanistan. He has twice been part of NPR News teams awarded the Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University Silver Baton for coverage of Iraq.

On days of bad news, Inskeep is inspired by the Langston Hughes book, Laughing to Keep From Crying . Of hosting Morning Edition during the 2008 financial crisis and Great Recession, he told Nuvo magazine when "the whole world seemed to be falling apart, it was especially important for me ... to be amused, even if I had to be cynically amused, about the things that were going wrong. Laughter is a sign that you're not defeated."

Inskeep is the author of Instant City: Life and Death in Karachi , a 2011 book on one of the world's great megacities. He is also author of Jacksonland , a history of President Andrew Jackson's long-running conflict with John Ross, a Cherokee chief who resisted the removal of Indians from the eastern United States in the 1830s.

He has been a guest on numerous TV programs including ABC's This Week, NBC's Meet the Press, MSNBC's Andrea Mitchell Reports, CNN's Inside Politics and the PBS Newshour . He has written for publications including The New York Times , Washington Post , the Wall Street Journal , and The Atlantic .

extraction.body: The Justice Department has charged a suspected Iranian operative for allegedly plotting to assassinate former Trump national security adviser John Bolton. Shahram Poursafi offered to pay contacts in the U.S. up to $300,000 to murder Bolton, according to court papers unsealed Wednesday . The Justice Department says the plot was likely in retaliation for the U.S. killing of top Iranian commander Qassem Soleimani in January 2020. Bolton, an Iran-hawk who served as former President Donald Trump's national security adviser from 2018 to 2019, thanked the Justice Department and FBI for uncovering and foiling the alleged plot. "While much cannot be said publicly right now, one point is indisputable: Iran's rulers are liars, terrorists, and enemies of the United States," he said. "Their radical anti-American objectives are unchanged; the commitments are worthless; and their global threat is growing." Poursafi, who is 45 and believed to be in Iran, was charged by criminal complaint with two counts: use of interstate commerce in the commission of murder for hire; and providing material support to a transnational murder plot. The court papers provide a wealth of details into Poursafi's alleged efforts to arrange the assassination from afar. In October 2021 he first contacted a person only identified as Individual A over social media and asked them to take photographs of Bolton for a book Poursafi was writing, according to prosecutors. That person put Poursafi in touch with a second individual, identified as a government confidential human source, or CHS, who could take the pictures. A few weeks later, Poursafi asked the CHS on an encrypted messaging app if they could hire someone for $200,000 to "eliminate someone." He then provided Bolton's name and made clear that he was the target. Court papers say that Poursafi and the CHS negotiated potential payments, and the price tag eventually rose to $300,000 to compensate the CHS as well as the person the CHS was hiring to carry out the murder. Poursafi allegedly instructed the CHS to open a cryptocurrency account for eventual payment, but he stressed that "his group" would only pay for completed work. Court papers say Poursafi then provided the CHS with Bolton's office address in Washington, D.C., including the name and contact details for someone in the office. In mid-November, the CHS told Poursafi that arrangements had been made with an individual who would carry out the murder. A few days later, the CHS traveled from Texas to Washington, went to Bolton's office, and sent Poursafi two photos of the building. Poursafi said the facility's parking garage would be a good place to carry out the hit. On Dec. 2, the CHS said the person hired to kill Bolton was at Bolton's home taking pictures. Poursafi appeared to be growing concerned that the plot might not come to fruition, and told the CHS that if one took too much time planning something, the window of opportunity could pass. "The CHS thanked Poursafi for his advice and said he/she had no experience in the spy world or any training in killing people," court papers said. By mid-January, the CHS told Poursafi that they'd acquired three vans as well as weapons, silencers and ammunition. But later that month said there was a problem and security concerns. Poursafi pushed for the CHS to "finish the job," and dangled more work in the future. The two sides stayed in touch through April, although no action was ultimately taken against Bolton. "The Justice Department has the solemn duty to defend our citizens from hostile governments who seek to hurt or kill them," said Assistant Attorney General Matthew G. Olsen, who leads the Justice Department's National Security Division. "This is not the first time we have uncovered Iranian plots to exact revenge against individuals on U.S. soil and we will work tirelessly to expose and disrupt every one of these efforts."

The findings aren’t necessarily groundbreaking, but they’re aimed at communicating the rapidly evolving threat landscape in space to the general public: That was then… The DIA says that US adversaries paid attention to 30+ years of space-supported US military operations (take the Gulf War, and precision-guided munitions, as one example). And this is now… Adversaries “are now seeking ways to expand their own capabilities and deny the US a space-enabled advantage.” The report opens by noting that China and Russia grew their combined operational space fleets by 70% in just over two years (after 200+% growth from 2015 to 2018). The two major spacefaring nations are simultaneously upgrading their space and counterspace capabilities. A continuum of counterspace capabilities, via the DIA: Competition to exploit resources on the Moon, Mars, and even asteroids, “while a nascent endeavor today,” could become a bigger driver for top spacefaring states and alliances in the future. extraction.body: TODD BREASSEALE: Hey, good afternoon, everyone. Today we're going to discuss the Defense Intelligence Agency's release of its latest, unclassified, foundational report, “Challenges to Security in Space 2022.” This is the second edition of DIA’s series of reports designed to inform the public on key challenges and foreign military threats in space. DIA’s foundational reports foster informed dialogues between America's leaders, the national security community, warfighters, academia, allies and partners about key national security challenges facing the United States. We're joined today by DIA’s foremost experts in the space field, Dr. John Huth, DIA’s Defense Intelligence Officer for Space and Counterspace, and Mr. Kevin Ryder DIA Senior Defense Intelligence Analyst for Space and Counterspace. Gentlemen, I'll hand it over to you. DEFENSE INTELLIGENCE OFFICER DR. JOHN F. HUTH: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss DIA’s report that we're releasing today, “Challenges to Security in Space 2022.” This is an unclassified report and it's a follow-on to the first “Challenges to Security in Space” DIA released in 2019. Like its predecessor, this report examines the space and counterspace programs that pose or potentially pose a significant challenge to U.S. or partner interests by China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran. The second iteration addresses increases in the pace and scope of competitive space operations since early 2019, which you're about to hear have been dramatic. DIA produces reports that provide both broad overviews of country military capabilities known as the Military Power Series, and more narrowly focused functional threat reports such as “Challenges to Security in Space” and “Global Nuclear Landscapes.” These are designed to help the public achieve a deeper understanding of key challenges and threats to U.S. national security. This new edition of “Challenges to Security in Space” provides an updated unclassified overview of current threats to U.S. space-based capabilities. Particularly from China and Russia, but also to a lesser extent, those emerging from North Korea and Iran. This edition examines the expansion of space operations and details Earth-focused space services, as well as growing efforts to explore the moon and beyond. And it also includes an expanded assessment of impacts of space debris. Space-based capabilities impact many day-to-day aspects of the American way of life. They enable functions that affect our homes, transportation, electric power grids, banking and communications. From watching television, to predicting weather patterns to avoiding traffic on our daily commutes, satellites enable many real-time conveniences that have become integral to our daily lives. On the national security front, space-based capabilities afford the United States and our allies with crucial ability to project combat power to areas of conflict and instability. They enable our armed forces to collect vital intelligence on foreign threats, navigate and maneuver rapidly, and communicate with one another to support global military and humanitarian crises. Meanwhile, Russia and China, our primary strategic competitors, are taking steps to undercut the United States and our allies in the space domain. Both nations view space as a requirement for winning modern wars, especially against Western nations, and look to prove themselves as world leaders. Since early 2019, competitor space operations have increased in pace and scope across nearly all major categories — communications, remote sensing, navigation, and science and technology demonstration. SENIOR DEFENSE ANALYST KEVIN RYDER: And China and Russia value superiority in space. And as a result, they'll seek ways to strengthen their space and counter-space programs and determine better ways to integrate them within their respective militaries. Both nations seek to broaden their space exploration initiatives together and individually with plans to explore the moon and Mars during the next 30 years. And if successful, these efforts will likely lead to attempts by Beijing and Moscow to exploit the moon's natural resources. Beijing and Moscow have integrated space-based capabilities into their individual, national and warfighting strategies with the intent of denying the United States a space-enabled advantage. Evidence of both nations’ intent to undercut the United States and allied leadership in the space domain can be seen in the growth of combined in-orbit assets of China and Russia, which grew approximately 70% in just two years. This recent and continuing expansion follows a more than 200% increase between 2015 and 2018. China has launched a robotic lander and rover to the far side of the moon, and an orbiter lander and rover in one mission to Mars. It has also launched multiple missiles, capable of destroying satellites, and deployed mobile jammers to deny satellite communications and GPS. Moscow on the other hand, has developed a suite of counter-space weapons capabilities, including electronic warfare, to deny, degrade, and disrupt communications, and to not - to deny the use of space-based imagery. Russia is also developing a mobile missile that is able to destroy satellites and crewed space vehicles. Now as the number of spacefaring nations grow, and counter-space capabilities become more integrated into military operations, the U.S. Space Posture will be increasingly challenged and orbit assets will face new risk. A secure, stable, and accessible space domain is crucial as challenges to the United States and our allies’ space capabilities continue to increase. “Challenges to Security in Space — 2022” offs the insights from top intelligence experts on current threats to the United States Space Posture posed by our strategic competitors, and key space issues through 2030 and beyond. Thank you for your time, we will now take questions. MR. BREASSEALE: So, if you have a question for these gentlemen, please just raise your hand and I'll call on you. passages: TODD BREASSEALE: Hey, good afternoon, everyone. Today we're going to discuss the Defense Intelligence Agency's release of its latest, unclassified, foundational report, “Challenges to Security in Space 2022.”

This is the second edition of DIA’s series of reports designed to inform the public on key challenges and foreign military threats in space. DIA’s foundational reports foster informed dialogues between America's leaders, the national security community, warfighters, academia, allies and partners about key national security challenges facing the United States.

We're joined today by DIA’s foremost experts in the space field, Dr. John Huth, DIA’s Defense Intelligence Officer for Space and Counterspace, and Mr. Kevin Ryder DIA Senior Defense Intelligence Analyst for Space and Counterspace. Gentlemen, I'll hand it over to you.

DEFENSE INTELLIGENCE OFFICER DR. JOHN F. HUTH: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss DIA’s report that we're releasing today, “Challenges to Security in Space 2022.” This is an unclassified report and it's a follow-on to the first “Challenges to Security in Space” DIA released in 2019. The second iteration addresses increases in the pace and scope of competitive space operations since early 2019, which you're about to hear have been dramatic. DIA produces reports that provide both broad overviews of country military capabilities known as the Military Power Series, and more narrowly focused functional threat reports such as “Challenges to Security in Space” and “Global Nuclear Landscapes.”

These are designed to help the public achieve a deeper understanding of key challenges and threats to U.S. national security. This new edition of “Challenges to Security in Space” provides an updated unclassified overview of current threats to U.S. space-based capabilities. Particularly from China and Russia, but also to a lesser extent, those emerging from North Korea and Iran. This edition examines the expansion of space operations and details Earth-focused space services, as well as growing efforts to explore the moon and beyond. And it also includes an expanded assessment of impacts of space debris.

From watching television, to predicting weather patterns to avoiding traffic on our daily commutes, satellites enable many real-time conveniences that have become integral to our daily lives. On the national security front, space-based capabilities afford the United States and our allies with crucial ability to project combat power to areas of conflict and instability. They enable our armed forces to collect vital intelligence on foreign threats, navigate and maneuver rapidly, and communicate with one another to support global military and humanitarian crises.

Meanwhile, Russia and China, our primary strategic competitors, are taking steps to undercut the United States and our allies in the space domain. Both nations view space as a requirement for winning modern wars, especially against Western nations, and look to prove themselves as world leaders.

Since early 2019, competitor space operations have increased in pace and scope across nearly all major categories — communications, remote sensing, navigation, and science and technology demonstration.

SENIOR DEFENSE ANALYST KEVIN RYDER: And China and Russia value superiority in space. Moscow on the other hand, has developed a suite of counter-space weapons capabilities, including electronic warfare, to deny, degrade, and disrupt communications, and to not - to deny the use of space-based imagery.
