extraction.body: TODD BREASSEALE: Hey, good afternoon, everyone. Today we're going to discuss the Defense Intelligence Agency's release of its latest, unclassified, foundational report, “Challenges to Security in Space 2022.” This is the second edition of DIA’s series of reports designed to inform the public on key challenges and foreign military threats in space. DIA’s foundational reports foster informed dialogues between America's leaders, the national security community, warfighters, academia, allies and partners about key national security challenges facing the United States. We're joined today by DIA’s foremost experts in the space field, Dr. John Huth, DIA’s Defense Intelligence Officer for Space and Counterspace, and Mr. Kevin Ryder DIA Senior Defense Intelligence Analyst for Space and Counterspace. Gentlemen, I'll hand it over to you. DEFENSE INTELLIGENCE OFFICER DR. JOHN F. HUTH: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss DIA’s report that we're releasing today, “Challenges to Security in Space 2022.” This is an unclassified report and it's a follow-on to the first “Challenges to Security in Space” DIA released in 2019. Like its predecessor, this report examines the space and counterspace programs that pose or potentially pose a significant challenge to U.S. or partner interests by China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran. The second iteration addresses increases in the pace and scope of competitive space operations since early 2019, which you're about to hear have been dramatic. DIA produces reports that provide both broad overviews of country military capabilities known as the Military Power Series, and more narrowly focused functional threat reports such as “Challenges to Security in Space” and “Global Nuclear Landscapes.” These are designed to help the public achieve a deeper understanding of key challenges and threats to U.S. national security. This new edition of “Challenges to Security in Space” provides an updated unclassified overview of current threats to U.S. space-based capabilities. Particularly from China and Russia, but also to a lesser extent, those emerging from North Korea and Iran. This edition examines the expansion of space operations and details Earth-focused space services, as well as growing efforts to explore the moon and beyond. And it also includes an expanded assessment of impacts of space debris. Space-based capabilities impact many day-to-day aspects of the American way of life. They enable functions that affect our homes, transportation, electric power grids, banking and communications. From watching television, to predicting weather patterns to avoiding traffic on our daily commutes, satellites enable many real-time conveniences that have become integral to our daily lives. On the national security front, space-based capabilities afford the United States and our allies with crucial ability to project combat power to areas of conflict and instability. They enable our armed forces to collect vital intelligence on foreign threats, navigate and maneuver rapidly, and communicate with one another to support global military and humanitarian crises. Meanwhile, Russia and China, our primary strategic competitors, are taking steps to undercut the United States and our allies in the space domain. Both nations view space as a requirement for winning modern wars, especially against Western nations, and look to prove themselves as world leaders. Since early 2019, competitor space operations have increased in pace and scope across nearly all major categories — communications, remote sensing, navigation, and science and technology demonstration. SENIOR DEFENSE ANALYST KEVIN RYDER: And China and Russia value superiority in space. And as a result, they'll seek ways to strengthen their space and counter-space programs and determine better ways to integrate them within their respective militaries. Both nations seek to broaden their space exploration initiatives together and individually with plans to explore the moon and Mars during the next 30 years. And if successful, these efforts will likely lead to attempts by Beijing and Moscow to exploit the moon's natural resources. Beijing and Moscow have integrated space-based capabilities into their individual, national and warfighting strategies with the intent of denying the United States a space-enabled advantage. Evidence of both nations’ intent to undercut the United States and allied leadership in the space domain can be seen in the growth of combined in-orbit assets of China and Russia, which grew approximately 70% in just two years. This recent and continuing expansion follows a more than 200% increase between 2015 and 2018. China has launched a robotic lander and rover to the far side of the moon, and an orbiter lander and rover in one mission to Mars. It has also launched multiple missiles, capable of destroying satellites, and deployed mobile jammers to deny satellite communications and GPS. Moscow on the other hand, has developed a suite of counter-space weapons capabilities, including electronic warfare, to deny, degrade, and disrupt communications, and to not - to deny the use of space-based imagery. Russia is also developing a mobile missile that is able to destroy satellites and crewed space vehicles. Now as the number of spacefaring nations grow, and counter-space capabilities become more integrated into military operations, the U.S. Space Posture will be increasingly challenged and orbit assets will face new risk. A secure, stable, and accessible space domain is crucial as challenges to the United States and our allies’ space capabilities continue to increase. “Challenges to Security in Space — 2022” offs the insights from top intelligence experts on current threats to the United States Space Posture posed by our strategic competitors, and key space issues through 2030 and beyond. Thank you for your time, we will now take questions. MR. BREASSEALE: So, if you have a question for these gentlemen, please just raise your hand and I'll call on you. And you can please state your name and outlet for which you're reporting. I saw your hand first. Yes, ma'am. Q: Hi, Tara Copp with Defense One. I was wondering if you could both talk about the extent to which China has been watching Russia's invasion of Ukraine and how it's shaping what counter-space capabilities it's pursuing? And what sort of - is it gathering lessons learned? Will it make it more difficult in future conflicts based on what we've seen happen over Ukraine? DR. HUTH: So, as far as the scope of the document really doesn't cover that, that's fairly new, and I’ll say, evolving information. So, really don't have a whole lot to – to add on that right now. MR. RYDER: So, I will say that, from a DIA perspective, what we do is we provide information on the threats and the challenges that are posed by our adversaries. And we provide that to our policymakers and our warfighting planners to make those determinations on the type of systems and mitigation strategies that are needed. DR. HUTH: And certainly, the acquisition community, the NRO [National Reconnaissance Office], SDA – Space Development Agency, et cetera. But as Kevin said, that's really for us to inform them. It's for them to figure out, based on that threat information, what they want to do. MR. BREASSEALE: Let’s take a caller, Theresa Hitchens, from Breaking Defense. MR. BREASSEALE: I want to go to the phones real quickly. Bill Gertz, Washington Times. Q: Yes. Hi. I want to follow up on Tony's question on the fractional orbital launch. Can you say whether this is a nuclear system, or it's a conventional system? And it is reported in the report as part of space weapons that are used to hit targets on the earth, on the sea and in the air. Can you elaborate a little bit more on that? MR. RYDER: Could you repeat the question? I'm sorry. And I know, Ukraine happened after this is published, but to the extent that that is occurring on the current battlefield, what sort of guidance are you providing, or helping shape future U.S. defenses for future potential conflict? DR. HUTH: So again, I'd say the report, and the information from an intelligence perspective stands as it is. So those types of things are what we provide to our customers, for them to consider as they are acquiring new capabilities with the understanding that both China and Russia are expanding their kit, if you will, in counter-space capabilities. And those are all factored into design of U.S. systems. MR. BREASSEALE: Let's go to the phones again. Poonam Sharma from Global Straits. MR. RYDER: So, from my perspective, all of the capabilities are equal in nature. It depends on how and why and when the adversary would tend to use them or choose to use them. DR. HUTH: And if I could just reemphasize my last point and pile on what Kevin said. So, it's not just a capability, it's the fact that they have a space force or each have space forces, China and Russia. And their intent is to make space part of that combined arms effort in any conflict. Q: Can I follow up on that a little bit, on John's question? Which capability are they the most advanced in, that's the most alarming to you? Q: Thank you so much. Just a couple of short questions. Does DIA also produce a classified version of this report or just the unclassified? And the second part of the question, in your discussion on China's capabilities, do you consider all Chinese space capabilities military? Or do you make a distinction between civilian space and military space? Thank you. MR. RYDER: So, for your first question, while DIA does publish a number of classified documents, “Challenges to Security in Space” is only produced in an unclassified format. DR. HUTH: I think with regard to your second question, Kevin, and I think I, had already both talked about what the Chinese refer to as civil-military fusion. So sometimes, things can look very distinct as to whether they lay on one side or another, at least for the time being. And that can change because of that, and there's a lot of gray area in there. They - they don't conduct business the way - certainly the way the U.S. or other Western countries do. Q: Hi, I'm Luis Martinez with ABC News. I have two questions. One, how does - in terms of the counter-space activities we're seeing from Russia and China, how does this report compare with what the conclusions from the 2019 report? You know, broad strokes, what's the main difference between those two? MR. RYDER: Well, as you said, 2022 builds on our 2019 report. It expands a little bit more on some of the future developments. It also takes a harder look at space debris and the causes - the potential impact of that in space. And it also looks at development to get out - exploration out beyond the moon. DR. HUTH: And I think we go a little bit deeper on space domain awareness and command and control as well in the new report.

extraction.body: The PHP development team released updated Windows builds on October 26 to fix CVE-2026-111497 , an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Brotli’s decompression code. The flaw can cause memory corruption and potentially allow an attacker to execute code when an application processes malicious compressed data. According to PHP’s official announcement , the affected decoder can be reached through PHP’s cURL extension when automatic HTTP response decompression is enabled. Although cURL disables that functionality by default, applications and HTTP client libraries can activate it. The rebuilt packages incorporate Brotli 1.2.1. The release highlights a practical challenge for security teams: updating a programming language does not necessarily resolve vulnerabilities in every component distributed with it. A separate dependency update can require another deployment even when the language’s own version number has not changed. PHP published the following replacement builds: The -1 suffix identifies a Windows package rebuild with refreshed dependencies. The PHP source release and runtime version remain unchanged. Updated packages are available through the official PHP downloads page . Consequently, administrators need to verify the installed package rather than rely solely on the PHP version reported by an application or inventory tool. A check that only recognises the underlying runtime release may fail to distinguish the original distribution from its replacement. Brotli is a compression technology used to reduce the size of data transferred over the web. The security issue arises during decompression, when a receiving application converts compressed content back into its original form. The Node.js security advisory describes the underlying decoder failure: an invalid block transition can be treated as a temporary shortage of input instead of a permanent formatting error. Processing then continues, allowing data to be written beyond an internal buffer. Depending on the affected application and execution environment, the resulting memory corruption can cause a crash, expose process memory or enable remote code execution. The advisory credits OpenAI Codex Security researchers Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer with reporting the vulnerability. For PHP, the documented exposure involves the application acting as an HTTP client. It contacts another server, receives a compressed response and passes that response to a vulnerable decoder. The potential impact extends beyond a theoretical decoder crash. In research published by Imperva , Ron Masas described a working proof of concept against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image. The researchers demonstrated execution of code supplied through Brotli-compressed data, while the fixed Node.js 24.22.1 release rejected the same input. Their testing covered both responses consumed through Node.js’s built-in fetch() function and incoming request bodies processed by configured middleware. Exploitation required multiple attempts in the tested environment. PHP’s October 26 announcement does not report active attacks against its Windows builds. The appropriate distinction is between a confirmed vulnerable component, demonstrated exploitation in a particular runtime, and evidence of attacks against deployed PHP systems. Google’s Brotli release history lists security fixes in versions 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10 , released on October 21. The release notes identify CVE-2026-111497 as an out-of-bounds write capable of permitting remote code execution. Other projects have also issued updates or advisories for the same dependency. Microsoft published an out-of-band .NET security update on October 25. Its associated advisory says exposure depends on applications enabling Brotli decompression or explicitly using decompression APIs on attacker-controlled input. Microsoft states that .NET Framework is unaffected. The Envoy project’s advisory similarly identifies deployments with the Brotli decompressor configured as the relevant exposure. Operationally, an operating-system package update should not be assumed to replace a component embedded inside a separate runtime or vendor-distributed application. Each supplier’s remediation guidance needs to be checked against the software actually deployed. The Windows rebuilds arrive five days after the October 21 security releases addressing CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , the vulnerabilities collectively known as PHP2Shell. The UK National Cyber Security Centre’s alert describes those earlier issues as flaws involving out-of-memory handling and stale internal request state. Under certain conditions, they can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. The NCSC urged organisations to identify PHP installations across their infrastructure, prioritise exposed systems and monitor updates from suppliers whose products bundle PHP. It also illustrates the limitations of broad patch-status labels. A system marked “PHP updated” after an earlier deployment may still require further attention when a bundled library receives a fix. For organisations using the official Windows packages, the immediate priority is to deploy the replacement build appropriate to their PHP branch and verify the package’s identity. A practical rollout should also include checking application compatibility, restarting affected processes so they load the updated components, and confirming that background workers, scheduled jobs and secondary installations use the intended runtime. The emergency security releases for PHP (addressing critical flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) have triggered a massive scramble across global IT and web infrastructure. Affecting PHP installations across Windows and Unix environments alike, these high-severity vulnerabilities highlight the delicate balance underlying the web applications powering a significant portion of the internet. 🔄📊⚡ This is a good example of why “patched” and “remediated” are not the same thing. What also stands out is how quickly this moved across the software supply chain. OpenAI publicly discussed the Brotli vulnerability on X after its Codex Security researchers identified the security impact, and within days multiple downstream projects were issuing or preparing updates. That matters operationally because one dependency can create several separate remediation paths. If the runtime version does not change, a version-only inventory check may still report the system as current while missing whether the rebuilt package with the corrected dependency was actually deployed. For me, the proof has to go deeper: Which exact build is installed? Which vulnerable component was replaced? Did every affected process reload it? Are secondary installations and background workers using the fixed package? And did validation confirm the vulnerable path is no longer reachable? Fixing PHP does not prove the same vulnerable Brotli library is gone from every other runtime or application that may bundle it. extraction.body: PHP has rebuilt its official Windows packages for PHP 8.2 through 8.5 to fix CVE-2026-111497 , a flaw in the Brotli compression library that the packages include. The flaw can let an attacker corrupt memory and potentially run code. PHP says the flaw can be reached through the cURL extension when the extension decompresses HTTP responses automatically. cURL leaves that off by default, but applications and HTTP client libraries can turn it on. The rebuilt packages, numbered 8.5.12-1 , 8.4.27-1 , 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1 , come five days after the October 21 releases that fixed the two PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws . They use the same PHP source, so those fixes stay in place, and they now include Brotli 1.2.1 , the fixed version. PHP publishes a software bill of materials , a list of the components inside, with each package. For last week's x64 Non Thread Safe builds of all four versions, those lists show Brotli 1.2.0, one of the affected versions. PHP advises Windows users to install the new builds from its downloads page . Because the PHP version itself is unchanged, php -v shows the same number before and after. The -1 in the file name, as in php-8.5.12-1-nts-Win32-vs17-x64.zip , and the SHA-256 hash listed on the downloads page identify the new build. Automatic decompression means cURL asks the server for a compressed response and unpacks it. In PHP code, the CURLOPT_ENCODING option turns it on, and an empty value accepts every format cURL supports. Guzzle, a PHP HTTP client library, sets that empty value by default for requests it sends through cURL, according to the code in its 7.16.1 release and in 8.3.1. Based on that code and PHP's own description, an application that keeps Guzzle's default settings meets the condition for reaching the flaw on last week's Windows builds. The Hacker News has not tested this on a Windows system. An attack would come as a crafted compressed response from a server that the PHP application contacts. Google rates the flaw 9.2 out of 10, or Critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Red Hat rates it 8.1 , or Important, on the CVSS 3.1 scale. Imperva researchers ran code through the flaw on one official Node.js build, and it took them several attempts. PHP's notice does not mention any attacks. CISA's assessment of October 23 recorded no exploitation, and the flaw was not in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of that day's update. Researchers at OpenAI found the flaw. Google fixed it in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10 when it was first disclosed on October 21 . Node.js, Bun and other software that ships its own copy of Brotli have also released fixes. PHP's notice offers no workaround for systems that cannot be updated yet. OpenAI advises turning off automatic Brotli decompression in HTTP clients until the update is installed, and warns that removing br, Brotli's name in the Accept-Encoding header, "alone does not stop a server from sending it." In PHP code, following that advice means not setting CURLOPT_ENCODING , because cURL does not decompress responses without it. In Guzzle, it means setting the decode_content request option to false , which stops all automatic decoding, so gzip responses also arrive compressed. extraction.body: The PHP development team released updated Windows builds on October 26 to fix CVE-2026-111497 , an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Brotli’s decompression code. The flaw can cause memory corruption and potentially allow an attacker to execute code when an application processes malicious compressed data. According to PHP’s official announcement , the affected decoder can be reached through PHP’s cURL extension when automatic HTTP response decompression is enabled. Although cURL disables that functionality by default, applications and HTTP client libraries can activate it. The rebuilt packages incorporate Brotli 1.2.1. The release highlights a practical challenge for security teams: updating a programming language does not necessarily resolve vulnerabilities in every component distributed with it. A separate dependency update can require another deployment even when the language’s own version number has not changed. PHP published the following replacement builds: The -1 suffix identifies a Windows package rebuild with refreshed dependencies. The PHP source release and runtime version remain unchanged. Updated packages are available through the official PHP downloads page . Consequently, administrators need to verify the installed package rather than rely solely on the PHP version reported by an application or inventory tool. A check that only recognises the underlying runtime release may fail to distinguish the original distribution from its replacement. Brotli is a compression technology used to reduce the size of data transferred over the web. The security issue arises during decompression, when a receiving application converts compressed content back into its original form. The Node.js security advisory describes the underlying decoder failure: an invalid block transition can be treated as a temporary shortage of input instead of a permanent formatting error. Processing then continues, allowing data to be written beyond an internal buffer. Depending on the affected application and execution environment, the resulting memory corruption can cause a crash, expose process memory or enable remote code execution. The advisory credits OpenAI Codex Security researchers Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer with reporting the vulnerability. For PHP, the documented exposure involves the application acting as an HTTP client. It contacts another server, receives a compressed response and passes that response to a vulnerable decoder. The potential impact extends beyond a theoretical decoder crash. In research published by Imperva , Ron Masas described a working proof of concept against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image. The researchers demonstrated execution of code supplied through Brotli-compressed data, while the fixed Node.js 24.22.1 release rejected the same input. Their testing covered both responses consumed through Node.js’s built-in fetch() function and incoming request bodies processed by configured middleware. Exploitation required multiple attempts in the tested environment. PHP’s October 26 announcement does not report active attacks against its Windows builds. The appropriate distinction is between a confirmed vulnerable component, demonstrated exploitation in a particular runtime, and evidence of attacks against deployed PHP systems. Google’s Brotli release history lists security fixes in versions 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10 , released on October 21. The release notes identify CVE-2026-111497 as an out-of-bounds write capable of permitting remote code execution. Other projects have also issued updates or advisories for the same dependency. Microsoft published an out-of-band .NET security update on October 25. Its associated advisory says exposure depends on applications enabling Brotli decompression or explicitly using decompression APIs on attacker-controlled input. Microsoft states that .NET Framework is unaffected. The Envoy project’s advisory similarly identifies deployments with the Brotli decompressor configured as the relevant exposure. Operationally, an operating-system package update should not be assumed to replace a component embedded inside a separate runtime or vendor-distributed application. Each supplier’s remediation guidance needs to be checked against the software actually deployed. The Windows rebuilds arrive five days after the October 21 security releases addressing CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , the vulnerabilities collectively known as PHP2Shell. The UK National Cyber Security Centre’s alert describes those earlier issues as flaws involving out-of-memory handling and stale internal request state. Under certain conditions, they can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. The NCSC urged organisations to identify PHP installations across their infrastructure, prioritise exposed systems and monitor updates from suppliers whose products bundle PHP. It also illustrates the limitations of broad patch-status labels. A system marked “PHP updated” after an earlier deployment may still require further attention when a bundled library receives a fix. For organisations using the official Windows packages, the immediate priority is to deploy the replacement build appropriate to their PHP branch and verify the package’s identity. A practical rollout should also include checking application compatibility, restarting affected processes so they load the updated components, and confirming that background workers, scheduled jobs and secondary installations use the intended runtime. The emergency security releases for PHP (addressing critical flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) have triggered a massive scramble across global IT and web infrastructure. Affecting PHP installations across Windows and Unix environments alike, these high-severity vulnerabilities highlight the delicate balance underlying the web applications powering a significant portion of the internet. 🔄📊⚡ This is a good example of why “patched” and “remediated” are not the same thing. What also stands out is how quickly this moved across the software supply chain. OpenAI publicly discussed the Brotli vulnerability on X after its Codex Security researchers identified the security impact, and within days multiple downstream projects were issuing or preparing updates. That matters operationally because one dependency can create several separate remediation paths. If the runtime version does not change, a version-only inventory check may still report the system as current while missing whether the rebuilt package with the corrected dependency was actually deployed. extraction.body: PHP has rebuilt its official Windows packages for PHP 8.2 through 8.5 to fix CVE-2026-111497 , a flaw in the Brotli compression library that the packages include. The flaw can let an attacker corrupt memory and potentially run code. PHP says the flaw can be reached through the cURL extension when the extension decompresses HTTP responses automatically. cURL leaves that off by default, but applications and HTTP client libraries can turn it on. The rebuilt packages, numbered 8.5.12-1 , 8.4.27-1 , 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1 , come five days after the October 21 releases that fixed the two PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws . They use the same PHP source, so those fixes stay in place, and they now include Brotli 1.2.1 , the fixed version. PHP publishes a software bill of materials , a list of the components inside, with each package. For last week's x64 Non Thread Safe builds of all four versions, those lists show Brotli 1.2.0, one of the affected versions. PHP advises Windows users to install the new builds from its downloads page . Because the PHP version itself is unchanged, php -v shows the same number before and after. The -1 in the file name, as in php-8.5.12-1-nts-Win32-vs17-x64.zip , and the SHA-256 hash listed on the downloads page identify the new build. Automatic decompression means cURL asks the server for a compressed response and unpacks it. In PHP code, the CURLOPT_ENCODING option turns it on, and an empty value accepts every format cURL supports. Guzzle, a PHP HTTP client library, sets that empty value by default for requests it sends through cURL, according to the code in its 7.16.1 release and in 8.3.1. Based on that code and PHP's own description, an application that keeps Guzzle's default settings meets the condition for reaching the flaw on last week's Windows builds. The Hacker News has not tested this on a Windows system. An attack would come as a crafted compressed response from a server that the PHP application contacts. Google rates the flaw 9.2 out of 10, or Critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Red Hat rates it 8.1 , or Important, on the CVSS 3.1 scale. Imperva researchers ran code through the flaw on one official Node.js build, and it took them several attempts. PHP's notice does not mention any attacks. CISA's assessment of October 23 recorded no exploitation, and the flaw was not in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of that day's update. Researchers at OpenAI found the flaw. Google fixed it in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10 when it was first disclosed on October 21 . Node.js, Bun and other software that ships its own copy of Brotli have also released fixes. PHP's notice offers no workaround for systems that cannot be updated yet. OpenAI advises turning off automatic Brotli decompression in HTTP clients until the update is installed, and warns that removing br, Brotli's name in the Accept-Encoding header, "alone does not stop a server from sending it." In PHP code, following that advice means not setting CURLOPT_ENCODING , because cURL does not decompress responses without it. In Guzzle, it means setting the decode_content request option to false , which stops all automatic decoding, so gzip responses also arrive compressed. extraction.body: This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: Tumors beneath the surface of the liver can be difficult to locate during laparoscopic, or keyhole, surgery. The new technology uses augmented reality to overlay a 3D visualization of the tumor and other anatomical structures on the surgeon's camera view. The visualization is updated as the camera changes position. "We have brought together the geometric tools needed to show where the tumor would be visible if the liver were semitransparent," says Torbjörn Lundh, professor at the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Gothenburg. "You can think of it as a GPS inside the organ. Instead of just having a map before surgery, we get continuous guidance based on the current camera angle," says Niclas Kvarnström, transplant surgeon and head of the Transplant Centre at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, and a researcher at Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg. In June 2026, the technology was used in surgery on a patient for the first time. "The system could be used as planned during the operation, and the workflow worked well. The patient was able to go home the following day," says Kvarnström. To use the technology, the surgeon places a special sticker on the surface of the liver. The sticker is approximately one square centimeter (0.16 square inches) in size and has a QR code. As long as the camera can see the marker, the system can show the tumor or other structures beneath the surface. "The sticker acts as an artificial landmark on the surface of the liver, which is otherwise as smooth and even as a polished floor. Put very simply, the marker, together with the camera's position and the X-ray image taken before surgery, helps us calculate where the tumor should appear. That information can then easily be overlaid on the camera view," says Lundh. Further liver operations are planned for fall 2026. In parallel, work continues on clinical validation, product development, quality management systems and the steps required to obtain regulatory approval. In the longer term, a larger international study is planned in collaboration with the Intervention Centre at Oslo University Hospital and hospitals in Washington. Although the first clinical application has been in liver surgery, the researchers also see potential in other areas. "Our next major step is to make the method more widely applicable to other laparoscopic procedures. This is a new project that we have just started together with Chalmers Next Labs," says Lundh. "This technology can be used in many routine procedures, for tumors in other organs or to keep track of a particular anatomical structure. We are starting with liver surgery, but in the longer term the technology could have much broader applications," says Kvarnström. The collaboration behind the technology began 10 years ago, when surgeons Kvarnström and Mårten Falkenberg contacted mathematicians Lundh and Klas Modin. "This is an excellent example of research rooted in a real need in the operating room. Together with our master's thesis students, Klas and I have used and developed the mathematics needed to see where the tumor is hidden," says Lundh. He emphasizes the importance of collaboration across professional boundaries. "We hope our collaboration shows that really good things can happen when doctors and mathematicians work together in interdisciplinary teams that focus on the problem rather than the scientific tools, and where team members have a high degree of trust in one another and curiosity about each other's work," says Lundh. extraction.body: A research collaboration in Gothenburg has developed technology that creates an interactive 3D image of an organ during surgery. This makes it easier, for example, to remove a tumor that would otherwise remain hidden beneath the organ's surface. With the new technology, the surgeon places a small sticker with a QR code on the organ being operated on. So far, the technology has only been tested on the liver. As long as the camera can track the marker, the surgeon can see tumors and other structures beneath the surface. "It is a bit like having GPS navigation inside the organ. Instead of simply having a map before surgery, we receive continuous guidance based on the current camera angle," says Niclas Kvarnström. He is a transplant surgeon and Head of the Transplant Center at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, and a researcher at Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg. Niclas Kvarnström, researcher, Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg The new technology links a three-dimensional image of the patient's anatomy to the surgical field and displays it in relation to the surgeon's camera view. Using augmented reality, tumors, blood vessels, and other anatomical structures hidden beneath the organ's surface can be made visible to the surgeon directly in the surgical field. The information is continuously updated as the camera changes position. "This means that computer-generated content is overlaid on the physical world. It is a bit like Pokémon GO, but with much greater precision." The technology was developed through a collaboration between Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Chalmers University of Technology, and the University of Gothenburg. Chalmers Ventures helped establish a company to develop the technology further. The collaboration dates back ten years, to when the Imaging and Intervention Centre at Sahlgrenska University Hospital had recently opened. Surgeons Niclas Kvarnström and Mårten Falkenberg were in contact with Chalmers researchers Torbjörn Lundh and Klas Modin, professors in the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Chalmers and the University of Gothenburg. The initial focus was on using diagnostic imaging in hybrid operating rooms and developing minimally invasive methods, including in liver and tumor surgery. The road to the first operation has been long, involving several years of technical development, preclinical studies, and testing of the system in different scenarios. The first operation on a human patient was performed in June of this year. "The system could be used as planned during the operation, and the workflow ran smoothly. The patient was able to go home the following day," says Niclas Kvarnström. Further operations are planned for the fall. In parallel, work continues on clinical validation, product development, quality management systems, and the regulatory pathway to market approval. In the longer term, a larger international study is planned. Although the first clinical application has been in liver surgery, Niclas Kvarnström sees potential in other areas too. "This technology can be used in many routine procedures, for tumors in other organs, or to track specific anatomical structures. We are starting with liver surgery, but in time the technology could have much broader applications," he says. Torbjörn Lundh considers this a good example of needs-driven research: "This was not something we came up with in isolation at Chalmers. It grew out of a real need in the operating room. Together with our thesis students, Klas and I have applied and developed the mathematics needed to visualize where the tumor is hidden." extraction.body: This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: Tumors beneath the surface of the liver can be difficult to locate during laparoscopic, or keyhole, surgery. The new technology uses augmented reality to overlay a 3D visualization of the tumor and other anatomical structures on the surgeon's camera view. The visualization is updated as the camera changes position. "We have brought together the geometric tools needed to show where the tumor would be visible if the liver were semitransparent," says Torbjörn Lundh, professor at the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Gothenburg. "You can think of it as a GPS inside the organ. Instead of just having a map before surgery, we get continuous guidance based on the current camera angle," says Niclas Kvarnström, transplant surgeon and head of the Transplant Centre at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, and a researcher at Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg. In June 2026, the technology was used in surgery on a patient for the first time. "The system could be used as planned during the operation, and the workflow worked well. The patient was able to go home the following day," says Kvarnström. To use the technology, the surgeon places a special sticker on the surface of the liver. The sticker is approximately one square centimeter (0.16 square inches) in size and has a QR code. As long as the camera can see the marker, the system can show the tumor or other structures beneath the surface. "The sticker acts as an artificial landmark on the surface of the liver, which is otherwise as smooth and even as a polished floor. Put very simply, the marker, together with the camera's position and the X-ray image taken before surgery, helps us calculate where the tumor should appear. That information can then easily be overlaid on the camera view," says Lundh. Further liver operations are planned for fall 2026. In parallel, work continues on clinical validation, product development, quality management systems and the steps required to obtain regulatory approval. In the longer term, a larger international study is planned in collaboration with the Intervention Centre at Oslo University Hospital and hospitals in Washington. Although the first clinical application has been in liver surgery, the researchers also see potential in other areas. "Our next major step is to make the method more widely applicable to other laparoscopic procedures. This is a new project that we have just started together with Chalmers Next Labs," says Lundh. "This technology can be used in many routine procedures, for tumors in other organs or to keep track of a particular anatomical structure. We are starting with liver surgery, but in the longer term the technology could have much broader applications," says Kvarnström. The collaboration behind the technology began 10 years ago, when surgeons Kvarnström and Mårten Falkenberg contacted mathematicians Lundh and Klas Modin. "This is an excellent example of research rooted in a real need in the operating room. Together with our master's thesis students, Klas and I have used and developed the mathematics needed to see where the tumor is hidden," says Lundh. He emphasizes the importance of collaboration across professional boundaries. "We hope our collaboration shows that really good things can happen when doctors and mathematicians work together in interdisciplinary teams that focus on the problem rather than the scientific tools, and where team members have a high degree of trust in one another and curiosity about each other's work," says Lundh. extraction.body: A research collaboration in Gothenburg has developed technology that creates an interactive 3D image of an organ during surgery. This makes it easier, for example, to remove a tumor that would otherwise remain hidden beneath the organ's surface. With the new technology, the surgeon places a small sticker with a QR code on the organ being operated on. So far, the technology has only been tested on the liver. As long as the camera can track the marker, the surgeon can see tumors and other structures beneath the surface. "It is a bit like having GPS navigation inside the organ. Instead of simply having a map before surgery, we receive continuous guidance based on the current camera angle," says Niclas Kvarnström. He is a transplant surgeon and Head of the Transplant Center at Sahlgrenska University Hospital, and a researcher at Sahlgrenska Academy at the University of Gothenburg. Niclas Kvarnström, researcher, Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg The new technology links a three-dimensional image of the patient's anatomy to the surgical field and displays it in relation to the surgeon's camera view. Using augmented reality, tumors, blood vessels, and other anatomical structures hidden beneath the organ's surface can be made visible to the surgeon directly in the surgical field. The information is continuously updated as the camera changes position. "This means that computer-generated content is overlaid on the physical world. It is a bit like Pokémon GO, but with much greater precision." The technology was developed through a collaboration between Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Chalmers University of Technology, and the University of Gothenburg. Chalmers Ventures helped establish a company to develop the technology further. The collaboration dates back ten years, to when the Imaging and Intervention Centre at Sahlgrenska University Hospital had recently opened. Surgeons Niclas Kvarnström and Mårten Falkenberg were in contact with Chalmers researchers Torbjörn Lundh and Klas Modin, professors in the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Chalmers and the University of Gothenburg. The initial focus was on using diagnostic imaging in hybrid operating rooms and developing minimally invasive methods, including in liver and tumor surgery. The road to the first operation has been long, involving several years of technical development, preclinical studies, and testing of the system in different scenarios. The first operation on a human patient was performed in June of this year. "The system could be used as planned during the operation, and the workflow ran smoothly. The patient was able to go home the following day," says Niclas Kvarnström. Further operations are planned for the fall. In parallel, work continues on clinical validation, product development, quality management systems, and the regulatory pathway to market approval. In the longer term, a larger international study is planned. Although the first clinical application has been in liver surgery, Niclas Kvarnström sees potential in other areas too. "This technology can be used in many routine procedures, for tumors in other organs, or to track specific anatomical structures. We are starting with liver surgery, but in time the technology could have much broader applications," he says. Torbjörn Lundh considers this a good example of needs-driven research: "This was not something we came up with in isolation at Chalmers. It grew out of a real need in the operating room. Together with our thesis students, Klas and I have applied and developed the mathematics needed to visualize where the tumor is hidden." WASHINGTON—October 26, 2026— The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) today released the Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: ONC Deregulatory Actions to Unleash Prosperity (HTI-5) Final Rule. This final rule aligns with President Trump’s Executive Order (EO) 14192, Unleashing Prosperity through Deregulation , and EO 14267, Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers , and is projected to save more than $1.5 billion in regulatory costs. The HTI-5 Final Rule significantly reduces administrative burdens for health IT developers participating in the ONC Health IT Certification Program (Certification Program). These deregulatory changes free up resources for health IT developers that can now be applied toward enhancing user experiences for patients and clinicians. “American doctors and patients need better technology, not more Washington paperwork,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “The Trump Administration is eliminating unnecessary regulations that cost more than $1.5 billion and hold back innovation. We are freeing America’s health technology innovators to build better tools, lower costs, and help doctors spend more time caring for patients.” As outlined in the 2026 Unified Agenda of Federal Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions, ONC intends to continue to address chronic disease, increase market competition, and lower healthcare costs by improving the access, exchange, and use of electronic health information (EHI). As such, the agency plans to put forth proposals in the future to advance interoperability and EHI sharing through standards adoption; additional updates to the Certification Program to support expanded uses of application programming interfaces (APIs) and potential successor technologies; and targeted conditions of certification. “Through HTI-5, we have taken decisive action to significantly lower the administrative compliance burden for developers so that they can spend more of their time developing solutions that improve interoperability, automation, and better healthcare for Americans,” said Tom Keane, M.D., National Coordinator for Health IT. Comments submitted in response to the HTI-5 Proposed Rule’s information blocking proposals remain under consideration as part of HHS’ ongoing efforts to address and eliminate information blocking. More information about the final rule can be found at healthit.gov/hti5 , on LinkedIn , or by following @ONC_HealthIT on X. passages: If you had invested $1,000 in Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH), XRP (CRYPTO:XRP), or Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) five years ago, you bought in close to the peak of a major market rally.
Bitcoin closed October 2021 at $61,340 and hit a high of $68,770 in November 2021, shortly before the market began to decline.
As a result, investors bought all four cryptocurrencies near their highs.
Bitcoin emerged as the top performer, yielding a 36.6% gain over five years, while XRP followed closely with a 29.5% increase.
In contrast, Ethereum and Solana are still trading significantly below their prices from October 2021.
To break even, Ethereum would need to surpass $3,954, an increase of about 70%, and Solana would need to rise above $185, about 83% higher.
On the other hand, Ethereum fell 41.1%, reducing $1,000 to about $589, while Solana fell 45.1%, leaving about $549.
Even Ethereum and XRP investors faced significant losses after experiencing gains.
Unfortunately, both coins saw declines of 51.0% for XRP and 44.0% for Ethereum in the following year.
Over the past 90 days, all four coins have recovered some ground, with Bitcoin up 25.6% and Solana up 37.6%.
However, they are all still significantly down compared to a year ago.
Bitcoin may maintain its leading position as it has gained the most of these coins since 2021.
If Bitcoin stays above $79,107 (its low in October 2026), the initial $1,000 investment keeps showing a solid profit.
However, if it falls below $58,681, that gain could disappear entirely.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Its lowest monthly price during this period was $348 in October 2022, a 24% dip—much less severe than Bitcoin's or Solana's drops.
It then surged to its all-time high in October 2025, making that stake worth around $2,150.
It plummeted to a low of $8.12 in December 2022, cutting the initial investment down to about $44, a staggering 95.6% loss.
However, it rebounded to $295 in January 2025, bringing that stake back up to about $1,597.
Of the four cryptocurrencies, two gained value while two lost almost half their value.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) tracks large U.S. companies and closed at $459 in October 2021.

facts.text: If you had invested $1,000 in Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH), XRP (CRYPTO:XRP), or Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) five years ago, you bought in close to the peak of a major market rally.
Bitcoin closed October 2021 at $61,340 and hit a high of $68,770 in November 2021, shortly before the market began to decline.
As a result, investors bought all four cryptocurrencies near their highs.
Bitcoin emerged as the top performer, yielding a 36.6% gain over five years, while XRP followed closely with a 29.5% increase.
In contrast, Ethereum and Solana are still trading significantly below their prices from October 2021.
To break even, Ethereum would need to surpass $3,954, an increase of about 70%, and Solana would need to rise above $185, about 83% higher.
On the other hand, Ethereum fell 41.1%, reducing $1,000 to about $589, while Solana fell 45.1%, leaving about $549.
Even Ethereum and XRP investors faced significant losses after experiencing gains.
Unfortunately, both coins saw declines of 51.0% for XRP and 44.0% for Ethereum in the following year.
Over the past 90 days, all four coins have recovered some ground, with Bitcoin up 25.6% and Solana up 37.6%.
However, they are all still significantly down compared to a year ago.
Bitcoin may maintain its leading position as it has gained the most of these coins since 2021.
If Bitcoin stays above $79,107 (its low in October 2026), the initial $1,000 investment keeps showing a solid profit.
However, if it falls below $58,681, that gain could disappear entirely.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Its lowest monthly price during this period was $348 in October 2022, a 24% dip—much less severe than Bitcoin's or Solana's drops.
It then surged to its all-time high in October 2025, making that stake worth around $2,150.
It plummeted to a low of $8.12 in December 2022, cutting the initial investment down to about $44, a staggering 95.6% loss.
However, it rebounded to $295 in January 2025, bringing that stake back up to about $1,597.

If you had invested $1,000 in Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ), or Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) five years ago, you bought in close to the peak of a major market rally. Bitcoin closed October 2021 at $61,340 and hit a high of $68,770 in November 2021, shortly before the market began to decline. As a result, investors bought all four cryptocurrencies near their highs.
Over the past 90 days, all four coins have recovered some ground, with Bitcoin up 25.6% and Solana up 37.6%. However, they are all still significantly down compared to a year ago.
We examined a $1,000 investment in each coin made on October 27, 2021, and evaluated their worth recently. Of the four cryptocurrencies, two gained value while two lost almost half their value.
Bitcoin turned a $1,000 investment into about $1,366, a 36.6% increase over five years. XRP closely followed with a value of approximately $1,295 after a 29.5% gain.
On the other hand, Ethereum fell 41.1%, reducing $1,000 to about $589, while Solana fell 45.1%, leaving about $549.

If you had split your $1,000 investment equally among the four coins, with $250 in each, your total would be about $950 based on today’s price. The two gainers absorbed most of the losses from the two decliners, but the overall investment still lost money over five years.

Bitcoin’s journey was turbulent. At its June 2022 monthly low, Bitcoin fell to $17,698, dropping the initial $1,000 investment to about $302, a 69.8% decline. It then surged to its all-time high in October 2025, making that stake worth around $2,150.

Solana had an even more dramatic ride. It plummeted to a low of $8.12 in December 2022, cutting the initial investment down to about $44, a staggering 95.6% loss. However, it rebounded to $295 in January 2025, bringing that stake back up to about $1,597.

Even Ethereum and XRP investors faced significant losses after experiencing gains. In late October 2025, XRP was priced at $2.65, and Ethereum hit $4,159, both above their prices from October 2021. Unfortunately, both coins saw declines of 51.0% for XRP and 44.0% for Ethereum in the following year.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) tracks large U.S. companies and closed at $459 in October 2021. By October 23, 2026, it climbed to $760. With dividends reinvested, a $1,000 investment would have grown to about $1,770, for a total return of 77.0%—better than any of the cryptocurrencies mentioned.
The ETF also had a smoother ride. Its lowest monthly price during this period was $348 in October 2022, a 24% dip—much less severe than Bitcoin’s or Solana’s drops.

A dollar-cost averaging strategy—investing a fixed amount regularly regardless of price—would have helped as well. If you had invested $200 in Bitcoin at the end of each October from 2021 through 2025, you would have paid $61,340, $20,504, $34,650, $70,347, and $109,555 per coin.

Overall, those five investments would be worth about $1,880 based on recent prices, outperforming the one-time investment of $1,366 made in October 2021. The 2022 purchase played a crucial role because it bought Bitcoin near its market low.

Bitcoin emerged as the top performer, yielding a 36.6% gain over five years, while XRP followed closely with a 29.5% increase. In contrast, Ethereum and Solana are still trading significantly below their prices from October 2021. To break even, Ethereum would need to surpass $3,954, an increase of about 70%, and Solana would need to rise above $185, about 83% higher.

Meanwhile, an S&P 500 index fund outperformed all four cryptocurrencies, and the strategy of investing in Bitcoin over five years yielded the best result of the group. Bitcoin may maintain its leading position as it has gained the most of these coins since 2021. If Bitcoin stays above $79,107 (its low in October 2026), the initial $1,000 investment keeps showing a solid profit. However, if it falls below $58,681, that gain could disappear entirely.

Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst and the editor of 24/7 Wall St.'s Crypto Desk, where he covers Bitcoin, XRP, Ethereum, Solana and the altcoins investors search for most. His work focuses on price levels, spot ETF flows, on-chain data and the regulatory decisions that move crypto markets, written so a first-time buyer and a seasoned trader can both use it. Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles. Before joining 24/7 Wall St., he wrote for crypto media outlets and Web3 companies and ghostwrote for crypto founders and token launches. His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites. He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives. When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.

We assessed this ranking against current prices to identify which levels are crucial for these cryptocurrencies.
Based on Grok AI's analysis, ETH is likely to hold up best in a market drop.
Grok assigns a 52% probability that ETH will recover first, followed by AVAX at 30% and SUI at 18%.
All three cryptocurrencies are already experiencing declines.

For SUI, its crucial line is $0.65, and it has the weakest one-year performance, down 65.6%.

Both Sui and Avalanche also face the challenge of recent gains that may be vulnerable to retracement.
ETH's larger market capitalization helps explain this ranking.

A smaller market cap generally means less selling pressure is needed to drive the price down.
Avalanche's gap is narrower, with a fully diluted valuation of about $4.2 billion.

passages: Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst and the editor of 24/7 Wall St.'s Crypto Desk, where he covers Bitcoin, XRP, Ethereum, Solana and the altcoins investors search for most.

Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.

sources.title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips as Musk warns of neocloud shakeout - Cryptopolitan
passages: According to Elon Musk, SpaceX has completed a deal for $40 billion in debt financing to purchase Nvidia graphics chips.
The transaction proves the strongest AI buyers can still raise money even though Musk warned that weaker companies are being increasingly denied access to the credit markets.
Musk confirmed the financing in a post on X on Sunday.
In a follow-up post, Musk described the money as mostly callable debt.
The chips the debt is set to pay for are due in the first and second quarters of 2027, and are not seen as a major point this quarter, according to Musk.
SpaceX ended September with $51.3 billion in cash and $38.6 billion in marketable securities, against a total debt figure of $38.8 billion, Yahoo Finance reported.
In the event that the full $40 billion is secured, total debt would roughly double to about $79 billion.

Last week, Musk also said a merger between Tesla and SpaceX would be “a good idea.” He added that both companies had formed independent committees to consider the deal but laid emphasis on the fact no decision had been made at the time.
Apollo Global Management was also expected to lead the financing.
SpaceX has raised large sums through debt before.
In June, the company raised $25 billion in its first bond sale, attracting nearly $90 billion in orders.
The proceeds from the bond sale were used to repay a bridge loan.
Musk said SpaceX’s investment-grade status and revenue from Starlink and rocket launches helped in securing the funding.
SpaceX’s third-quarter revenue rose 161% from a year earlier to $14.58 billion, according to Reuters.
CoreWeave and Nebius are examples of neoclouds that rent out Nvidia GPUs and rely on debt to expand.
SpaceX is spending far more than it brings in from its operations.
SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs, but we’re investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue.
The second half of Musk’s message carried a warning for the rest of the industry.
He stated that debt markets have “almost entirely shut off access to money” over the last few weeks, especially for any company lacking substantial revenue outside AI data centers.
“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote.
At that rate, the new loan would cover about a quarter of its spending.
Reuters reported that it was uncertain whether lenders had agreed to the deal.
Musk also did not name any banks or disclose interest rates or repayment dates.
Bloomberg later reported that the borrowing would be done via a separate entity, keeping it off SpaceX’s balance sheet and helping to protect the company’s credit rating.

SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk said his company closed on $40 billion in financing to pay for specialized chips used to power AI, but warned that access to debt is drying up for companies that solely rely on data center revenue. "As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," wrote Musk on X on Sunday. Musk went on to say that SpaceX ( SPCX ) closed $40 billion in debt for Nvidia's ( NVDA ) GPUS, or graphics processing units, used for AI, but highlighted that the space company is "investment-grade" and has Starlink & rocket launch revenue. In a follow-up post, Musk noted this "is primarily callable debt for GPU purchases that will arrive in Q1 and Q2. Not a major factor this quarter." Musk's comments reignited concerns about the rising cost of capital and the business models of so-called neoclouds, which rent computing power to train and run AI models. The debt disclosure comes on the heels of SpaceX's better-than-expected quarter. The company's AI segment brought in $7.6 billion in the third quarter, more than Starlink and the rocket business combined, and more than half of SpaceX's $14.6 billion in total revenue. Musk also took a shot at neoclouds, companies that rent out computing power and AI chips, saying they are "going to see guppy-level death and consolidation." "Some will make it through, but not many," said Musk. The comments following a viral chart earlier this month highlighted neocloud provider CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) spiking bond yields, underscoring concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet. Shares of CoreWeave recovered during Monday's session after opening in red territory. The stock has tumbled more than 30% over the past month. Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Read the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance

sources.title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt deal for AI chips as Musk warns of neocloud shakeout - Cryptopolitan
passages: According to Elon Musk, SpaceX has completed a deal for $40 billion in debt financing to purchase Nvidia graphics chips.
The transaction proves the strongest AI buyers can still raise money even though Musk warned that weaker companies are being increasingly denied access to the credit markets.
Musk confirmed the financing in a post on X on Sunday.
In a follow-up post, Musk described the money as mostly callable debt.
The chips the debt is set to pay for are due in the first and second quarters of 2027, and are not seen as a major point this quarter, according to Musk.
SpaceX ended September with $51.3 billion in cash and $38.6 billion in marketable securities, against a total debt figure of $38.8 billion, Yahoo Finance reported.
In the event that the full $40 billion is secured, total debt would roughly double to about $79 billion.

Last week, Musk also said a merger between Tesla and SpaceX would be “a good idea.” He added that both companies had formed independent committees to consider the deal but laid emphasis on the fact no decision had been made at the time.
Apollo Global Management was also expected to lead the financing.
SpaceX has raised large sums through debt before.
In June, the company raised $25 billion in its first bond sale, attracting nearly $90 billion in orders.
The proceeds from the bond sale were used to repay a bridge loan.
Musk said SpaceX’s investment-grade status and revenue from Starlink and rocket launches helped in securing the funding.
SpaceX’s third-quarter revenue rose 161% from a year earlier to $14.58 billion, according to Reuters.
CoreWeave and Nebius are examples of neoclouds that rent out Nvidia GPUs and rely on debt to expand.
SpaceX is spending far more than it brings in from its operations.
SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs, but we’re investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue.
The second half of Musk’s message carried a warning for the rest of the industry.
He stated that debt markets have “almost entirely shut off access to money” over the last few weeks, especially for any company lacking substantial revenue outside AI data centers.
“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote.
At that rate, the new loan would cover about a quarter of its spending.
Reuters reported that it was uncertain whether lenders had agreed to the deal.
Musk also did not name any banks or disclose interest rates or repayment dates.
Bloomberg later reported that the borrowing would be done via a separate entity, keeping it off SpaceX’s balance sheet and helping to protect the company’s credit rating.
